items.title: Deep Work Summary & Practical Guide: How to Do Real Work in a Distracted World (+ Free 1-Page Playbook)
items.summary: The Quick Take : Most of us spend eight hours a day answering emails, jumping on "quick calls," and juggling 25 browser tabs—only to hit 5:00 PM feeling exhausted with zero real progress. Here is our plain-English Deep Work summary , how to separate needle-moving work from everyday busywork, and a free 1-page printable Daily Playbook you can keep on your desk. 1. The 5:00 PM Question Nobody Likes Answering Have you ever worked hard from 9:00 AM to 5:00 PM—answering 60 emails, replying to dozens of team chat messages, sitting through four status meetings, and drinking three cups of coffee—only to look at your screen at the end of the day and think: "Wait... what did I actually finish today?" Figure 1.1: Why feeling super busy all day and actually moving your main project forward are two completely different things. You weren't slacking off. Your hands were moving on the keyboard all day. Yet the one big thing that actually mattered—the strategy proposal, the tricky software feature, the dense industry report you needed to digest—barely moved an inch. When computer science professor Cal Newport wrote his book Deep Work , he put a simple name to this exact trap. And once you see the difference between the two types of work competing for your day, you can never unsee it. 2. What Is Deep Work? (Deep Work vs. Shallow Work in Plain English) If you are looking for a quick Deep Work book summary , the entire philosophy comes down to one simple distinction: almost everything you do at your desk falls into one of two buckets. Figure 1.2: Shallow busywork keeps you running in place for 8 hours; 3 hours of Deep Work actually builds the bridge. Bucket 1: Shallow Work (Looking Busy) Shallow work is all the small, logistical busywork you can do while half-distracted: Replying to routine emails and "quick questions" in Slack or Teams. Sitting in status-update calls where five people listen to one person read a slide. Formatting spreadsheets, moving tickets around a board, or bouncing between 25 open browser tabs. Shallow work feels great in the moment because checking off tiny tasks gives your brain a quick burst of relief. The problem? You can spend 40 hours a week doing shallow work and have almost nothing lasting to show for it. Bucket 2: Deep Work (Moving the Needle) Deep work is when you close the door, silence every notification, and give 100% of your undivided attention to one hard, valuable task : Writing a clear strategy document, client proposal, or research brief. Building or debugging a complex piece of software architecture. Reading a dense 50-page report or learning a difficult new skill and actually connecting the dots in your head. Here is the secret most workplaces miss: three focused hours of Deep Work produce more real value than two full days of distracted multitasking. 3. items.title: Alter Zero: a Rust agent harness for coding, cybersecurity, and automation
items.summary: Debugging a failing test, tracing an access-control issue, and automating a repetitive shell workflow have something in common: they require more than a chat response. You need tools, context, and a way to check the result. Alter Zero is an open-source agent harness for coding, cybersecurity, and automation , written in Rust. That is also how the project describes itself in its Cargo.toml . It works in your terminal with tools for reading and editing files, running commands, managing long-running processes, and delegating focused work to subagents. You choose a supported model provider or connect a local model server. Here is what that looks like across the three workflows—and how to try it. See it in action Watch the video demo . 1. Coding: go from investigation to a verified change Alter Zero can inspect a repository, edit files, run build or test commands, and show the output as it happens. Syntax-highlighted file views, readable diffs, and task checklists help you follow the work instead of relying only on the final summary. A focused starting prompt: Find why this test fails. Trace the cause, make the smallest fix, and run the relevant tests. Explain what changed and what you verified. You can steer a running turn, queue a follow-up, and resume saved sessions later. Optional per-directory checkpoints support restoring working files when rewinding a conversation. The important distinction: the harness gives the model tools to investigate and verify. It does not make every proposed fix correct—review the diff and test results yourself. 2. Cybersecurity: investigate code and systems with evidence The same file and shell tools can support security reviews, technical investigations, and authorized testing. For example, ask the agent to trace authentication and authorization paths rather than simply list generic vulnerabilities: Review this repository's authentication and authorization flow. Trace each potential issue to specific code, distinguish confirmed findings from hypotheses, and suggest fixes and regression tests. Do not modify files yet. For a system you own or have permission to assess, another useful task is to summarize supplied service configurations or security logs and identify what needs manual verification. The repository also includes an optional headless Kali Rolling container for Docker or Podman. It packages Alter Zero with a selected set of CLI tools, including nmap , curl , jq , rg , and Python—not the entire Kali toolset. See the container guide for setup, networking, and workspace options. The container runs as root, and a mounted workspace exposes those files to edits. Treat it as a working environment, not a guarantee of isolation. Keep testing within an explicitly authorized scope. 3. Automation: work with the tools already in your shell Automation is not limited to generating scripts. Alter Zero can execute commands, inspect their output, and handle programs that pause for input. Its shell tools support interactive prompts, REPLs, and full-screen terminal programs. Long-running commands can be started in the background, inspected, waited on, sent input, or stopped. A practical first task: Write a script that summarizes these logs and flags recurring errors. Test it on a small sample, show the expected output, and do not alter or delete the original logs. For repeatable workflows, you can add reusable skills, lifecycle hooks, and project instructions. Hooks are off by default and can be enabled per working directory. MCP servers connect additional tools; what the agent can do through an integration depends on the server you configure. A harness you can extend Several capabilities tie these workflows together: Subagents: delegate focused work with separate context and tool access. The main agent can check progress, send follow-ups, stop an agent, and resume a finished agent's conversation. Skills: reusable SKILL.md folders loaded when needed. Built-in skills include web search, Jina Reader, skill creation, media-download guidance, and localhost-tunnel guidance. MCP: connect servers over stdio, HTTP, or SSE, with OAuth support for remote servers that use it. Hooks and AGENTS.md : add lifecycle automation and project-specific instructions. Session continuity: use /resume , alter-zero --continue , or alter-zero --resume to pick up earlier work. Skills are instructions and, in some cases, supporting scripts—not bundled versions of every external tool. For example, the yt-dlp skill uses the separately installed downloader, and flaredantic uses the external flare CLI. Loading the tunnel skill does not itself expose a service. Choose your model provider Supported providers include OpenRouter, Anthropic, GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT Codex, Venice, Cline/ClinePass, and Ollama, among others. Use /login to connect and /model to select a model. Sign-in methods and available capabilities vary by provider. You can add OpenAI-compatible services or local servers in ~/.alter-zero/providers.toml ; custom providers appear alongside the built-ins. The harness is open source. Hosted model access may require a subscription or API credits, and local inference quality and speed depend on your model and hardware. Permissions, secrets, and privacy: know the boundaries Alter Zero offers four permission modes: Mode General behavior manual Asks before file changes and commands edit Allows file changes; commands still require approval auto Adds a reviewer for routine commands master Runs unattended Start with manual , review proposed actions, and keep a clean Git working tree or backups. Project-defined agents, hooks, and MCP servers have a trust review through /trust . Permission controls are not an operating-system sandbox. The /secrets feature lets tools use stored credentials through placeholders, with expansion at execution and redaction in model-visible output. This reduces direct exposure to the model; it is not an encrypted vault or a promise that arbitrary commands cannot leak data. The secrets documentation explains storage and raw-log caveats. Telemetry is enabled by default. The documented ping contains an install ID, app version, and platform information—not prompts, code, or command history. You can disable it for a run with: ALTER_ZERO_TELEMETRY = 0 alter-zero DO_NOT_TRACK=1 is also supported. The separate GitHub update check has its own setting and is not disabled by DO_NOT_TRACK . Model-provider requests are separate from telemetry: using a hosted model still sends the context needed for inference to that provider. Read the telemetry policy before using sensitive workspaces. Try Alter Zero on Linux or macOS Install the native build through npm: npm install -g @linuztx/alter-zero cd your-project alter-zero Then: Run /login to connect a supported provider or local model server. Run /model to choose a model. Start with a focused task and review approval prompts. Without a configured provider, the app opens an offline demo with scripted turns so you can explore the interface. Prefer building from source? With rustup and a C compiler installed: git clone https://github.com/linuztx/alter-zero.git cd alter-zero cargo install --path . alter-zero The repository pins its Rust toolchain. See the quick-start guide for the shell installer and other options. What is new in v0.15.0? At the time of writing, GitHub's latest release is v0.15.0 . Its changelog includes: Custom OpenAI-compatible providers through providers.toml . Streaming file writes in the UI: see generated file content line by line while the model produces the tool call, rather than waiting for the whole call to finish. The flaredantic skill for guiding localhost sharing and webhook testing with an external CLI. macOS screenshot-paste fixes and removal of metadata from pasted images. This does not apply to images read directly from a file path. These are released features; changes under Unreleased are not included here. Explore the project Alter Zero is licensed under Apache-2.0 . Source, documentation, and issues → github.com/linuztx/alter-zero If an extensible terminal agent for coding, cybersecurity, and automation fits your workflow, give it a try. A GitHub star helps others discover the project , and a reproducible bug report or contribution helps improve it. Start with the contributing guide . Which workflow would you try first: fixing a failing test, reviewing access controls, or automating a repetitive CLI task? AI disclosure: This article was prepared and published with AI assistance, based on the project's Cargo metadata, README, changelog, and technical documentation. Prompts are suggested starting points, not benchmarks or claims of tested outcomes.
items.summary_html:
Debugging a failing test, tracing an access-control issue, and automating a repetitive shell workflow have something in common: they require more than a chat response. You need tools, context, and a way to check the result.

Alter Zero is an open-source agent harness for coding, cybersecurity, and automation, written in Rust. That is also how the project describes itself in its Cargo.toml.

It works in your terminal with tools for reading and editing files, running commands, managing long-running processes, and delegating focused work to subagents. You choose a supported model provider or connect a local model server.

Here is what that looks like across the three workflows—and how to try it.

See it in action

Watch the video demo.

1. Coding: go from investigation to a verified change

Alter Zero can inspect a repository, edit files, run build or test commands, and show the output as it happens. Syntax-highlighted file views, readable diffs, and task checklists help you follow the work instead of relying only on the final summary.

A focused starting prompt:

Find why this test fails. Trace the cause, make the smallest fix,
and run the relevant tests. Explain what changed and what you verified.

You can steer a running turn, queue a follow-up, and resume saved sessions later. Optional per-directory checkpoints support restoring working files when rewinding a conversation.

The important distinction: the harness gives the model tools to investigate and verify. It does not make every proposed fix correct—review the diff and test results yourself.

2. Cybersecurity: investigate code and systems with evidence

The same file and shell tools can support security reviews, technical investigations, and authorized testing. For example, ask the agent to trace authentication and authorization paths rather than simply list generic vulnerabilities:

Review this repository's authentication and authorization flow.
Trace each potential issue to specific code, distinguish confirmed
findings from hypotheses, and suggest fixes and regression tests.
Do not modify files yet.

For a system you own or have permission to assess, another useful task is to summarize supplied service configurations or security logs and identify what needs manual verification.

The repository also includes an optional headless Kali Rolling container for Docker or Podman. It packages Alter Zero with a selected set of CLI tools, including nmap, curl, jq, rg, and Python—not the entire Kali toolset. See the container guide for setup, networking, and workspace options.

The container runs as root, and a mounted workspace exposes those files to edits. Treat it as a working environment, not a guarantee of isolation. Keep testing within an explicitly authorized scope.

3. Automation: work with the tools already in your shell

Automation is not limited to generating scripts. Alter Zero can execute commands, inspect their output, and handle programs that pause for input.

Its shell tools support interactive prompts, REPLs, and full-screen terminal programs. Long-running commands can be started in the background, inspected, waited on, sent input, or stopped.

A practical first task:

Write a script that summarizes these logs and flags recurring errors.
Test it on a small sample, show the expected output, and do not alter
or delete the original logs.

For repeatable workflows, you can add reusable skills, lifecycle hooks, and project instructions. Hooks are off by default and can be enabled per working directory. MCP servers connect additional tools; what the agent can do through an integration depends on the server you configure.

A harness you can extend

Several capabilities tie these workflows together:

  • Subagents: delegate focused work with separate context and tool access. The main agent can check progress, send follow-ups, stop an agent, and resume a finished agent's conversation.
  • Skills: reusable SKILL.md folders loaded when needed. Built-in skills include web search, Jina Reader, skill creation, media-download guidance, and localhost-tunnel guidance.
  • MCP: connect servers over stdio, HTTP, or SSE, with OAuth support for remote servers that use it.
  • Hooks and AGENTS.md: add lifecycle automation and project-specific instructions.
  • Session continuity: use /resume, alter-zero --continue, or alter-zero --resume to pick up earlier work.

Skills are instructions and, in some cases, supporting scripts—not bundled versions of every external tool. For example, the yt-dlp skill uses the separately installed downloader, and flaredantic uses the external flare CLI. Loading the tunnel skill does not itself expose a service.

Choose your model provider

Supported providers include OpenRouter, Anthropic, GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT Codex, Venice, Cline/ClinePass, and Ollama, among others. Use /login to connect and /model to select a model. Sign-in methods and available capabilities vary by provider.

You can add OpenAI-compatible services or local servers in ~/.alter-zero/providers.toml; custom providers appear alongside the built-ins.

The harness is open source. Hosted model access may require a subscription or API credits, and local inference quality and speed depend on your model and hardware.

Permissions, secrets, and privacy: know the boundaries

Alter Zero offers four permission modes:

Mode General behavior manual Asks before file changes and commands edit Allows file changes; commands still require approval auto Adds a reviewer for routine commands master Runs unattended

Start with manual, review proposed actions, and keep a clean Git working tree or backups. Project-defined agents, hooks, and MCP servers have a trust review through /trust. Permission controls are not an operating-system sandbox.

The /secrets feature lets tools use stored credentials through placeholders, with expansion at execution and redaction in model-visible output. This reduces direct exposure to the model; it is not an encrypted vault or a promise that arbitrary commands cannot leak data. The secrets documentation explains storage and raw-log caveats.

Telemetry is enabled by default. The documented ping contains an install ID, app version, and platform information—not prompts, code, or command history. You can disable it for a run with:

ALTER_ZERO_TELEMETRY=0 alter-zero

DO_NOT_TRACK=1 is also supported. The separate GitHub update check has its own setting and is not disabled by DO_NOT_TRACK. Model-provider requests are separate from telemetry: using a hosted model still sends the context needed for inference to that provider. Read the telemetry policy before using sensitive workspaces.

Try Alter Zero on Linux or macOS

Install the native build through npm:

npm install -g @linuztx/alter-zero
cd your-project
alter-zero

Then:

  1. Run /login to connect a supported provider or local model server.
  2. Run /model to choose a model.
  3. Start with a focused task and review approval prompts.

Without a configured provider, the app opens an offline demo with scripted turns so you can explore the interface.

Prefer building from source? With rustup and a C compiler installed:

git clone https://github.com/linuztx/alter-zero.git
cd alter-zero
cargo install --path .
alter-zero

The repository pins its Rust toolchain. See the quick-start guide for the shell installer and other options.

What is new in v0.15.0?

At the time of writing, GitHub's latest release is v0.15.0. Its changelog includes:

  • Custom OpenAI-compatible providers through providers.toml.
  • Streaming file writes in the UI: see generated file content line by line while the model produces the tool call, rather than waiting for the whole call to finish.
  • The flaredantic skill for guiding localhost sharing and webhook testing with an external CLI.
  • macOS screenshot-paste fixes and removal of metadata from pasted images. This does not apply to images read directly from a file path.

These are released features; changes under Unreleased are not included here.

items.title: A review signal: what 1,120 one and two-star reviews say about 30 UK energy suppliers, and who answers them
items.summary: Every unhappy customer who writes a review is telling the market something specific: the phone line that never answers, the estimated bill, the smart meter that stopped sending readings, the refund that takes three months. For the company's competitors that is the most useful data there is. It says where the other side is weak right now, in the customers' own words, with a date on it. If you run marketing or customer experience at a challenger brand, sell to companies in a crowded consumer market, broker contracts, or advise on service quality, that is the signal you want: across a whole category, how many recent reviews are negative, what they are about, and which companies answer them. We built it for 30 UK energy suppliers on 15 October 2026 with our trustpilot-reviews Actor on Apify. It reads each company's public Trustpilot page the way a logged-out visitor sees it: star rating, title, text, dates, whether the review was invited, and the company's reply with its date. Every number below is from those runs. Reviews are written by members of the public, so this post shows counts only: no reviewer names, and no review text. The signal, written as two inputs The 30 suppliers: 16 household suppliers in Great Britain, 4 in Northern Ireland and 10 that sell to businesses, from Octopus Energy and British Gas to Crown Gas & Power. Brands that have closed or moved their customers to another supplier (Shell Energy, Bulb, Boost, Rebel Energy) were left out. The list is recipe-3-companies.txt . The first run is a snapshot: every review from the last 90 days, newest first, up to 100 per company, plus one business row each with the TrustScore and review counts. { "companies" : [ "octopus.energy" , "britishgas.co.uk" , "edfenergy.com" , "eonnext.com" , "ovoenergy.com" ], "maxReviewsPerCompany" : 100 , "dateFrom" : "90 days" , "sort" : "recency" , "includeCompanyInfo" : true } The second run is the complaint pull: only one and two-star reviews from the last 30 days, again up to 100 per company. { "companies" : [ "octopus.energy" , "britishgas.co.uk" , "edfenergy.com" , "eonnext.com" , "ovoenergy.com" ], "stars" : [ "1" , "2" ], "maxReviewsPerCompany" : 100 , "dateFrom" : "30 days" , "sort" : "recency" , "includeCompanyInfo" : false , "onlyNew" : true } Three notes on the fields: companies takes the website domain or a Trustpilot review link from any country site. We checked the 30 first with maxReviewsPerCompany: 0 , which returns only the business row, so a wrong guess costs next to nothing. 18 of our 72 guessed domains had no Trustpilot page and came back as free rows, and one, eon.co.uk , turned out to be a film production company. dateFrom takes a date or a period like 30 days . With newest-first order the Actor stops reading a company at that date, so it only reads the pages it needs. onlyNew remembers which reviews it has already returned for this exact input, in your own Apify account. It is what makes the weekly version below cheap. What came back The snapshot: 2,358 reviews and 30 business rows. At $0.25 per 1,000 rows, a user on the free or Starter plan pays $0.58 for the main run and $0.03 for one retry (E.ON Next's page timed out after 40 reviews, so we ran that company again on its own). Only 319 of the 2,358 recent reviews (13.5%) are one or two stars. 1,858 (79%) are five stars. But 1,599 of them (68%) were invited by the company, and invited reviews are a different population. 4% of invited reviews are one or two stars. Of the 759 organic reviews, written by people who went to Trustpilot on their own, 34% are. items.summary_html:
Every unhappy customer who writes a review is telling the market something specific: the phone line that never answers, the estimated bill, the smart meter that stopped sending readings, the refund that takes three months. For the company's competitors that is the most useful data there is. It says where the other side is weak right now, in the customers' own words, with a date on it.

If you run marketing or customer experience at a challenger brand, sell to companies in a crowded consumer market, broker contracts, or advise on service quality, that is the signal you want: across a whole category, how many recent reviews are negative, what they are about, and which companies answer them.

We built it for 30 UK energy suppliers on 15 October 2026 with our trustpilot-reviews Actor on Apify. It reads each company's public Trustpilot page the way a logged-out visitor sees it: star rating, title, text, dates, whether the review was invited, and the company's reply with its date. Every number below is from those runs. Reviews are written by members of the public, so this post shows counts only: no reviewer names, and no review text.

The signal, written as two inputs

The 30 suppliers: 16 household suppliers in Great Britain, 4 in Northern Ireland and 10 that sell to businesses, from Octopus Energy and British Gas to Crown Gas & Power. Brands that have closed or moved their customers to another supplier (Shell Energy, Bulb, Boost, Rebel Energy) were left out. The list is recipe-3-companies.txt.

The first run is a snapshot: every review from the last 90 days, newest first, up to 100 per company, plus one business row each with the TrustScore and review counts.

{
  "companies": ["octopus.energy", "britishgas.co.uk", "edfenergy.com", "eonnext.com", "ovoenergy.com"],
  "maxReviewsPerCompany": 100,
  "dateFrom": "90 days",
  "sort": "recency",
  "includeCompanyInfo": true
}

The second run is the complaint pull: only one and two-star reviews from the last 30 days, again up to 100 per company.

{
  "companies": ["octopus.energy", "britishgas.co.uk", "edfenergy.com", "eonnext.com", "ovoenergy.com"],
  "stars": ["1", "2"],
  "maxReviewsPerCompany": 100,
  "dateFrom": "30 days",
  "sort": "recency",
  "includeCompanyInfo": false,
  "onlyNew": true
}

Three notes on the fields:

  • companies takes the website domain or a Trustpilot review link from any country site. We checked the 30 first with maxReviewsPerCompany: 0, which returns only the business row, so a wrong guess costs next to nothing. 18 of our 72 guessed domains had no Trustpilot page and came back as free rows, and one, eon.co.uk, turned out to be a film production company.
  • dateFrom takes a date or a period like 30 days. With newest-first order the Actor stops reading a company at that date, so it only reads the pages it needs.
  • onlyNew remembers which reviews it has already returned for this exact input, in your own Apify account. It is what makes the weekly version below cheap.
What came back
  • The snapshot: 2,358 reviews and 30 business rows. At $0.25 per 1,000 rows, a user on the free or Starter plan pays $0.58 for the main run and $0.03 for one retry (E.ON Next's page timed out after 40 reviews, so we ran that company again on its own).
  • Only 319 of the 2,358 recent reviews (13.5%) are one or two stars. 1,858 (79%) are five stars.
  • But 1,599 of them (68%) were invited by the company, and invited reviews are a different population. 4% of invited reviews are one or two stars. Of the 759 organic reviews, written by people who went to Trustpilot on their own, 34% are.
  • The complaint pull: 1,120 one and two-star reviews from the last 30 days, at 28 of the 30 suppliers, in 3 minutes 53 seconds, for $0.28. firmus energy and SEFE Energy had none in the period.
  • 43% of the 1,120 are about getting through to someone: hold times, call-backs that never come, emails with no answer. Billing comes second (30%) and smart meters third (28%).
  • 86% of the one and two-star reviews that were at least three days old had a reply from the company. 61% of those at least a day old were answered within 24 hours. The median reply came after 15 hours.
Invited and organic reviews are two different signals

Trustpilot shows how each review arrived. Most of these suppliers send customers an invitation after a call or a meter fitting, and those customers are mostly happy. People who go looking for the review page are mostly not.

Reviews in the snapshot Reviews Five stars One or two stars Invited by the company 1,599 86.9% 4.0% Organic 759 61.8% 33.6% All 2,358 78.8% 13.5%

That is why two suppliers with similar service can show very different scores. British Gas has a TrustScore of 4.4; 86 of its 100 newest reviews were invited. British Gas Lite, a separate brand in the same group, has 1.1; 44 of its 45 reviews in the 90 days were organic, and 44 of the 45 were one or two stars. At the business suppliers that invite few customers, the organic reviews are mostly good: Corona Energy (98 organic reviews of 100) and Pozitive Energy (88 of 100) have 5% and 8% one or two-star reviews.

So for a competitor signal, ignore the TrustScore and read two things: the organic reviews, and the one and two-star reviews whichever way they arrived. 37% of the 1,120 one and two-star reviews in the complaint pull came through an invitation, which means the customer was unhappy enough to say so in the company's own survey.

What the unhappy customers write about

We grouped the 1,120 complaint reviews with keyword lists in code: a review counts for a theme when its title or text contains one of the theme's phrases, ignoring case. A review can count for several themes. 146 (13%) matched none, mostly reviews of a line or two that only say the service was bad.

Complaint theme Reviews Share Example phrases we match Getting through to someone 482 43% on hold, call back, no response, chase, live chat Billing and estimated bills 338 30% bill, estimated, overcharged, statement Smart meters and readings 308 28% smart meter, meter, readings, in-home display Switching, moving and closing accounts 293 26% switched, moving home, final bill, cancel Tariffs and prices 198 18% tariff, unit rate, standing charge, price Engineers and appointments 182 16% engineer, appointment, installation, no-show Refunds and credit balances 179 16% refund, credit balance, money back, owed Rude or unhelpful staff 156 14% rude, unhelpful, attitude, no idea Direct debit and payments 150 13% direct debit, payment plan, monthly payments Formal complaints and the ombudsman 131 12% ombudsman, formal complaint, escalated Contracts and renewals 113 10% contract, renewal, rolled over, deemed, broker Debt collection and court 91 8% debt, collectors, court, warrant, credit file Broadband, phone and other services 85 8% broadband, home phone, mobile, boiler Solar, EV and export 74 7% solar, export, EV, heat pump, battery Prepayment and top-ups 36 3% prepay, top up, emergency credit

The full phrase lists are in recipe-3-analysis.py. Change them for your own market; the method is the same.

The mix changes by customer type, and that is where the signal gets specific:

  • Business suppliers: billing leads (41% of their 181 complaint reviews), then getting through (40%), contracts and renewals (26%) and formal complaints (21%). A business customer who is unhappy is often in a contract dispute, not just on hold.
  • Household suppliers: getting through leads (44% of 924), with smart meters and billing tied at 28%.
  • One supplier at a time: British Gas's complaints mention engineers and appointments in 39% of cases, because it also sells boiler cover and repairs. At OVO, direct debits come up in 26%. At Utility Warehouse, which sells broadband and mobile too, 37% are about those other services.
Who answers bad reviews, and how fast

A reply is public, it has a date, and it shows how a company treats an unhappy customer in front of the next one. We measured it on the complaint pull, and only counted reviews that were old enough to have had a fair chance: at least 24 hours old for "answered within a day", at least three days old for "answered at all".

Supplier One and two-star reviews a day Answered within 24 hours Median time to reply E.ON Next 35.9 69 of 69 4.7 hours Octopus Energy 26.6 21 of 68 23.3 hours British Gas 15.6 87 of 87 0.5 hours ScottishPower 15.3 47 of 77 22.6 hours OVO 10.3 84 of 90 17.5 hours Utility Warehouse 10.3 69 of 86 2.6 hours EDF 8.0 58 of 86 11.3 hours Yü Energy 3.1 13 of 86 21.3 hours So Energy 2.2 35 of 60 21.5 hours Fuse Energy 1.7 4 of 49 96.0 hours SmartestEnergy 1.0 26 of 28 2.9 hours Pozitive Energy 0.4 0 of 13 108.6 hours

Reviews a day is over the 30 days, or over the days our 100 reviews covered when a supplier had more than 100 in the month (E.ON Next's 100 covered under three days). The other 18 suppliers and every column are in companies.csv.

Three patterns stand out:

  • The big suppliers run reply desks. British Gas answered all 87 of its one and two-star reviews that were a day old within 24 hours, and its median reply came 30 minutes after the review. E.ON Next and Utility Warehouse also reply within hours.
  • Some reply to everything, slowly. Pozitive Energy answered all 11 of its older complaint reviews, but none within a day; the median was four and a half days. Fuse Energy took four days at the median and had answered 33 of 48.
  • Some don't reply at all. British Gas Lite answered none of its 13 one and two-star reviews that were three days old or more, and Corona Energy none of 5. Yü Energy, with the lowest TrustScore among the active business suppliers (3.7), had answered 25 of 77.
Read the themes once

Keyword grouping is fast and you can check every match, but it is crude, so read a sample before you act on it:

  • It finds words, not meaning. "No issues with the meter" counts for smart meters. That is rare in one-star reviews, but check a few per theme.
  • Short reviews match nothing. 13% of the complaint reviews fall in no theme. Add phrases when you see a pattern; don't stretch the lists until everything matches.
  • Reviews are not a random sample of customers. They are the people who chose to write, plus the ones a company invited. Compare a supplier with itself over time, or one theme across suppliers, rather than reading a share as a fact about all customers.
  • A reply date is the date Trustpilot shows for the reply. Some companies edit their replies, which can move the date.
The weekly version: a competitor's unhappy customers, in Slack

The useful form of this signal is a message every Monday: for each competitor, how many one and two-star reviews arrived in the last seven days, what they were about, and how many got a reply, with links to the newest few. It is a view of where each competitor is struggling, for your product, marketing and service teams. It is not a list of people to contact: the Actor's terms ask you not to contact or profile reviewers, and the workflow never touches reviewer names.

We use an n8n workflow with five nodes for it:

  1. Schedule Trigger, every Monday at 08:00.
  2. Competitors and filters (a Set node): the companies' domains, one per line, the stars to keep (1, 2) and the period (7 days).
  3. Apify, Run actor and get dataset: runs trustpilot-reviews with onlyNew: true, up to 200 reviews per company and 2,000 rows in all, with a $1 cap on the run.
  4. Code: groups the reviews by company, counts the themes with the same phrase lists as this post, works out the reply share, and builds one message with links to the three newest reviews per company (titles only). A quiet week sends nothing.
  5. Slack: posts it to the channel you pick.

Download review-signal-to-slack.json. It comes with this post's 30 suppliers filled in; replace them with your own competitors.

Setup takes about five minutes:

  1. In n8n, open Workflows > Import from file and pick the JSON.
  2. The workflow uses the verified Apify node (@apify/n8n-nodes-apify). n8n Cloud installs it from the canvas; on self-hosted n8n, add it under Settings > Community nodes.
  3. In the Apify node, create an Apify API credential with your token from the Apify console (Settings > API & Integrations).
  4. In Post to Slack, pick your Slack credential and the channel.
  5. Edit Competitors and filters. Run it once by hand: the first run returns the last seven days, and from then on each Monday brings only the new week.

What it costs: across these 30 suppliers, about 136 one and two-star reviews arrive a day, so a weekly run is about 950 rows, or $0.24. A supplier with more than 200 bad reviews a week (E.ON Next had about 250) will hit the per-company limit on a weekly schedule; for those, set the trigger to daily and the period to 2 days, and the same message works as a daily digest. On Apify's free plan a run returns up to 1,000 rows; any paid plan removes the cap.

If you work from Claude Code or another MCP client

With the Apify MCP server connected, this prompt does the same job for your own category and gives you tables:

Use the Apify Actor locaihost/trustpilot-reviews. First run it with maxReviewsPerCompany 0 on these
domains to check each one has a Trustpilot page: [your 10 to 30 competitors]. Then run it on the ones
that exist with stars ["1","2"], dateFrom "30 days", maxReviewsPerCompany 100, includeCompanyInfo false.
The price is $0.25 per 1,000 rows; tell me the expected row count before the second run.
Do not show or store reviewerName. Group the reviews into complaint themes with keyword lists you
show me first, and give me per company: one and two-star reviews a day, the top three themes with
their share, the share of reviews older than 24 hours that got a reply within 24 hours, and the
median hours to reply. List any theme where one company's share is twice the average.
More ways to use the review signal
  • Positioning and ads. If 43% of a market's complaints are about getting through to someone, "a person answers in two minutes" is a claim worth testing, and the theme counts tell you which competitor to compare yourself with.
  • Your own service team. Put your own domain in the list. The themes and reply times sit next to your competitors', in the same format, every week.
  • Category research. Any market with busy Trustpilot pages works the same way: banks and fintech apps, broadband, airlines, delivery firms, online retailers, VPNs. Swap the domains and the phrase lists.
  • Brokers and switching services. A rise in contract and renewal complaints at one business supplier is a reason to call the customers you placed there before their renewal date.
  • Investors and analysts. A sudden jump in one theme (billing after a system migration, say) shows up in reviews within days, long before it shows up in a regulator's complaint figures.
  • Score tracking. Keep includeCompanyInfo on with onlyNew, and a business row comes back only when the TrustScore or review count changed.
Notes
  • The sample. 30 UK energy suppliers with an active Trustpilot page, picked by us: 16 household suppliers in Great Britain, 4 in Northern Ireland, 10 business suppliers. It is not every supplier in the market.
  • The runs. Snapshot run MpDPBn28NabBlLoRS on 15 October 2026 at 04:57 UTC (395 seconds, 2,298 reviews and 30 business rows), then lTXbPzQw9ciFlIYSc for E.ON Next alone (100 reviews), whose rows replace the 40 from the first run. Complaint run 2wJfjfHnZ91cXV9M2 (233 seconds, 1,120 reviews), then wU4Q8947iivcb8Jgn with the same input, which returned nothing and charged nothing because onlyNew had already sent every review.
  • What "invited" means here. Any review whose source is not Trustpilot's "Organic": invitation emails, invitation links and the links a company shares itself.
  • No personal data in the outputs. The run script drops reviewer names before saving anything, and the files next to this post hold counts per company only.
  • Reproduce it. The company list, the run script and the analysis script are next to this post, with the computed results.

If you run this on your own category, post two numbers in the comments: the share of one and two-star reviews among organic reviews, and among invited ones. If the gap is as wide as it was here, the next reader will know how little a TrustScore says on its own.

items.title: How CoreWeave’s Debt Binge Brought a Perilous Moment of Reckoning
items.summary: In early 2023, Blackstone CEO Steve Schwarzman gathered with Jas Khaira, the company’s lead AI investor, and other top executives at the finance giant’s Park Avenue headquarters in Manhattan for a debate: Should they give billions of dollars to a little-known data center developer—CoreWeave—that they had turned down just a few months earlier? CoreWeave had gotten Blackstone to return to the table after landing a multiyear, multibillion-dollar contract to sell cloud computing services to Microsoft. It needed $2.3 billion to buy Nvidia GPUs and secure a data center to house them. In Blackstone’s discussion of the deal, several executives in the room had deep misgivings, according to a person who attended the meeting. CoreWeave was still something of a mystery, a six-year-old, privately held firm that had generated only $16 million in revenue in the previous year. Schwarzman himself was personally worried his investment team could be making a mistake, the person said.

items.title: Will Rust Replace Python in AI? The Real Battle Is Happening Underneath
items.summary: Rust isn’t coming for your Jupyter notebook. It’s coming for everything around it. If you write AI code, you write Python. Training loops, fine-tuning scripts, eval harnesses, the FastAPI wrapper around your model: it’s Python almost all the way down. Or at least it looks that way. Open up the tools you pip install every day and a different picture shows up. The tokenizer behind most Hugging Face models is written in Rust. So is safetensors, the format most open model weights now ship in. So is Polars, the DataFrame library that keeps eating into pandas' benchmarks. Even Python's own tooling is shifting: uv and ruff, two of the fastest-growing Python dev tools, are Rust binaries. That raises a fair question. Is Rust going to replace Python in AI? And if it’s already sitting under Python, could it push further down and take over from C and C++ inside the frameworks themselves? The short answer is no, and also yes, depending on which layer of the stack you’re looking at. To see why, you have to stop thinking of an “AI app” as a model and start thinking of it as a system. 1. items.title: Part XV — Adaptive Query Execution: What AQE Actually Rewrites at Runtime
items.summary: Spark plans your query before it has seen your data. AQE is the engine’s admission that the planner was guessing — and the machinery that lets the runtime rewrite the plan after every shuffle, using statistics that only exist once the bytes have actually moved. Part I | Part II | Part III | Part IV | Part V | Part VI | Part VII | Part VIII | Part IX | Part X | Part XI | Part XII | Part XIII | Part XIV | Part XV The Job That Ran 4 Hours 47 Minutes Every Night for a Year Friday, 1:12 AM. The clickstream sessionization job — 1.8TB of raw events, keyed by session_id, shuffled, windowed, written out — finished in 4 hours 47 minutes. It had finished in roughly that time every night for a year. The on-call runbook said "sessionization is slow, it's just big," and everyone believed it, because the Spark UI showed the same shape every night: 200 shuffle partitions, three of them glowing red, each holding ~78% of the data between them while 197 partitions finished in minutes and sat idle. The standard playbook had been tried. More executors: no change — the three hot partitions still had to be processed serially by three tasks. spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=2000: worse, now there were 2,000 tiny files and the same three hot keys. Salting (Part VII's playbook): worked, but it meant rewriting the sessionization logic around salted keys and un-salting downstream, and nobody wanted to touch a pipeline that "worked." Then someone noticed a config line inherited from the Spark 2.4 migration, three years stale: spark.sql.adaptive.enabled=false. AQE had shipped in Spark 3.0, been enabled by default in 3.2, and this cluster had been carrying the opt-out like a vestigial organ. We flipped it on for the next run. The job finished in 52 minutes. Same data, same cluster, same query. The planner had been flying blind for a year, and the fix was deleting one line. So: what does AQE actually rewrite at runtime, which knobs control each rewrite, and where does the adaptive machinery run out of road? The Mechanic Underneath: The Plan Is Re-Planned After Every Shuffle The static Spark planner (Part III’s Catalyst) optimizes your query once, before execution, using table statistics that are frequently stale, missing, or lies. It picks join strategies, partition counts, and build sides based on estimates. AQE replaces that single planning moment with a loop: Execute a stage → collect runtime statistics from the actual shuffle output → re-optimize the rest of the plan → repeat. The unit of adaptivity is the query stage : a subtree of the plan that ends at a shuffle boundary. AQE wraps each one in a QueryStageExec, runs it, and harvests real numbers — actual partition sizes, actual row counts — from the shuffle files that were just written. The remaining plan is then re-planned with truth instead of estimates. In the Spark UI's SQL tab you'll see it as AdaptiveSparkPlan with collapsed stages; each collapse point is a place where the plan changed its mind. Three rewrites happen in that loop, each controlled by its own configs, each fixing a different way the static planner guesses wrong. They are: coalescing shuffle partitions, switching join strategies, and splitting skewed partitions. Coalescing: 200 Empty Partitions Were Never a Plan spark.sql.shuffle.partitions (default 200) is a static guess made before the query runs. Set it for your biggest shuffle and every small shuffle pays the tax: 200 partitions for a 50MB shuffle means 200 tasks, 200 files, and scheduling overhead that dwarfs the actual work. Set it for the small shuffle and the big one gets 200 giant partitions. With spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.enabled=true (default), AQE measures the actual shuffle output after the stage completes and merges adjacent small partitions until each is close to spark.sql.adaptive.advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes (default 64MB ). Your 50MB shuffle becomes 1 partition. Your 1.8TB shuffle keeps its parallelism. One config, both problems gone. The coalescing respects a floor: it won’t merge below the advisory size target, and spark.sql.adaptive.coalescePartitions.initialPartitionNum (defaulting to spark.sql.shuffle.partitions) caps how many it starts from. The practical upshot is that spark.sql.shuffle.partitions stops being a tuning knob you agonize over and becomes a rough upper bound. Set it generously; AQE trims. Join Switching: Sort-Merge at Plan Time, Broadcast at Runtime Part VI covered the static join strategy choice: broadcast hash join for small build sides, sort-merge for everything else. The static planner makes that call from estimated sizes. When the estimate is wrong — the “small” table is actually 40GB, or the “huge” table filtered down to 3MB — you’re locked into the wrong algorithm for the entire query. AQE re-evaluates the join strategy after each stage using runtime statistics . The classic win: the planner chose sort-merge join because the build side was estimated at 2GB, but after filters and the actual shuffle the build side is 8MB. AQE converts the sort-merge join into a broadcast hash join mid-flight — no shuffle of the big table, no re-plan by you. The threshold it uses is spark.sql.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold, which defaults to the familiar spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold (10MB). It can also demote to a shuffled hash join where that fits. This is the feature that quietly retires a whole class of BROADCAST hints. Part XIV showed what happens when a hint fossilizes a wrong size assumption; AQE's runtime join selection is the engine doing that decision with fresh data instead of your eighteen-month-old guess. It doesn't make broadcast free — the driver still collects (Part XIV's bottleneck is still real) — but it makes the decision correct. Skew Handling: Splitting the Partition the Planner Couldn’t See This is the one that fixed our sessionization job. AQE detects skew after a shuffle stage completes , by looking at actual partition sizes: a partition is skewed if it’s larger than spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes (default 256MB ) and larger than spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.skewedPartitionFactor (default 5 ) times the median partition size. Both conditions — absolute and relative — must hold, which is why it doesn't fire on uniformly large shuffles. When it fires, on a sort-merge or shuffled-hash join, AQE splits the skewed partition into sub-partitions and replicates the corresponding partition of the other side to each split. The hot key’s work fans out across many tasks instead of serializing on one. In our job, the three monster partitions — 78% of 1.8TB — were split into dozens of pieces, each paired with a replicated copy of the small side. The 4h47m wall clock was three tasks; the 52-minute wall clock was hundreds. Two details matter. First, skew splitting only applies to sort-merge and shuffled-hash joins — if AQE already converted the join to broadcast, there’s nothing to split, because every executor holds the full build side anyway. Second, the split count derives from the skewed partition’s size relative to the advisory partition size, so advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes quietly controls skew handling granularity too. Reading an Adaptive Plan: Where the Rewrites Show Up AQE is invisible if you don’t know where to look, which is why teams run with it for years without realizing what it’s doing — or run without it for years without realizing what they’re missing. In the Spark UI’s SQL tab, an adaptive query shows AdaptiveSparkPlan at the root, with stages that render collapsed : each collapsed node is a QueryStageExec whose final plan was chosen at runtime. Expand the final stage and you'll see AQEShuffleRead nodes where the static plan had plain Exchange — those are the reads that got coalesced or skew-split. The "Details" for a stage show the runtime statistics AQE collected: actual size, actual rows. The fastest diagnostic: EXPLAIN the same query with spark.sql.adaptive.enabled true and false, and diff them. The non-adaptive plan is what Catalyst guessed. The adaptive plan's final form is what the data required. The distance between them is the value AQE added — and on our sessionization job, that distance was 200 static partitions versus 34 coalesced ones with three skew splits. The Fix, and What It Cost The naive state of the sessionization pipeline: AQE disabled by a three-year-old migration config, a static partition count tuned by superstition, and a manual salting design doc nobody wanted to implement. # Naive: static planning with a fossilized opt-out. The planner guesses 200 # partitions and sort-merge join from stale stats; skew is discovered by humans # at 1 AM instead of by the engine at runtime. spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "false") # carried over from the Spark 2.4 migration spark.conf.set("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "200") # tuned once, wrong for every query shape sessions = ( events .groupBy("session_id") .agg(...) # 3 partitions hold 78% of 1.8TB; 197 sit idle ) # Result: 4h47m nightly, three red partitions in the UI, "just big" in the runbook. The engine-aware fix: delete the opt-out, set the advisory size to match the workload, and let the runtime see the skew. # Optimized: let the runtime plan with real statistics. No query rewrite needed. spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "true") # default since 3.2; we had opted out spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.advisoryPartitionSizeInBytes", 128 * 1024 * 1024) # 128MB: our files are large spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled", "true") # default true; explicit for the runbook # skewJoin.skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes=256MB, skewedPartitionFactor=5: defaults were fine sessions = ( events .groupBy("session_id") .agg(...) # identical query text ) # AQE coalesced 200 -> 34 partitions, skew-split the 3 hot ones, runtime: 52 minutes. No salting, no query rewrite, no logic changes downstream. The query text is byte-identical; only the planning loop changed. Before/after: 4h47m wall clock → 52 minutes . Shuffle partitions 200 static → 34 coalesced with skew splits. EMR cost per run ~$96 → ~$18. The three red partitions in the UI are gone — not because the skew disappeared, but because the engine finally saw it and split it. The Catch: Where the Adaptive Machinery Runs Out of Road AQE is powerful the way a good autopilot is powerful: within its envelope. Outside it, you’re hand-flying again. First, AQE needs a shuffle to learn from. The first query stage runs on static planning, always — there are no runtime statistics yet. A query with no shuffles gets zero adaptivity. A query whose only shuffle is at the very end gets its statistics too late to matter. Second, skew handling only covers sort-merge and shuffled-hash joins. If your skew is in a groupBy aggregation or a window function, AQE watches it happen and does nothing. That's still Part VII territory: salt it yourself. Third, runtime statistics cost scheduling. Each query stage boundary is a synchronization point — stages can’t overlap the way a fully pipelined static plan might. For queries with many small stages, the stage-scheduling overhead can eat the coalescing gains. It’s usually worth it. Usually is doing work in that sentence. Fourth, AQE’s broadcast conversions still hit Part XIV’s bottleneck. Converting a sort-merge join to a broadcast hash join at runtime means the driver collects the build side right then . If the runtime statistics say the build side is 9GB and your driver has 8g of heap, AQE will cheerfully schedule a driver OOM. The adaptive threshold deserves the same scrutiny as the static one. Fifth, join reordering still wants real table statistics. AQE can change strategies mid-flight, but the initial join order comes from Catalyst, and Catalyst without CBO stats is guessing. ANALYZE TABLE ... COMPUTE STATISTICS remains the cheapest performance work nobody does. Takeaways The static planner guesses; AQE measures — every rewrite is funded by runtime statistics collected at shuffle boundaries. Coalescing retires spark.sql.shuffle.partitions as a tuning knob — set it as a generous upper bound and let the 64MB advisory size trim the rest. Runtime join switching is the anti-hint — it makes the broadcast decision with fresh data instead of your eighteen-month-old guess. Skew splits fire at 256MB and 5× median, on sort-merge/shuffle-hash joins only — aggregation skew is still yours to salt. Read the adaptive plan, not the query text — collapsed stages and AQEShuffleRead nodes are where the rewrites show up in the UI. ANALYZE TABLE is still the cheapest optimization — AQE fixes strategy, but join order still needs real statistics to start from. The most expensive query in your warehouse is the one the planner imagined and the data never matched. If this saved you a 3 AM pager incident, follow me on Medium for Twice a week for the next 3 Months of Advanced Data Engineering & AI. Let’s connect on LinkedIn and X . Part XV — Adaptive Query Execution: What AQE Actually Rewrites at Runtime was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

# Naive: static planning with a fossilized opt-out. The planner guesses 200
# partitions and sort-merge join from stale stats; skew is discovered by humans
# at 1 AM instead of by the engine at runtime.
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "false")  # carried over from the Spark 2.4 migration
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.shuffle.partitions", "200")  # tuned once, wrong for every query shape
sessions = (
    events
    .groupBy("session_id")
    .agg(...)  # 3 partitions hold 78% of 1.8TB; 197 sit idle
)
# Result: 4h47m nightly, three red partitions in the UI, "just big" in the runbook.

# Optimized: let the runtime plan with real statistics. No query rewrite needed.

# skewJoin.skewedPartitionThresholdInBytes=256MB, skewedPartitionFactor=5: defaults were fine
sessions = (
    events
    .groupBy("session_id")
    .agg(...)  # identical query text
)
# AQE coalesced 200 -> 34 partitions, skew-split the 3 hot ones, runtime: 52 minutes.

For queries with many small stages, the stage-scheduling overhead can eat the coalescing gains. It’s usually worth it. Usually is doing work in that sentence.

Fourth, AQE’s broadcast conversions still hit Part XIV’s bottleneck. Converting a sort-merge join to a broadcast hash join at runtime means the driver collects the build side right then. If the runtime statistics say the build side is 9GB and your driver has 8g of heap, AQE will cheerfully schedule a driver OOM. The adaptive threshold deserves the same scrutiny as the static one.

Fifth, join reordering still wants real table statistics. AQE can change strategies mid-flight, but the initial join order comes from Catalyst, and Catalyst without CBO stats is guessing. ANALYZE TABLE ... COMPUTE STATISTICS remains the cheapest performance work nobody does.

Takeaways
  • The static planner guesses; AQE measures — every rewrite is funded by runtime statistics collected at shuffle boundaries.
  • Coalescing retires spark.sql.shuffle.partitions as a tuning knob — set it as a generous upper bound and let the 64MB advisory size trim the rest.
  • Runtime join switching is the anti-hint — it makes the broadcast decision with fresh data instead of your eighteen-month-old guess.
  • Skew splits fire at 256MB and 5× median, on sort-merge/shuffle-hash joins only — aggregation skew is still yours to salt.
  • Read the adaptive plan, not the query text — collapsed stages and AQEShuffleRead nodes are where the rewrites show up in the UI.
  • ANALYZE TABLE is still the cheapest optimization — AQE fixes strategy, but join order still needs real statistics to start from.

The most expensive query in your warehouse is the one the planner imagined and the data never matched.

If this saved you a 3 AM pager incident, follow me on Medium for Twice a week for the next 3 Months of Advanced Data Engineering & AI. Let’s connect on LinkedIn and X.

items.title: are you building a model or a model factory
items.summary: Subscribe • Previous Issues The Model Factory Matters More Than the Model A couple of months ago, I wrote about the growing post-training stack that lets teams turn general-purpose models into something better suited to their own work. I recently spoke with Joel Hron , CTO of Thomson Reuters, about a more ambitious version of the same idea. His team starts with a strong open-weight model, continues pre-training it on Thomson Reuters data, then puts it through several stages of post-training. I am going to call this deep model customization . Thomson Reuters is not alone. Cursor, C3 AI, ByteDance, Cisco, and Reddit are exploring variations of the same approach, and their experiences already point to a few useful lessons. A frequent reader? Consider becoming a paid supporter Why Fine-Tuning Is Not Always Enough The companies going down this path generally tried easier options first. Thomson Reuters started with commercial models and relatively simple LoRA fine-tuning. The models improved on the tasks being targeted, but other capabilities deteriorated. C3 AI ran into a different problem. Its proprietary Type System does not appear in public training data, so retrieval alone produced an 11 percent pass rate on its internal coding evaluation. Adding agents and tools pushed frontier models to around 60 percent, but responses took roughly two minutes. The information was available, but the models had not really learned how C3’s system worked. The lesson is not that RAG or fine-tuning are ineffective. They solve different problems. Retrieval is useful when information changes or is too large to put into model weights. Post-training can reshape behavior and improve specific tasks. Continued pre-training goes deeper by changing what the model knows about a domain. That matters when a company’s advantage comes from knowledge, language, workflows, or judgment that is poorly represented in public training data . ByteDance wanted Valley3 to understand multimodal commerce. Cisco wanted a small model that understood cybersecurity. Reddit wanted a model that understood community behavior and moderation context. The Checkpoint Is Just the Starting Point The common recipe begins with model selection. These teams are generally not pre-training a general model from scratch. They evaluate open models against their own workloads and pick the best starting point. Thomson Reuters selected Qwen using its internal evaluations. Cursor chose Kimi K2.5 after testing candidate models on coding knowledge and its own code. C3 AI has repeated its process across five generations as stronger open models have appeared. Next comes continued pre-training. The company mixes domain data into the model while usually retaining general data so specialization does not wipe out useful capabilities. Thomson Reuters trained on a 200 billion token mixture drawn from a much larger collection of legal, regulatory, news, and other material. ByteDance added an e-commerce training phase to Valley3. Cisco continued training Llama 3.1 8B on billions of tokens of cybersecurity text. This is where data engineering matters. Teams have to decide what goes into the mixture, what gets removed, and whether more data is actually improving the model. Then comes post-training. Teams use supervised examples, preference data, reinforcement learning, or some combination. What stood out to me is how often the training environment resembles the actual product. Cursor trains Composer inside coding environments with tools similar to those used in Cursor. Thomson trains its model to use Thomson Reuters search and research systems. Valley3 learns to operate a multimodal product-search engine. The goal is not only to teach the model what to know. It is also to teach it how work gets done inside the company. These Models Do Not Have to Replace Everything One of the key lessons from Thomson Reuters is that success does not require replacing every commercial model. Hron told me their frontier model ( Thomson ) currently handles about 5 to 10 percent of inference inside CoCounsel. Its main production job is high-volume document analysis, such as reviewing large collections of contracts during M&A due diligence. CoCounsel still uses Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, and smaller models. Thomson gets the work where its legal specialization, control, and economics make it a better fit. Other deployments follow a similar pattern. C3’s Narwhal handles C3-specific coding, documentation, customer support, and agent tooling while the broader platform remains model-agnostic. Cursor offers Composer alongside third-party models. Cisco is putting its security model into XDR and other security workflows. Reddit reports that its Nova-based moderation work has reduced missed threats while consolidating work previously handled by multiple models. A specialized model does not need to handle every request to be worthwhile. It can be valuable simply by owning the high-volume or highly differentiated parts of the workload. The Hard Part Is Everything Around the Training Run Thomson Reuters gives a clear sense of what this takes. Its core effort involved roughly 30 scientists and engineers, seeded partly through the acquisition of Safe Sign . It also had something most companies cannot quickly recreate: more than 3,000 legal and tax experts, decades of curated metadata, several trillion tokens of content, mature retrieval products, and evaluations that could detect whether the model was improving in law while getting worse elsewhere. The final training run cost less than $450,000 in compute, but Hron estimates the broader two-year effort at roughly $40 million including people and infrastructure. The other examples vary widely. C3 credits a small data-science group and already had proprietary code, documentation, production feedback, and internal evaluations. Cursor built much more infrastructure itself, including distributed training, large-scale RL , and sandboxed coding environments. Reddit took the opposite route and used Amazon Nova Forge , which provides model checkpoints and managed training infrastructure. This connects to a point I have made before about data . A pile of proprietary documents is not much of an advantage by itself. The useful asset is the machinery that turns data, expert judgment, production failures, and evaluations into better models. The Model Factory May Matter More Than the Model The most interesting part of these projects is that several teams already treat the underlying model checkpoint as replaceable. Thomson Reuters expects to start from newer open models as they appear. C3 AI has already repeated its process across multiple bases. Cursor reused its training machinery for Composer 2.5. The durable asset is increasingly a model factory : the data pipelines, evaluations, training recipes, RL environments, serving infrastructure, and people who know how to run the loop again. The most interesting part of these projects is that several teams already treat the underlying model checkpoint as replaceable. Thomson Reuters expects to start from newer open models as they appear. C3 AI has already repeated its process across multiple bases. Cursor reused its training machinery for Composer 2.5. I recently saw the next step in this progression in a conversation with Ameet Talwalkar of Datadog . Datadog went further with Toto and pre-trained its own time-series foundation model from scratch, using the huge volume of observability data it already had. Taken together, these examples suggest that the durable asset is increasingly a model factory : the data pipelines, evaluations, training recipes, RL environments, serving infrastructure, and people who know how to run the loop again. I’m not suggesting that every large company should start training its own model. Most teams should exhaust prompting, retrieval, better harnesses, and conventional post-training first. Deep model customization is still expensive and operationally demanding. But the threshold is moving. As open-weight models improve and AI infrastructure gets easier to rent or buy, more companies with distinctive data and high-volume workloads will be able to go further. I suspect the interesting question will shift from whether enterprises can customize models this deeply to which parts of their businesses are valuable enough to justify it. items.title: AI’s Midas problem: When code is free, features are worthless
items.summary: Every team that adopted Claude Code, Cursor, or Copilot to produce more code has the same problem: When output is free, offering volume stops being a viable strategy. In fact, teams accelerating their software development with AI may be giving up the very thing that makes their software valuable. It’s time to remember what makes software valuable and why racing to produce a mountain of code and features leads to failure. The Midas touch In Ovid’s tale, Midas, king of Phrygia, took in the missing satyr Silenus, whom Phrygian peasants had found drunk, granted him ten days of hospitality, and then returned him to Dionysus. In return, he was offered the reward of his choice: whatever he wished for. Famously, he wished that everything he touched would turn to gold. Testing his new ability on an oak twig and then a stone, Midas was delighted. Nathaniel Hawthorne, who retold the myth for children in 1851, added a rose garden: His Midas turns every bloom to gold, still delighted, though his daughter Marygold mourns that the roses no longer smell sweet. In both versions, the celebration ends at the table, where food and drink turn to gold in his hands. That’s when Midas realized his reward was a bane, not a blessing, and asked to be rid of it. Many leaders who force-fed AI to developers are now coming to a realization similar to that of Midas. Though the process is gradual, many organizations and leaders who force-fed AI to developers are now reaching a similar conclusion. Reports show organizations slashing budgets and limiting tool use. With Microsoft and Meta reportedly cutting internal spending on Anthropic’s Claude, and Uber and Accenture capping what employees can spend on AI tools, it’s time to acknowledge that the return on investment might not be there — McKinsey’s own 2026 research found record AI spending hasn’t moved earnings for 94% of enterprises — and it’s easy to see why. The economics of plenty If Midas had depended on the value of gold, perhaps hoping to trade the gold he created to fund his lavish lifestyle of hosting ten-day-long parties, he would have quickly learned that his gold was no longer valuable. His touch would cause hyperinflation, and gold’s price would plummet. His skill would be as useful as turning everything you touch to ash. In the modern, non-mythical world, everything you touch with AI becomes a commodity. If you can get Claude or ChatGPT to create something for you, then everyone else can. They have access to the same tools. Whether you’re building software or writing a book, when you use AI, its perceived value is little more than the cost of the tokens you used. When coding looked like magic to most people, basic coding competence was sufficient value. You could build a career translating human-language requirements into code. This value rolled up to the team, department, and organization level, with code magicians performing their arcane translations in return for money, whether the software was internal, built for a customer, or sold as a product. If your software expresses user requirements translated into code, it’s now worthless. If your software expresses user requirements translated into code, it’s now worthless. We know that a page that adds nothing beyond the AI summary is worthless, and software built by translating a user’s wants into code is the same. How to avoid incinerating your software’s value There is hope for us, though. When Midas asked to be rid of his power, he had to wash in the Pactolus River. Our touch isn’t directly connected to the generation machine, so it won’t inevitably turn our work to ash. The answer is conceptually simple, though it takes a lot of effort in practice, which seems to be exactly what people want to avoid. Nevertheless, for your work to be immune to AI’s mortally ruinous touch, you need to provide something beyond what someone could achieve with their own Claude subscription. For your work to be immune to AI’s mortally ruinous touch, you need to provide something beyond what someone could achieve with their own Claude subscription. That means moving away from the feature-factory model of software development, where the value is primarily in the translation of “human wants” into code. Instead, teams building software must develop a deeper understanding of the jobs users do and the challenges they face, so they can generate novel ideas and commercial insights users wouldn’t reach on their own. This second mode of building means you may deliver something completely different from what users ask for, yet one that gracefully solves many of the challenges they face in their work. Combining deep business domain knowledge with an understanding of abstract, reusable solutions lets you deliver something exceptional. DORA’s State of DevOps research has highlighted this need for user-centricity. That doesn’t mean doing whatever users ask; it means understanding their work and challenges so you can provide software they value. DORA’s 2024 report says this approach improves product performance, regardless of delivery speed. We are living through a time of excess code, sentences, and images. The path forward isn’t more; it’s better.

I put a friend who'd never flown into its virtual cockpit and didn't worry one bit. items.title: How governments worldwide are shaping what AI can say about politics
items.summary: With the U.S. midterms approaching, about 1 in 5 voters has asked AI chatbots about elections and politics, a recent survey found. But many voters may not know that governments around the world increasingly shape what chatbots can say. And because many tech companies apply the same policies worldwide, the answers American voters get may be shaped by governments at home and abroad. I’m a researcher at a nonpartisan think tank at Vanderbilt University, where I study free speech policy . In two reports published in 2025 and 2026 , my colleagues and I worked with global legal experts to examine how governments in 12 countries and regions regulate artificial intelligence. Our research shows that they often use existing rules , such as national security or anti-state propaganda laws, rather than new AI laws to control what AI models can say. Censorship masked as safety AI can cause real harm, from launching cyberattacks to generating sexualized images of children . It’s important that governments tackle these harms. But, in our assessment, some governments use legitimate concerns like these as a pretext to control political discussion , particularly chatbot responses about those in power. In 2024, an Indian journalist asked Google’s Gemini chatbot whether the policies of India’s prime minister, Narendra Modi, were fascist . Gemini responded that some experts say yes . The government reacted by requiring official permission before “unreliable” AI models could be released . Although authorities later dropped this requirement , the case shows how terms like “under-testing” or “unreliable” can be used for political purposes. India is not alone. China requires AI models to uphold “socialist core values.” And in Turkey, a court blocked posts by Grok , the chatbot built into the social platform X, that allegedly insulted President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, founding father Mustafa Kemal Atatürk and religious values. Research by Turkish law scholar Yaman Akdeniz identifies the Turkish rulings as among the earliest documented cases of state censorship of chatbots . Vietnam shows what such content controls can mean for dissidents, including those in exile. A Vietnamese court sentenced two activists , who live in Germany, to 17 years each in prison in December 2025 for spreading anti-state material. Prosecutors accused them of using AI to fake voices and images of Vietnamese leaders, illustrating how prosecutions can target political criticism . The governments studied often used national security or anti-state propaganda laws to control what AI models could say. Vertigo3d/Getty Images Foreign rules, domestic impact Some of these government measures only affect people residing in their countries. Other statutes cross borders. The European Union’s AI Act , adopted in 2024, requires any company offering AI tools in Europe, wherever it is based, to mark AI-generated content . Anthropic, for one, applies the marks globally because it has no reliable way to apply them by region . This is an example of the Brussels Effect , in which rules adopted in the EU end up applying elsewhere. European rules also affect what chatbots say about politics. In August 2026, the EU placed ChatGPT under the strictest tier of its Digital Services Act , Europe’s online safety rulebook. OpenAI, creator of ChatGPT, now must assess and reduce the “systemic risks” of its service, including risks to elections, such as the spread of disinformation. And the Dutch Data Protection Authority tested four chatbots before the 2025 national election and found that the political middle ground “virtually disappears” in their voting advice. It urged providers to “prevent their systems from being used for voting advice.” These rules can be used to pressure platforms. In 2024, Thierry Breton, then the EU’s top digital rules enforcer, reminded Elon Musk of his legal obligations before Musk’s live interview with then-presidential candidate Donald Trump on X, warning against the spread of “harmful content.” The United States is no exception Threats to Americans’ access to information do not come only from abroad. In 2025, President Trump issued an executive order on “Preventing Woke AI in the Federal Government.” It requires the AI models the government buys to be “truth-seeking,” ideologically neutral and not favoring ideas such as “diversity, equity and inclusion.” “Truth-seeking” may sound like an objective, neutral term, but it can mean very different things to different people. Take media reporting: The president recently banned three news outlets from the White House for reporting “FICTION and LIES” and dismissed media polls as “fake.” More recently, the Federal Trade Commission has suggested that AI companies that steer answers toward undisclosed ideological or biased objectives might break consumer protection law. A 2025 Pew Research Center survey found that 8 in 10 Americans believe Republican and Democratic voters cannot agree on basic facts . In other words, as our report notes, government mandates to seek truth are often driven by ideological belief systems, particularly on political issues. Meanwhile, dozens of states have passed laws restricting AI-generated political deepfakes. California and Hawaii , for example, are two states that have banned sharing deceptive AI content about candidates in the months around an election. U.S. courts have blocked both of those laws , citing the First Amendment. What does this mean for voters? When you ask your chatbot about the elections, treat the answer as a starting point. Keep in mind that governments, both foreign and domestic, may try to influence the answer. AI responses should not replace your critical thinking at the ballot box. Jordi Calvet-Bademunt is affiliated with The Future of Free Speech, a nonpartisan, nonprofit think tank located at Vanderbilt University. The organization is supported by foundations and individual donors, and it retains full independence and final authority over its work, including research, methodology, analysis, conclusions, and presentation.
