Data is as of Oct. 5, 2026. Note that data lags are most pronounced at the earliest stages of venture activity, with seed funding amounts increasing significantly after the end of a quarter/year. Please note that all funding values are given in U.S. dollars unless otherwise noted. Crunchbase converts foreign currencies to U.S. dollars at the prevailing spot rate from the date funding rounds, acquisitions, IPOs and other financial events are reported. Even if those events were added to Crunchbase long after the event was announced, foreign currency transactions are converted at the historic spot price. items.title: The Googlebook work test: Can an Android laptop get the job done?
items.summary: In a weird way, I’ve been thinking about the idea of a Googlebook for well over a decade now — despite the fact that such a product has only officially existed for a matter of months. I’m relatively unusual in the world of tech journalism, y’see, in that I’ve been both writing about Android and ChromeOS since the platforms’ earliest days and actively using devices from both ends of those ecosystems in my own day-to-day life that entire time. Most tech writers tend to be iPhone owners and Chromebook skeptics who see this part of the digital world from an outside view — once a year or so, when significant new devices come along for assessment — without having the perspective of someone who’s truly immersed in it day in and day out. That distinction is always painfully apparent when you read a review that waxes on endlessly with out-of-touch iPhone comparisons and comments about the limiting nature of Google’s ChromeOS concept — positions that simply aren’t accurate for those of us who live in these ecosystems and embrace the philosophies they offer. This won’t be one of those reviews, and I perhaps more than anyone have been champing at the bit to get my hands on one of Google’s new Android-ChromeOS-combining Googlebooks since the vaguest concept of these devices first appeared on the horizon earlier this year. So keep that in mind when I tell you, coming from the perspective of someone who very much wanted to love this: Using a Googlebook is an extraordinarily strange experience — especially when you’re treating it like a regular laptop, as it’s being positioned by Google, and relying on it to get real work done. But amidst all the oddness, there are some true high points along with plenty of intriguing, if unfinished-feeling, potential. Here’s what it’s been like trying to actually work on a Googlebook — specifically, the Lenovo Googlebook , which sells for $1,149 (and was provided to me as a short-term loaner from Lenovo for the purposes of this article). The Googlebook groundwork First things first, let’s back up a minute and set the stage for what we’re even talking about here. The Googlebook is a new type of laptop created by Google and built by a variety of third-party device-making partners — Acer, Asus, Dell, HP, and Lenovo, to start. It’s meant to represent an evolution of sorts from the Chromebook, the initially simple laptop Google launched in 2012 and slowly morphed from a barebones web portal into an “everything OS” — a system that runs web apps , Android apps , Linux apps , and even sometimes Windows apps , for businesses that have specific needs that can’t be addressed in any other way. But while ChromeOS and Android grew closer and more connected over time, Googlebook OS — the awkwardly clunky name of the operating system at the heart of every Googlebook — sets all of that aside to aim for a fresh start. The software here sports Android at its core alongside a variety of optimizations designed to bring in bits of ChromeOS-like elements and make everything seem more suited to a laptop setting. With that in mind, starting to use a Googlebook is both immediately familiar and vexingly confusing. The interface feels a lot like Android, which is nice, but it also doesn’t quite feel in line with how you expect to work on a desktop computer. It’s a jarring sort of mashup, and it’s tough to wrap your head around to get comfortable working. That’s true for relatively small touches like having the clock in the upper-left corner of the screen instead of in the lower-right corner, where’d you expect it on most non-Apple-made computers. It’s a little thing, but it keeps throwing me whenever I try to glance at the time during the day. items.title: Presentation: Beyond the Prototype: Scaling Framework Agnostic AI Agent Infrastructure with Ray
items.summary: The speakers discuss transitioning AI agents from local FastAPI prototypes to resilient production systems on Kubernetes using Ray. They share operational insights on RayCluster topology, stateful memory handling, auto-scaling on dynamic traffic, and robust control plane designs, while highlighting critical guardrails, multi-region setups, and LLM-as-a-judge evaluation pipelines. By Deepak Mohanakumar Chandramouli, Bhumik Vinodkumar Thakkar

items.title: SpaceX earnings put Elon Musk's Starlink cash cow to the test
items.summary: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk Bloomberg/Getty Images This post originally appeared in the Business Insider Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . The SpaceX business helping to fund Elon Musk's biggest bets is taking a swing of its own just in time for earnings. SpaceX reports earnings after the bell today, and Musk's goal of turning Starlink into a major mobile carrier is expected to be a focus. Taking on Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile is a huge endeavor. And it requires significant investment from a company that already has a long list of expensive bets. As a bit of a refresher, SpaceX is made up of three key parts: connectivity (Starlink), space (reusable rockets like Starship), and AI (Grok, X, and data centers). Among the three, connectivity is the only one generating an operating profit . That makes it incredibly valuable not only as a stand-alone business but as a way to offset the expensive investments made by SpaceX's space and AI segments. Turning Starlink into a mobile carrier complicates that arrangement. To offer service in more densely populated areas, SpaceX will need to launch more satellites into space and establish a ground footprint. How much SpaceX plans to set aside for that buildout and the impact it'll have on the bottom line are key questions analysts will have. Musk is no stranger to talking a big game. He recently said SpaceX could one day be worth more than Earth's economy . He's backed it up by accomplishing things others thought were impossible, like self-landing rockets . Just don't expect him to hit his self-imposed deadlines. (Case in point: Tesla Roadster , which has faced numerous delays and is now targeting production in 2028.) There's less at stake when you're starting from scratch. But with Starlink, it's also about Musk avoiding turning his cash cow into another capital drain. According to another Musk proclamation, a lot of us will have a vested interest in SpaceX's success. Early Monday morning, Musk said he'll give one of his SpaceX shares to every kid in America next year . "This will be the first of many," he added . Details on how that would work weren't clear, but many people immediately thought of the recently launched Trump Accounts . President Donald Trump predicted Musk would donate SpaceX stock to the accounts . And SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell already said she'd gift a share of her company stock to Trump Accounts . If that's how the shares are distributed, it's an example of the complexities the Trump Accounts can pose for some parents. Certain jobs, like those in financial services, have restrictions around the types of investments you can hold due to compliance reasons . Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Why Enterprise AI Prototypes Break in Production
items.summary: A generative AI prototype can answer questions, generate SQL or produce charts. But deploying it in an enterprise is a different challenge. The system must work with live data, enforce access controls, manage unreliable outputs and handle thousands of queries without compromising performance. At Cypher 2026, held in Bengaluru from October 7 to 9, Bhanu Prasad Mahanti and Sri Vallabha Deevi of Tiger Analytics discussed why moving from proof of concept (POC) to production demands a broader engineering effort. From POC to Production Mahanti described three categories of generative AI systems: agentic workflows with deterministic orchestration, single-agent systems that select and use tools, and autonomous multi-agent systems . He says the first two are relatively easier to productionise, while autonomous multi-agent systems are considerably harder. Citing a LangChain developer survey, Mahanti identified output quality as the leading challenge , followed by latency and security concerns. The acceptable level of accuracy also varies by application. Email personalisation may tolerate occasional errors, whereas other enterprise use cases demand much higher reliability. Teams may also need to build their own evaluation datasets. Production introduces further constraints around unbounded inputs and outputs, memory, latency and cost. Mahanti notes that guardrails are essential in production environments because, even if testing appears successful, actual performance remains unpredictable. Working With Live Data Deevi described a deployment for an electronics device manufacturer that collects device-health data in the cloud . The client had a platform where IT administrators could view summaries and run SQL queries, but not all were proficient in SQL. It wanted natural-language interaction with existing data, insights across multiple tables and flexibility as new tables were added. Tiger Analytics integrated an agent-based chatbot into the platform. The system supports multi-turn conversations, generates visualisations and lets administrators investigate data to identify root causes. The engagement has progressed through three versions, with the third being deployed, Deevi says. Tiger Analytics has also developed similar systems for retail and insurance claims. Data freshness posed another challenge. Different tables were updated at different frequencies, with some device data arriving every four hours. A single unified table could not reliably serve every query. Instead, the system identifies user intent, selects relevant tables, generates and executes SQL, and presents insights or visualisations. An earlier iteration achieved 90% accuracy with 10-second latency for complex queries, Deevi says. Privacy Becomes Architecture Production systems cannot always rely on the sanitised data used in prototypes. Personally identifiable information can appear in prompts, databases, charts and vector stores used for retrieval. “You'll encounter them in databases where the device data is stored. You will encounter them in the charts that people will talk about. You may encounter them in the vector stores,” Deevi says. Tiger Analytics replaces PII in prompts with reversible tokens before sending text to a model. Other safeguards include dynamic database masking and sanitising information before embedding it for retrieval. The company also uses small language models to detect attacks and deterministic rules to clean content from external sources. Threats include prompt injection, system prompt extraction, data poisoning and privilege escalation. Outputs from LLM-based tools are treated as untrusted, with human review available for high-impact applications. Access controls must also prevent users from viewing information outside their roles. “The marketing department should not really be seeing sales data. Operations guy should not be seeing HR data,” Deevi says. Role-based permissions and tenant IDs can restrict access. Stricter deployments may use separate databases or vector namespaces, alongside encryption and network isolation. These restrictions cannot depend on prompts alone. “System prompts are always soft instructions. They do not really impose hard restrictions on the data,” Deevi says. When AI Gets It Wrong Connecting a model to enterprise data does not eliminate hallucinations . Errors can occur during query generation, data retrieval or summarisation. “There can be hallucinations at the query level, data level, or the summarisation level,” Deevi says. For customer-facing systems, the consequences can be immediate. For instance, a chatbot offering an incorrect 90% discount could create a business liability. Tiger Analytics restricts query generation to fields in database schemas, attributes sources, enforces output structures and uses fallback mechanisms. Evaluation must continue after deployment. Deevi described using golden datasets, schema validation, small models for toxicity checks and an LLM judge to assess a sample of outputs. Sampling helps contain costs because evaluating every interaction with another LLM can become expensive. Deevi noted that the evaluation model cannot assess every response, raising questions about sampling strategies and the percentage of queries sent to a judge. User behaviour offers another signal. Abandoned conversations, ignored charts and negative feedback can indicate that an answer failed to meet expectations. Production Changes Architecture Moving beyond a prototype also requires rethinking system architecture. Deevi explained that while POCs rely on sequential monolithic designs, production systems must handle thousands of queries per minute. At scale, each request may involve multiple model calls, tools and database operations, creating several potential points of failure. Production systems therefore need asynchronous queues, routing, distributed tracing, failure handling and session-memory management. “So how do you break it into asynchronous queues? How do you gain time? How do you make sure that you handle failure, LLM failures, routing? All these are things that we also need to consider,” Deevi noted. As enterprises embed generative AI into internal and customer-facing systems, the models and frameworks will continue to change. The underlying requirements, however, remain: secure data, reliable outputs, continuous evaluation and resilient architecture. A successful prototype demonstrates what AI can do. Production engineering determines whether it can deliver that value consistently.

items.title: Why AI agents need workflows
items.summary: AIAI’s recent article, "System One models: why fast AI agents act wrong," describes a failure agent builders will recognize. The System One model covers "read agent state well and still pick the wrong action." The fix described is plain: the authors repaired the failures by combining the models' correct answers to factual questions in ordinary code. That points to a rule for an agent that can change something outside its own context window. The model proposes, and a workflow checks the proposal and takes the action. Anthropic's guide to building effective agents defines workflows as "systems where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths." Agents, in its words, are "systems where LLMs dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage." For most business processes I build a hybrid. A fixed workflow runs the steps someone can write down, and an agent handles the single step that calls for judgment, such as parsing a messy email. 7 reasons small language models belong in your 2027 roadmap A frontier model reformatting JSON is expensive overkill. Here are seven sourced reasons small language models earn a place in your 2027 roadmap, and how to start. The agent returns a choice Give the agent the data it needs and a short list of allowed answers. Make it return one of them: a category, a label or a yes or no. The workflow owns the rest: the trigger, the lookups, the write and the log. Take a refund request. The agent reads the customer's email and the order record, then returns "refund," "replacement" or "escalate." If it returns "refund," the workflow pulls the amount from the order record, compares it with the refund ceiling and issues the refund. 💡 An amount above the ceiling goes to a person for approval. The agent does not type an amount or call the payment system. The workflow rejects an answer outside the list and hands the case to a person. In this design a wrong answer surfaces at one known point. Rerun that step on the same input to see why the model chose as it did, and swap in a different model later without touching the rest of the process. Prompt rules did not hold I learned how far prompt rules go on a front-desk phone agent we run for a local service business. It can book new customers and send messages to the front desk. In one week of calls we reviewed in September, the agent told a caller that a message had already been sent. The notification call had been cut off when the caller spoke, and nothing confirmed it went out. The prompt already told it to acknowledge only actual notification results and never to resend an unconfirmed one. The backend was healthy that week, and all of its executions succeeded. The logs showed that the workflow ran. They said nothing about whether the agent chose the right action. We tried the prompt first, and prompt-only versions failed in testing. One model announced actions it had not taken. Another retried an abandoned notification. Switching models did not fix it by itself. How deeptech companies can use AI for smarter R&D bets Raising a big round is the easy part. A deeptech founder explains how project-level budgets, evidence-based milestones, and AI-assisted analysis help every pound of R&D capital buy down real risk. In testing, a procedure around the write held up. The procedure forces the call and reads the receipt. The agent may confirm only when four receipt fields agree: a submitted flag, a submitted status, a message ID from the provider and the matching action. Any other result takes a fixed uncertainty line. The first strict test exposed an edge case: a receipt with the ID absent rather than empty. We corrected the check, and three test cases then passed: a valid receipt, an interrupted submission and a missing ID. In October we tested the same idea on dates and identity. The test bank held ten scenarios drawn from three weeks of the business's real calls, run as text simulations with a simulated caller. On the live version, 17 of 20 runs had no defect. In one simulated booking, the agent invented the caller's details ("Caller Caller," an example.com email address and a birth date of 1990-01-01) and read "next Tuesday" as November 3. The other booking used the business's own email address. A simulated emergency callback carried an invented birth date. 💡 We moved date handling and identity checks into code. The model passes the caller's own words, such as "next Tuesday," to the availability tool, which returns the spoken date, whether the business is closed that day and the earliest open times. A new customer record requires the caller's own name, birth date and email, and the write tool refuses placeholders before it writes anything. The same ten scenarios ran 21 times with no defect. The test is small: text only, simulated callers, two or three runs per scenario and no audio. Four runs on earlier versions of the fix failed. The booking skipped intake, or an emergency callback carried the name "Caller." Two rules, emergency routing and cancellations, still live in the prompt, on top of a business-hours status that code supplies. 8 AI problems leaders face now, and the fix for each Eight problems keep landing on AI leaders' desks, and each has a fix backed by fresh data. Start with the two that cost you most this quarter. Limit what the agent can touch Start the agent with read-only access, and let it write only by asking the workflow, one action per request. OWASP's entry on excessive agency lists excessive functionality, excessive permissions and excessive autonomy as root causes. Its mitigations include implementing authorization in downstream systems rather than relying on the model to decide whether an action is allowed. A refund ceiling, a discount limit and a recipient list are rules the workflow checks. Choosing which customer record to open is an action too. In a customer-history lookup we built for a client, the call platform supplies the caller's phone number to the tool, so the model cannot choose which record opens. If two contacts share the number, the lookup returns no history. Treat anything the agent reads, including emails and web pages, as untrusted input. Hidden instructions in that text can steer a model that holds broad permissions. Write the handoff rules before launch. A person takes over in four cases: the customer asks for one, the agent's answer falls outside the allowed format, the conversation returns to the same question a second time, or the case involves money, legal terms or health information. Test the choice and price the run Test the agent step before it touches a customer. Build a set of a few hundred real past cases, including the ugly ones, and write down the right outcome for each. Score the agent against the set, and score it again after every prompt or model change. Then run in shadow mode: the agent makes real decisions on live traffic, and a reviewer approves each one before the workflow sends or writes anything. Automate the categories where the reviewer's change rate stays low. Price the run the same way. A fixed workflow costs what the automation tool charges. An agent also bills for model usage, which grows with the text it reads, the tools it calls and the loops it runs. A research agent that runs a search, opens five results and tries again can cost a multiple of one classification call. Anthropic's guide says autonomy "means higher costs, and the potential for compounding errors." A bounded choice puts a ceiling on the cost of each run, because the workflow makes one model call where an open agent makes as many as it decides to. 💡 Start with one action your agent can take today: a message sent, a record written or money moved. Put it behind a workflow step with a rule to check and a receipt to read, then run your test cases again. Emre Benian runs an AI consulting & implementation company in Chicago for owner-led businesses.

Test the agent step before it touches a customer. Build a set of a few hundred real past cases, including the ugly ones, and write down the right outcome for each. Score the agent against the set, and score it again after every prompt or model change.

Then run in shadow mode: the agent makes real decisions on live traffic, and a reviewer approves each one before the workflow sends or writes anything. Automate the categories where the reviewer's change rate stays low.

Price the run the same way. A fixed workflow costs what the automation tool charges. An agent also bills for model usage, which grows with the text it reads, the tools it calls and the loops it runs. A research agent that runs a search, opens five results and tries again can cost a multiple of one classification call.

Anthropic's guide says autonomy "means higher costs, and the potential for compounding errors." A bounded choice puts a ceiling on the cost of each run, because the workflow makes one model call where an open agent makes as many as it decides to.

💡
Start with one action your agent can take today: a message sent, a record written or money moved. Put it behind a workflow step with a rule to check and a receipt to read, then run your test cases again.

items.title: Internal docs reveal how Google is shaking up its interview process with AI
items.summary: Google CEO Sundar Pichai. Bloomberg/Getty Images Google is injecting more AI into the interview process. The company has been testing a new format that tests candidates on their AI fluency. The pilot has recently rolled out more broadly across Google, internal docs show. AI is changing how Google employees work — and how Google hires them. The company has been testing several AI-related changes to its hiring process for software engineers, according to documents reviewed by Business Insider. These changes, which Google has been rolling out in phases throughout this year, include allowing the use of AI in coding interviews and permitting interviewers to use Gemini to give candidates feedback. Many engineers are also now expected to show some degree of AI fluency as a bare minimum, the documents show. In May, Business Insider reported that Google was piloting ways to integrate AI into the interview process with a small handful of orgs. This included a new "code comprehension" interview in which candidates are assessed on AI fluency and prompt engineering. Candidates can also use Google's Gemini AI as an assistant during the interview. The new formats have since been rolled out more broadly across the company, according to the internal documents. However, a spokesperson said they were still considered to be in the pilot phase for now. "We're piloting updates to our interview process for software engineers, including evaluating for AI fluency, to be more reflective of how our teams are operating," Brian Ong, vice president of recruiting at Google, told Business Insider in a statement. Like other companies, Google is adapting its hiring process to keep pace with the huge transformation AI is having on software engineering . As developers increasingly rely on AI coding assistants, hiring companies want to know how competent they are with these tools. In April, Google said that three-quarters of new code created at the company is generated by AI and reviewed by humans, a trend that has since continued across the tech industry. Google has said that its employees are increasingly using the company's own Gemini models to both improve other Google products and to build the next generation of Gemini . The documents say that for some roles, including software engineering, AI fluency and AI product integration are now used as measures of a candidate's abilities. A Google spokesperson said that AI fluency is a requirement for all software engineering jobs, while AI product integration is required for most roles outside entry-level positions. Google is also piloting the use of Gemini for interview transcription and note-taking in some job interviews conducted via the company's videoconferencing platform, Google Meet, one document shows. Google wants to speed up the feedback process using AI, too. The same document states that Google is working to enable interviewers to use Gemini to draft role-tailored feedback. As Google builds out this new interview system, employees were told they may be asked to participate in some of the pilots — but were warned against using AI tools to generate their own interviewing "solutions." "Do not use GenAI or LLMs to create your own standalone solutions or agents for hiring or interviewing use cases," the document states, referring to large language models. Have something to share? items.title: I visited a coworking space where startup founders with tiny teams pay $9K a month to be around each other
items.summary: Inside the Series HQ office. Agnes Applegate/BI I visited an NYC coworking space, where startups spend up to $9,000 a month for a spot. There was a private chef, a robot, and a love for in-person work. The overall vibe more closely resembled a college campus than a midtown office. I've been following and interviewing tiny team founders for the last year. As part of my ongoing research, I popped into the Series HQ workspace last month to observe how these founders are running their small teams. As the elevator doors opened on the top floor of the Chelsea office building, the Series HQ office manager, a 21-year-old NYU student, greeted me. Balancing on a skateboard, the tall, young, and very casually dressed Gen Zer fit right in among the cohort of founders he works for. Most of the founders at Series HQ are either straight out of college or under 30, with many of their startups being in early funding rounds. "I do honestly think if you're 35 or 40 thinking about starting a company now, it's probably too late," Nathaneo Johnson, the 22-year-old Series cofounder, said. He recognizes that as a "harsh belief" but believes the average founder age at Series HQ reflects a growing community of young entrepreneurs . Series itself was launched in 2024 by Johnson and Sean Hargrow as an AI social networking app for iMessage. After they both graduated from Yale and raised $5.1 million in pre-seed funding , the pair signed a lease for over 10,000 square feet of office space. They tacked on "HQ" to distinguish between the coworking space and the business. When they moved their company into the building last October, they had roughly eight to 10 people on their team. The pair was preparing for growth, but AI has helped to keep their head count lean, and their tenants operate with similarly sized staff. As I scanned the still mostly empty office, it seemed the tiny teams didn't require much to function. What stood out to me — more than the young, mostly male office demographic — was each company's desire to be around more people, despite operating with as few employees as possible. Business Insider wants to talk to founders of AI-powered companies with fewer than 10 workers, and employees working alongside AI agents, to understand what the "Tiny Teams" era really feels like — the wins, the fears, and the human skills that stand out. Share your story by filling out this quick form . The tiny teams here can spend up to $9,000 a month for shared space I was at the office around 3 p.m. on a Thursday, and about a dozen people from at least five different companies were working, mostly young men and a few young women. The space usually hosts about 15 to 20 startups, and members have 24-hour access when possible, Johnson said. Founder work pods at Series HQ. Agnes Applegate/BI In August, Series HQ charged between $1,250 and $4,000 for workstation pods that hold up to four people. For more privacy, founders can rent the glass pods for $5,000 to $9,000 a month. The more expensive rental options include meals cooked on-site by the private chef they hired last year to curb their takeout costs. The kitchen at Series HQ Agnes Applegate/BI In the massive main room, across from the scattered row of founder workstations, was a basketball hoop and a roughly $21,000, beat-up robot holding a football. The robot propped up in the Series HQ main office room. Agnes Applegate/BI When they talked about their robot, which was slightly broken during my visit, the room lit up. It fascinated me that these founders would incur the expense to work in such a large office. They didn't need all of this physical space — which was, in some ways, obvious, as most of it still looked sparse with objects. The main office room at Series HQ. Agnes Applegate/BI Many of the founders I talked to are around my age — 23 — and graduated from high school during the pandemic, when so much social and work interaction moved online. Now building companies, the appeal of Series HQ seemed to be less about the fancy office with a private rooftop and chef, and mainly about having like-minded coworkers to build in-person with. Long hours mean more time together Zain Ahmad, who was a summer tenant at Series HQ, works at the AI startup Evos. He said Evos found Series from the promotional drone videos that took over their social media platforms all summer. "We figured if they're good enough to end up on both of our For You pages and get this much traction, there's a lot to learn from them and be in that space," he said. Evos rented one of the private glass pods and, during my visit, gave me a tour of their space. Inside the small glass office, we stood in front of their two desks, chatting directly across from a small couch and coffee cart. Evos rented one of the private glass pods at Series HQ. Agnes Applegate/BI In between investor calls, which he said were powered by cups of tea with creatine honey , Ahmad confessed he has taken quite a few naps on that couch. An average workday for them is around 8:30 a.m. to around 10 p.m., sometimes longer. As tenants of Series HQ, they were in the office around six days a week. He explained the concrete environmental benefits for Evos, which creates specialized agentic AI workflows for traditional industries. Ahmad said they were able to meet a new hire because the new hire was another tenant at Series. They even learned about their most-used AI tool at the moment through the Series team: Aside, an AI-powered browser. Turnover was high at the beginning of the experiment, Johnson said. Partly because some of the summer tenants were just in town between school semesters. But those tenants probably didn't feel too far from home, since the vibe here more closely resembled a college campus than a midtown office. Nathaneo Johnson, Series cofounder, on the office's private roof. Agnes Applegate/BI The most important piece of growing an AI startup is still the human network The majority of companies working in the space are AI or technology startups. Logan Milano, the 23-year-old founder of the drink brand Amryth, is one of the few non-tech founders. He recently graduated from college and said he spends well over 40 hours a week here despite living close by. Milano said all he needs to operate his business is "my laptop, a good place to lock in, and being around other people who are building." The main work room at Series HQ. Agnes Applegate/BI This was an overall sentiment I heard. Many of these young founders lived a hop, skip, and a jump away, based on the commutes they told me about. But simply being around others who are building is, in some ways, one of the biggest benefits. "Even if we're getting dinner or going out or something, it's like you're still kind of thinking about work and it's all kind of related," he said about the Series community. Adding that "sourcing opportunities" everywhere likely drew them together and is their biggest similarity. At a time when AI is making it possible to build companies with fewer employees and building solo can be the dream for many, these young founders don't need, or necessarily want to run their business with tons of employees, but they still seem to really want coworkers. When I asked Milano if he's ever spent the night at the Series office, he smiled, looked over at one of the Series team members, and said, "Am I allowed to say?" Do you have a story to share about working on a tiny team? If so, please reach out to the reporter at aapplegate@businessinsider.com . Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: ACM SIGAI Autonomous Agents Award 2027 open for nominations
items.summary: Nominations are solicited for the 2027 ACM SIGAI Autonomous Agents Research Award. This award is made for excellence in research in the area of autonomous agents. It is intended to recognize researchers in autonomous agents whose current work is an important influence on the field. The award is an official ACM award, funded by an endowment created by ACM SIGAI from the proceeds of previous Autonomous Agents conferences. The recipient of the award will receive a monetary prize and a certificate, and will be invited to present a plenary talk at the AAMAS 2027 conference. How to nominate Anyone can make a nomination. Nominations should be made by filling out this google form , and should consist of a short (< 1 page) statement that emphasizes not only the research contributions that the individual has made that merit the award but also how the individual’s current work is an important influence on the field. Note: a candidate can only be considered for the award if they are explicitly nominated. If you believe that someone deserves the award, then nominate them – don’t assume that somebody else will! Nomination link is here . Important Dates 5 December 2026 – Deadline for nominations 1 February 2027 – Announcement of winner 3-7 May 2027 – AAMAS-2027 conference in Hanoi, Vietnam For any questions please contact Sven Koenig (Award Chair) or Louise Dennis (SIGAI Vice Chair).

items.title: I created 'Diary of a Wimpy Kid.'  A good day is when I get my to-do list under 200 items — here's my routine.
items.summary: Simon Simard for BI This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Jeff Kinney, the 55-year-old author of the "Diary of a Wimpy Kid" series, who lives in Plainville, Massachusetts. It has been edited for length and clarity. Every year, when a new "Diary of a Wimpy Kid" book hits the shelves, I'm surprised that kids keep showing up. I started writing the first book in 1998, while working as a computer programmer and game designer. I wanted to be a newspaper cartoonist, but that didn't work out, so I set out to get my cartoons published somehow. I was inspired by my own childhood experiences. The first generation of kids who read my books is now almost 30 years old. It's wild to me that there's a new generation of kids encountering these books and finding them fresh. Business Insider's Power Hours series gives readers an inside look at how powerful people structure their workday. Reach out to editor Lauryn Haas to share your daily routine. As an author, I work within a few different spheres: books, my bookstore, movies, and development. I hop from one area to another. Here's a day in my life. I wake up before 7 a.m. I don't set an alarm, so I wake up at that time naturally every day. I stay in bed for a while because after an ankle injury, I have some PT to do, like ankle stretches, while I'm in bed. I meditate for about 10 minutes, set my intentions for the day, and organize my digital to-do list before I get out of bed. I do two hours of exercise before breakfast Right after I get up, I do about two hours of PT yoga, then weightlifting. I do that before I eat breakfast, which is often eggs and sausages. I'm really committed to my morning physical routine of PT, PT yoga, and exercise. That's now become non-negotiable. I also do some journaling because it orients me toward the day, and it's a calming mechanism. I've just had my most productive year, during which I wrote two books and two screenplays, so I attribute that to my morning routine. It grounds me. I stay organized with a habit tracker I've tried a million different to-do list apps that didn't work, including the pomodoro method and all sorts of others. Then I found a digital habit tracker . Simon Simard for BI I'm pretty diligent about checking off my daily habits. These include eating enough fiber, drinking enough water, waking up by a certain time, meditating, and doing stretches and yoga. My workday starts at around 9:30 a.m. I have about five or six workspaces, and I like to balance between them. One is a really colorful studio with my whole staff on the top floor of my bookstore, which is about three miles away from my home. When I'm not touring or working on a script, I go into the bookstore. The bookstore is always top of mind for me, though the day-to-day operations are handled by the staff. Every so often, I'll get involved because we'll have a big author that comes to the store, and I'll interview them. Another is my guest house, where I sit in the quiet living room. I also have a dark room in the basement where I'll go if I need to shut out everything. The other one is sitting in my car at the cemetery, where it's also very quiet. I can't listen to music because it occupies the same part of my brain needed for creating. Sometimes I write for 8 to 12 hours a day I feel most creative in the early morning hours, but sometimes I might write for eight to 12 hours a day. If I'm illustrating, which I basically do all summer, I'll draw from maybe 9 a.m. until about 9 or 10 p.m. every day for months. When I'm working on a book, I'll write the jokes first, then the manuscript, and finally I'll illustrate. I do all the illustrations myself. I don't usually combine those activities together. I'm always stuck creatively, so I use a system Simon Simard for BI When I get stuck, I use something called systematic creative thinking, which helps me to produce material even if I'm not feeling creative. I start with the components. If I'm writing about an airplane, I'll list the parts of the plane inside and out: the wings, the pilots, the lavatory, everything. Then I'll go through each component with a few different tools like subtraction and multiplication, and that's what gives me my raw material. I'll use my iPad or my computer, or I have this device called a Freewrite, which is a super simple word processor that's not connected to the internet. I don't stop for lunch I only eat two meals a day, so I don't really step away for lunch — this is how I roll. I do have an energy drink, but it's more of a habit than a need. I also don't typically take breaks. I don't have many work boundaries A good day is when I can get my to-do list to under 200 items, which is really hard to do. When I'm not illustrating, my wife might say, "Hey, let's have dinner," and that's my backstop for when I stop working. Work is always on my mind, and I really don't have any boundaries. I don't tell people when I'm going on vacation because they'll reach me anyway, and I don't want to stop them from making progress. I usually make myself available, even if I'm away. Simon Simard for BI My team mostly communicates with me by text Texting is how my team communicates with me. Email has become less useful for me because I get so many emails in a day that I feel like I'm a hockey goalie, and pucks keep whizzing past me. I can really only answer emails right when I get them. Once they get too far down my list, I'll forget about them. I have a lot of challenges with executive functioning . I really struggle with having a lot of choices. I've always answered my own emails, and I don't use AI to write. I'm not often bored; I need stimulation I don't play a lot. I sometimes go to Celtics games, or I'll go out to dinner with my wife, my friends, or my kids. I'm not often bored. In fact, I feel very understimulated. I often feel like I'm not getting enough information, or there's not enough that's happening. For example, if I were to drive through the McDonald's drive-thru and get my food, I'd turn on the radio, tune in to some news program, and eat while reading the news on my phone. Chicken McNuggets with sweet and sour sauce are probably my guilty pleasure. As far as watching TV goes, Survivor is always a staple in our house. I go to sleep around 9:45 p.m. These days I go to bed pretty early. I get in bed around 9:45 p.m., put in an earbud, and fall asleep with the news in my ear. Simon Simard for BI

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Jeff Kinney, the 55-year-old author of the "Diary of a Wimpy Kid" series, who lives in Plainville, Massachusetts. It has been edited for length and clarity.

Every year, when a new "Diary of a Wimpy Kid" book hits the shelves, I'm surprised that kids keep showing up.

I started writing the first book in 1998, while working as a computer programmer and game designer. I wanted to be a newspaper cartoonist, but that didn't work out, so I set out to get my cartoons published somehow. I was inspired by my own childhood experiences.

The first generation of kids who read my books is now almost 30 years old. It's wild to me that there's a new generation of kids encountering these books and finding them fresh.

Business Insider's Power Hours series gives readers an inside look at how powerful people structure their workday. Reach out to editor Lauryn Haas to share your daily routine.

As an author, I work within a few different spheres: books, my bookstore, movies, and development. I hop from one area to another.

Here's a day in my life.

I wake up before 7 a.m.

I don't set an alarm, so I wake up at that time naturally every day. I stay in bed for a while because after an ankle injury, I have some PT to do, like ankle stretches, while I'm in bed.

I meditate for about 10 minutes, set my intentions for the day, and organize my digital to-do list before I get out of bed.

I do two hours of exercise before breakfast

Right after I get up, I do about two hours of PT yoga, then weightlifting. I do that before I eat breakfast, which is often eggs and sausages.

I'm really committed to my morning physical routine of PT, PT yoga, and exercise. That's now become non-negotiable. I also do some journaling because it orients me toward the day, and it's a calming mechanism.

I've just had my most productive year, during which I wrote two books and two screenplays, so I attribute that to my morning routine. It grounds me.

I stay organized with a habit tracker

I've tried a million different to-do list apps that didn't work, including the pomodoro method and all sorts of others. Then I found a digital habit tracker.

Simon Simard for BI

I'm pretty diligent about checking off my daily habits. These include eating enough fiber, drinking enough water, waking up by a certain time, meditating, and doing stretches and yoga.

My workday starts at around 9:30 a.m.

I have about five or six workspaces, and I like to balance between them. One is a really colorful studio with my whole staff on the top floor of my bookstore, which is about three miles away from my home. When I'm not touring or working on a script, I go into the bookstore.

The bookstore is always top of mind for me, though the day-to-day operations are handled by the staff. Every so often, I'll get involved because we'll have a big author that comes to the store, and I'll interview them.

Another is my guest house, where I sit in the quiet living room. I also have a dark room in the basement where I'll go if I need to shut out everything. The other one is sitting in my car at the cemetery, where it's also very quiet. I can't listen to music because it occupies the same part of my brain needed for creating.

Sometimes I write for 8 to 12 hours a day

I feel most creative in the early morning hours, but sometimes I might write for eight to 12 hours a day.

If I'm illustrating, which I basically do all summer, I'll draw from maybe 9 a.m. until about 9 or 10 p.m. every day for months.

When I'm working on a book, I'll write the jokes first, then the manuscript, and finally I'll illustrate. I do all the illustrations myself. I don't usually combine those activities together.

I'm always stuck creatively, so I use a system

Simon Simard for BI

When I get stuck, I use something called systematic creative thinking, which helps me to produce material even if I'm not feeling creative.

I start with the components. If I'm writing about an airplane, I'll list the parts of the plane inside and out: the wings, the pilots, the lavatory, everything. Then I'll go through each component with a few different tools like subtraction and multiplication, and that's what gives me my raw material.

I'll use my iPad or my computer, or I have this device called a Freewrite, which is a super simple word processor that's not connected to the internet.

I don't stop for lunch

I only eat two meals a day, so I don't really step away for lunch — this is how I roll.

I do have an energy drink, but it's more of a habit than a need. I also don't typically take breaks.

I don't have many work boundaries

A good day is when I can get my to-do list to under 200 items, which is really hard to do. When I'm not illustrating, my wife might say, "Hey, let's have dinner," and that's my backstop for when I stop working.

Work is always on my mind, and I really don't have any boundaries. I don't tell people when I'm going on vacation because they'll reach me anyway, and I don't want to stop them from making progress. I usually make myself available, even if I'm away.

Simon Simard for BI

My team mostly communicates with me by text

Texting is how my team communicates with me. Email has become less useful for me because I get so many emails in a day that I feel like I'm a hockey goalie, and pucks keep whizzing past me.

I can really only answer emails right when I get them. Once they get too far down my list, I'll forget about them. I have a lot of challenges with executive functioning. I really struggle with having a lot of choices.

I've always answered my own emails, and I don't use AI to write.

I'm not often bored; I need stimulation

I don't play a lot. I sometimes go to Celtics games, or I'll go out to dinner with my wife, my friends, or my kids. I'm not often bored.

In fact, I feel very understimulated. I often feel like I'm not getting enough information, or there's not enough that's happening. For example, if I were to drive through the McDonald's drive-thru and get my food, I'd turn on the radio, tune in to some news program, and eat while reading the news on my phone.

Chicken McNuggets with sweet and sour sauce are probably my guilty pleasure. As far as watching TV goes, Survivor is always a staple in our house.

I go to sleep around 9:45 p.m.

These days I go to bed pretty early. I get in bed around 9:45 p.m., put in an earbud, and fall asleep with the news in my ear.

Good morning, {{ first_name | AI enthusiasts }}, and welcome to our 5,481 new readers. Anthropic has spent 2026 warning that AI is moving faster than anyone is ready for. Now one of its co-founders says the moment has a name.

Jack Clark just said that the singularity, when AI-driven progress starts outrunning humanity’s ability to keep up, is officially underway. What comes with it? A possible $44T U.S. economy, serious job disruption, and a short window to decide if AI needs an intelligence cap.

In today’s AI rundown:

  • Anthropic co-founder says the singularity is underway

  • One hacker’s AI agents break into 100+ companies

  • Try ChatGPT’s new voices with GPT-Live-1.1

  • Inception’s Mercury 3 speeds past rivals

LATEST DEVELOPMENTS

ANTHROPIC🌌 Anthropic co-founder says the singularity is underway

Image source: IMF

The Rundown: Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark just told economists and policymakers at the IMF and World Bank’s annual meetings that the singularity, the point where AI speeds up discovery faster than humans can follow, has “now begun.”

The details:

  • Clark pointed to AI’s scores on Humanity’s Last Exam (expert-level questions) going from 8% to 67.7% since 2025, and FrontierMath improving from 2% to 94%.

  • One Anthropic model has U.S. GDP at $44T by 2030 if AI spreads fast, which Clark admitted sounds outlandish but also predicts “very disruptive” job impacts.

  • The world’s 10M scientists may soon direct “a billion virtual scientists,” Clark said while urging nations to build labs and robots before they run short.

  • He also said CEO Dario Amodei has floated limits on AI’s “ceiling of intelligence,” adding that he believes there is only “a small number of years” to act.

Why it matters: With the number of AI math and science breakthroughs in the last few months alone, 2026 has handed Clark plenty of evidence. Singularity talk used to live strictly in science fiction, and now one of the people building it is saying it out loud to the folks who run the global economy.

TOGETHER WITH ATLASSIAN📈 AI adoption has outpaced strategy

The Rundown: Atlassian’s 2026 State of the Developer Experience report, based on global research with 1,560 respondents including devs and engineering leaders, maps out clear paths for leaders to help their teams manage the speed vs. friction tension happening right now.

In the report, you’ll explore how:

  • Devs are managing more output

  • An AI-native SDLC fixes bottlenecks

  • Only 23% of leaders have an AI strategy

Download the full State of DevEx 2026 Report today.

AI & SECURITY🔓 One hacker’s AI agents break into 100+ companies

Image source: NorForge

The Rundown: Security firm NorForge revealed that a Chinese-speaking hacker let AI agents do nearly all the work to successfully break into the websites of 100+ companies, with Reuters identifying victims like Cummins, Deere, and SharkNinja in the hack.

The details:

  • NorForge watched the attacks after finding 20+ hacker control panels for Cairn, an open-source tool for AI agents, left online with no password.

  • The hacker fed the agents a pre-screened list of busy online stores and orders under 100 Chinese characters, then sent them after over 1,200 sites.

  • NorForge puts AI costs near $50 per successful break-in, with a typical one taking nearly a day using Claude Code and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash.

  • It’s unclear if any data was taken, with SharkNinja calling the threat contained, Deere citing “remediation actions,” and Cummins “investigating.”

Why it matters: A month ago, we were writing about “three guys with Claude” breaking into OpenAI, and now it’s one hacker with an estimated $5K in tokens and a short note to their agents hitting 100+ companies. AI’s offensive cyber capabilities are outpacing the defensive ones, and a lot of companies are about to be caught in the crosshairs.

AI TRAINING🎙️ Try ChatGPT’s new voices with GPT-Live-1.1

The Rundown: In this guide, you’ll try ChatGPT’s new voices, compare them with the same short passage, and check whether a spoken correction reaches the final answer.

Step-by-step:

  1. Open ChatGPT’s Voice settings and choose Live where available. Pick a voice and start a new chat with the guide’s fictional workshop notice

  2. Ask it to read the notice, then try the same words with another voice. Keep the language and instructions fixed so the comparison stays useful

  3. Try a regional voice in a language you know well. Listen for clear names, dates, and numbers, and ask for a slower repeat when needed

  4. Interrupt the notice with a new date and headcount. Check that those details change while the time and budget stay fixed

  5. Ask Voice to search OpenAI’s release notes. Open its source link and check the answer rather than trusting the spoken search cue alone

Pro tip: A new voice and a new model are different changes. Comparing Bubbie with your usual voice does not prove a gain over GPT-Live-1. Pro members get the practice prompts and listening checklist.

PRESENTED BY OPTIMIZELY🤖 Find high-value AI use cases

The Rundown: Most AI planning starts with the wrong question. Instead of asking “What should AI do?”, ask “Where does the work break?” Optimizely’s template helps you identify high-value AI use cases by finding the manual work slowing you down.

This template gives you:

  • A personalized AI use case in minutes

  • The same process that turned a 2-3 hour GA4 reporting task into a 5-minute one

  • A use case mapped to how your team actually works, not a generic list of ideas

Download the template.

INCEPTION⚡️ Inception’s Mercury 3 speeds past rivals

Image source: Inception

The Rundown: AI startup Inception just launched Mercury 3, a “diffusion” language model it says matches or beats OpenAI’s GPT-6 Luna and Anthropic’s Claude Haiku 5.5 by its own numbers at 4-8x their speed.

The details:

  • Language models write one at a time, while diffusion models draft many words at once and refine them, leading to outputs of 1,000+ tokens a second.

  • Inception pitches it as useful for apps where any lag shows, with early users running live tutors, voice customer support, and web-browsing agents on it.

  • Mercury 3 is priced at $0.20/$0.70 per million tokens, with the company saying the model is 40x the size of Mercury 1 while still maintaining the same speeds.

  • Co-founder Stefano Ermon said scaling diffusion is limited by “compute and data, not fundamental algorithmic barriers,” and a successor is already in training.

Why it matters: Mercury 3 won’t replace the frontier AI people use for hard reasoning, and Inception isn’t pretending it will. But with OpenAI’s Cerebras partnership and a new Ultrafast tier that pushes GPT-6 Astra as high as 300 tokens/s, speed is clearly the next battleground — and Inception is betting an alternative model type can win it.

QUICK HITS

COMMUNITY AI WORKFLOW OF THE DAY

▸ A reader built a voice-enabled task management system with Claude

Today’s workflow comes from an anonymous Rundown reader:

I’m 78, and I run a homestead, a home server, and a senior center, with dozens of jobs underway at once. Most jobs get done a piece at a time, while to-do apps only track whether something is “done” or “not done.”

So I built Taskmaster: a plain-text ledger inside a Claude Project. I first tried building a large custom app, then scrapped it. One of my own rules is, “Build the ugly version first.”

In the field, I speak notes into the Claude app on my phone. Claude saves my exact words, updates each job’s progress, and asks me one question at a time when something is unclear. When I ask, “What’s next?” it considers deadlines, weather, and my energy level, then gives me one to three things to do.

Anything tied to a specific time goes on my Google Calendar. Home Assistant then reads the reminder aloud through my hearing aids. Today, it checked the forecast and scheduled my paint job for the one day this week that stays above 50°F overnight. The machine carries the complexity, so I don’t have to.

  • 📽️ FLUX 3 Max - Black Forest Labs’ fast text-to-video AI with voices and sound

  • 💨 Mercury 3 - Inception’s speed-focused diffusion AI rivaling GPT-6 Luna

  • 🔎 Exa 3.0 - Exa’s SOTA web search for AI agents

Elon Musk said he will give a SpaceX share to “every kid in America” starting next year via Trump Accounts, responding to the news of Anthropic’s Public Benefit Fund.

The U.S. Dept. of Homeland Security formally banned DeepSeek from civilian agency systems, giving departments 60 days to request exceptions and extending the ban to third-party tools built on the Chinese lab’s models.

Black Forest Labs released FLUX 3 Max, a sped-up FLUX 3 built with fal that it says matches Seedance 2.5 on quality at 22x the speed, rendering 10s clips in 12 seconds.

Chinese AI lab MiniMax launched M3.1 Flash, a new model previously tested as “Space Bunny”, scoring well on coding and computer use at an extremely low price.

items.title: A visit to Samsung’s massive new semiconductor hub
items.summary: _____________ THE PLACE Pyeongtaek, South Korea Generative AI models run on powerful chips known as GPUs, which depend on stacks of specialized memory chips packaged with the processor. To meet growing demand for memory, Samsung is building a massive new semiconductor manufacturing complex in Pyeongtaek, South Korea. Three fabs already operate around the clock, and a fourth is coming online. Construction of a fifth was halted during a drop in demand for memory chips in 2024 but restarted when the AI boom sent demand soaring. It’s just before noon on a Monday, and construction workers are pouring out of Samsung’s fabs in Pyeongtaek, a farming city south of Seoul where rice paddies abut a sprawling chipmaking complex. Thousands of workers, dressed head to toe in black with sky-blue vests, take off helmets bearing their names and fab numbers. They walk to lunch, sweaty and flushed, in chunky sneakers capped with yellow rubber toe guards. Some hop on scooters or motorcycles to get around the campus, which covers an area about the size of New York City’s Central Park. They’ll dine at buffets, diners, and beef stew joints, walking past banners advertising short-term leases for studio apartments. Some stop by real estate offices to inquire, stepping up to the same counters where Samsung’s salaried engineers buy new homes . In front of the fourth fab, I meet Choi Hye-rin, a 35-year-old safety officer, as she wipes her forehead with a handkerchief. At dawn, she boarded one of the shuttle buses that ferry workers in from Songtan, an older, scrappier district. She oversees the safety of a crew responsible for building cable ducts. She writes reports, inspects equipment, and checks the chemicals the workers handle. She’s one of hundreds of women working on site, many employed as spotters who walk ahead of heavy equipment. Safety is a big deal here. After lunch, construction picks right back up. Excavators move past rust-red steel structures rising high under tower cranes. Banners that hang from the highest girders read, “Even if the work runs late, don’t rush.” A giant LED scoreboard announces the winners of a contest for writing a poem about safety. Helmets stickered with a pledge, “I will not work if it’s not safe,” perch atop lockers. The finished fabs glisten from across the street. Along with the cautionary messages, there’s a sense of urgency in the air. Samsung predicts that demand for memory chips will continue to surge through 2028. And for years the company watched its domestic rival SK Hynix pull ahead in the global market for the high-bandwidth models that power Nvidia’s AI accelerators. (Meanwhile, the Taiwanese chipmaker TSMC has dominated the foundry business, manufacturing chips that other companies design.) The Pyeongtaek build-out is Samsung’s attempt to reclaim its lead on memory chips. Although the heat can be brutal and the work zones are crowded, Hye-rin has no plans to leave. “The rate here is higher than other construction sites, and the work is relatively easy,” she says. She gets paid 140,000 won ($97) a day and expects the boom to keep her busy for some time: “You just keep coming back.”

Helmets stickered with a pledge, “I will not work if it’s not safe,” perch atop lockers. The finished fabs glisten from across the street. 

Along with the cautionary messages, there’s a sense of urgency in the air. Samsung predicts that demand for memory chips will continue to surge through 2028. And for years the company watched its domestic rival SK Hynix pull ahead in the global market for the high-bandwidth models that power Nvidia’s AI accelerators. (Meanwhile, the Taiwanese chipmaker TSMC has dominated the foundry business, manufacturing chips that other companies design.) The Pyeongtaek build-out is Samsung’s attempt to reclaim its lead on memory chips. 

Although the heat can be brutal and the work zones are crowded, Hye-rin has no plans to leave. “The rate here is higher than other construction sites, and the work is relatively easy,” she says. She gets paid 140,000 won ($97) a day and expects the boom to keep her busy for some time: “You just keep coming back.”

items.title: These startups hope “blended” food will cut our appetite for red meat
items.summary: In the fall of 2025, Jeff Dodge set up a six-foot folding table in the cafeteria of Cane Bay High School in Summerville, South Carolina, to conduct a taste test. When the first rush of about 150 hungry students hit, he was waiting with slow cookers filled with steaming marinara sauce and meatballs. Kids love a taste test, but they’re also discerning, and Dodge wasn’t sure what they would make of his product, a blend featuring both meat and mushrooms. As students swarmed the table and tapped out their opinions on an iPad or scanned a QR code to use their phones, Dodge asked those who lingered to guess what kind of vegetable might have been mixed into the meat. Few of them could—the meatballs had tasted like moist, flavorful beef. The school enrolls a few thousand students, and Dodge estimates that the majority of them came by. In the end, the survey showed that 92% of those who tried the meatballs wanted them on the menu; they easily cleared the bar to be added for the 2026–2027 school year. Comments described their flavor as “bussin’.” Through his consulting company, K–12 Food Solutions, Dodge was testing a new product called 50/Cut from the company Joyn. The proprietary blend of seemingly simple ingredients—available as meatballs, burgers, and ground meat—could help solve one of the most intractable challenges of the climate crisis, at least on the individual level: getting people to eat less meat, particularly beef. Livestock production accounts for somewhere between 10% and 20% of all greenhouse-gas emissions related to human activity, and nearly two-thirds of that comes from ruminants like cows raised for meat and dairy products. Beef herds create four times the emissions of dairy herds per kilo of food produced. And for US households, food makes up as much as 30% of emissions . Unlike other polluting sectors, such as electricity and transportation, cattle farming has little potential for a big fix. Ruminants produce about 30% of the methane associated with human activity, and this gas has 28 times more global-­warming potential than carbon dioxide. What’s more, it would be virtually impossible to raise them in a perfectly climate-­neutral manner. “We don’t have a technical solution to change the stomach of a ruminant,” says Fredrik Hedenus, a professor in sustainability and systems analysis at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden. Technologies to dampen the impact of their burps have been in the works for a while but have yet to scale. They also fix only part of the problem with red meat: Cows need a lot of land for pasture and for feed, which has made livestock a top driver of deforestation in the Amazon and elsewhere around the world. Even if the world stopped burning all fossil fuels tomorrow, emissions from agriculture would push the planet past 2 °C over preindustrial temperatures by 2070, Hedenus says. According to his research, more efficient livestock farming methods would still leave agriculture eating up over half of humanity’s carbon budget by that time. Only with the addition of dietary changes does his model show a winning scenario. He’s far from alone in his conclusions: A 2024 survey of more than 200 climate scientists, conducted at Harvard, found that the vast majority believe reducing emissions from livestock is important to meeting climate goals. People have to eat less beef. “Essentially, you need a culture shift,” Hedenus says. Yet the culture has proved intractable. Not only do people like the taste of meat, but across most of the world, meat-eating tends to be associated with status. As societies have grown wealthier, it has increased. A United Nations report showed that global meat production quadrupled between 1961 and 2022 , while vegetarianism has held steady at about 4% of the population in the US since 1999. What could move the needle is a carbon-light and delicious meat replacement. But from a food-tech standpoint, all we have to show is a menu of mostly failed solutions. Lab-grown meat has generated endless headlines since the 2000s but has yet to become commercially available (and affordable) at scale. And while breakthroughs in taste and texture inched plant-based meats from companies like Impossible Foods and Beyond Meat toward mass adoption, the hype—and the appetite—has somewhat fizzled. So instead of asking people to change their preferences, startups like Joyn are trying a different tack. They’re creating what are broadly referred to as blended meat products, which combine plant proteins with the real deal. The logic: The best meat replacement is … better meat. Paul Shapiro, cofounder of the startup BMC Ingredients, which markets a plant protein related to mushrooms, says the math is easy to understand: If we imagine that Impossible Whoppers at Burger King account for about 2% of sales, that’s only a 2% reduction in meat. But if a conventional Whopper were 20% plants, that would be a 20% cut right off the bat. Those aren’t quite the numbers climate models are calling for, but some estimates say they could lead to outsized gains relative to the status quo: A 2022 study in Nature found that replacing 20% of beef globally could halve the annual rate of deforestation. And unlike the other solutions tried thus far, this particular Hail Mary is one a lot of omnivores seem open to giving a try. The idea of blending meat and vegetables together is, of course, nothing new. Food cultures from around the world boast an array of dishes that combine small amounts of meat with plants. Today, home cooks still add veggies and legumes to dishes to stretch tight grocery budgets or to sneak extra greenery into their children’s supper. But in the mid to late 2010s, however, the focus was largely on companies that appeared to have cracked the code for ditching meat entirely. When Impossible debuted its namesake burger in 2016, it impressed with an ingredient called heme, an iron-rich molecule in the protein soy leghemoglobin that allowed all-plant burgers to “bleed” like beef. Impossible and its biggest competitor, Beyond, swaggered through the media and the markets. In 2019, Impossible’s founder told the New Yorker he intended to wipe out all animal agriculture by 2035. Beyond’s 2019 IPO was the most successful since the 2008 financial crisis. A flood of imitators followed. But within a few years, tastes shifted. In 2023, Impossible employees’ stock values tumbled 89% from a 2021 high. That same year, Beyond laid off 20% of its staff, and a bruising Businessweek feature labeled the entire sector a fad . Sales have been slipping for years, with a 10% year-over-year drop in 2025 , according to the Good Food Institute, a think tank focused on alternative proteins. Any quest to wipe out animal agriculture could now seem farcical. In 2025, Americans downed $45 billion worth of beef. Several factors were likely at play. Megan Krogius, a spokesperson for Impossible Foods, says the dip is a “correction not a crisis” after “an outsized pop in demand” between 2020 and 2022. She also says that a flurry of plant-based products muddied the category’s reputation. Indeed, some disruptors (and their imitators) have struggled to compete on the sensory level. Nectar, an organization that conducts research on meat alternatives, has found that taste and texture are among the major factors that keep people from adopting plant-based meats. “Our consumers identify products as having bad aftertaste and off flavors five to six times more than in animal counterparts,” says Caroline Cotto, the group’s director. At the same time, discourse around processed foods tarnished plant-based meat’s halo. In 2019, the Center for Consumer Freedom, a since-dissolved lobbying group backed by the meat industry, launched an ad campaign against plant-based alternatives, demonizing them as “ultra-­processed imitations.” While Impossible’s Krogius warns against conflating processed food with junk food (she points, for example, to a study in The Lancet finding mock meat to be nutritionally preferable to red meat), some of the bad press stuck. Now, the term “ultra-­processed” has become something of a political cudgel—one wielded by the meat-loving MAHA movement and the US secretary of health and human services, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. In 2025, he flipped the food pyramid and stacked a steak on top . Any quest to wipe out animal agriculture could now seem farcical. In 2025, Americans downed $45 billion worth of beef , and consumption rose by 4.3% over the previous year, according to an industry report. Rising prices could be slowing this down a bit, but cost can dampen only so much demand. Blended meat, which has meat’s own juiciness and texture, rose alongside the plant-based superstars, but it did not get New Yorker profiles or headlining IPOs. At the height of mock-meat hype, companies like Tyson and Perdue launched blended products, and firms working on lab-grown meat explored cutting their products with plants . The big advantage of blended meat is that large numbers of consumers—what some call “ flexitarians ”—are curious about it, and when they try it, they like it. A blind taste test co-funded by the USDA in 2022 showed that diners preferred blended burgers to fully plant-based ones . And a report from the major food processor ADM found that large proportions of every generation of Americans were interested in trying blended meats, including 75% of millennials . “This is a solution that we can do today, that consumers will accept today,” says Tim Dale, a director at Food Systems Innovations, the nonprofit group that oversees Nectar. Joyn’s 50/Cut meat blends beef with roasted mushrooms and cultivated mycelium— the rootlike threads extending from fungi. COURTESY OF JOYN At this point, even Impossible has acknowledged the potential. In a wide-ranging interview with the Wall Street Journal in 2025, the company’s former CEO Peter McGuinness admitted the brand’s struggle to win over consumers, and suggested a hybrid burger could bridge the divide. Plenty of newcomers are entering the fray. “Shiitake-infused beef burgers” from Australia-based Fable Foods are in restaurants and moving “incredibly well” at the high-end grocery store Central Market in Austin, Texas, says CEO Michael Fox. The Both Burger from Los Angeles–based 50/50 Foods is available in a smattering of California stores and eateries. And Spare Food in New York signed a deal with Premier, one of the nation’s biggest spenders in the health-care sector, for its blend of surplus produce and ground beef. One major insight for all these upstarts is that consumers react best when marketing focuses on pleasure, not environmental virtues or health benefits. Though many companies actually create a burger or meatball with a better nutritional profile (fiber!) and fewer of meat’s downsides, like saturated fat, that doesn’t get people to buy it. They like that it tastes good. Beef and mushrooms, for example, contain complementary flavor compounds, including the glutamates that yield deep umami, which is why they’re so often paired in dishes like beef Wellington and stroganoff. Food-production companies are a big target. BMC Ingredients, which collaborated with Perdue on a line of blended nuggets, markets a plant-based protein that can be mixed with meat to up its nutrition and flavor. BMC grows mycelium—the root-like structures of fungi. It underpins popular meat alternatives like Quorn and also features alongside mushrooms in Joyn’s 50/Cut. Shapiro likens his factory to a brewery, but instead of yeast fermenting barley, a fungus called Neurospora crassa digests starch to produce a protein with a dense network of fibers that makes for a meat-like chew. “We grow four hours before we get a harvest,” Shapiro says. “It’s among the most efficient ways to produce protein on Earth.” Joyn also sees its path forward outside the grocery store. Food eaten away from home accounts for more than half of what US consumers spend on grub, according to the USDA . Padraic Doherty, who joined Joyn from the meat distributor D’Artagnan and holds the title of chief growth officer, says its main areas of focus are K–12 and college cafeterias and other major food service providers, like stadiums. These organizations, he says, often have sustainability goals and also are pressured to find both nutritious and affordable options. The 50/Cut Joyn sells to cafeterias is between 5% and 15% cheaper than beef. But can cafeteria mushroom burgers prompt a larger cultural shift? The folks touting the idea of going halfway see it as a bridge. BMC’s Shapiro thinks the movement toward meat-light eating reflects the reality of how these changes happen. Nectar’s Cotto compares blended meat to a hybrid car. “Moving people toward blended products [is] a way to drive demand for some of the fully plant-based ingredients that don’t scale right now to bring the price down,” she says. “So it’s both a short- and a long-term approach.” Not everyone is so sure market forces will be enough, though. Nil Zacharias, a longtime entrepreneur in food sustainability who offers plant-based options to New York City delis through his company Plantega, isn’t sold on the notion. “Too many people in the space believe that as long as we create meat that is not from an animal but tastes like meat and costs the same, people will eat it,” he says. “I think the plant-based backlash to ultraprocessed foods shows you that’s not necessarily how things are going to go.” He believes blended meat’s main impact will be on institutional dining, in places like schools and health-care facilities. “People in this space believe that as long as we create meat that is not from an animal but tastes like meat, people will eat it.” Nil Zacharias, founder and CEO, Plantega Meat hybrids could, however, taste just familiar enough to open consumers’ minds to alternatives. Some research has found that thinking about mock meats prompts people to reconsider the whole system. In the 2010s, Clemens Driessen, a cultural geographer who teaches at Wageningen University & Research in the Netherlands, worked on a project that asked people in pubs, supermarkets, and other public spaces what they thought of lab-grown meat. “There’s a first response, which is ‘Oh, that sounds horrible,’” Driessen says. Then people tended to reflect that the meat they consume is also heavily industrialized. “A whole train of thought emerges out of proposing something very new,” he says. The Both Burger, made from beef and a mix of veggies, is available at a handful of restaurants and specialty retailers. It’s even been on the menu at Disneyland as the Meteorite Medley Burger. COURTESY OF 50/50 FOODS If the category succeeds, climate advocates will need to make peace with imperfection. A life-cycle analy­sis Joyn commissioned on the 50/Cut burger confirms that the product has half the greenhouse-gas footprint of a beef patty, which—if you go by company claims—means it has about five times the impact of a burger from Impossible or Beyond. Hedenus, the climate scientist, says that even if blended products don’t reduce impact as much as plant-based ones, he’s all for trying any solution that works. “It is very difficult to change how we eat, so I think most good suggestions should be explored,” he says. Meanwhile, the products are finding their way to more plates. They’re in cafeterias, high-end grocery stores, and small burger chains . They’re in the catalogues of major distributors like Sysco. The Both Burger has even been at Disneyland . The 50/Cut meatball is on the menu this school year in seven states. At Cane Bay High it’ll take the form of a sub. The school is buying 200 cases at a time, with 150 meatballs in a case. Jason Ciaccia, the systems specialist for child nutrition in the school district, says he won’t be using the word “mushroom” to describe it. “If they hear ‘mushroom,’ they’re going to skip over it,” he says. He is, however, considering his branding. He’s asked AI to help him come up with something fun. He thinks “Marvelous Meatball Sub” has a nice ring. Meghan McCarron is a food and culture journalist based in Los Angeles.
