items.title: Ganiga secures €2.5M to expand its AI-powered food waste technology
items.summary: Italian deeptech startup Ganiga has raised €1.5 million in an equity funding round to further develop its AI-powered waste management technology and support commercial expansion. The round was led by Italian contract catering company Vivenda, with participation from London-based NextSTEP and three angel investors. Together with €1 million secured through Smart&Start Italia, an incentive programme managed by Invitalia, Ganiga's total funding has reached €2.5 million. Founded in the province of Pisa by Nicolas Zeoli , Ganiga develops technologies combining artificial intelligence, computer vision and robotics to improve waste management and reduce food waste. The company initially focused on robotic waste sorting, developing devices that identify and separate different types of waste. It has sold more than 300 devices for use in airports, shopping centres and large businesses across Italy, Japan, Australia and other European countries. Building on data collected through these deployments, Ganiga expanded into food waste management with HooolyFood, an AI-powered system designed to help catering operators monitor and reduce waste. Using cameras installed above waste containers, the system identifies discarded food without requiring weighing and provides data to help operators identify inefficiencies, improve purchasing and menu planning, and manage costs. Developed in less than a year, the technology is already deployed in operations serving more than 30,000 meals daily. The company's proprietary data platform brings information from its devices into a single dashboard to analyse waste patterns, estimate costs and monitor container fill levels. Ganiga is also extending its technology to automate ingredient ordering and menu planning, while developing sensors for existing containers to monitor municipal and other waste streams. The development comes as the European Union introduces binding targets to reduce food waste by 2030. According to Eurostat, the EU generated approximately 58 million tonnes of food waste in 2023, highlighting the need for more efficient waste management across industries, including food services. Nicolas Zeoli, founder and CEO of Ganiga, said the investment will help scale technology already deployed in commercial settings. He added: For a canteen, knowing which dishes are being wasted and why provides actionable data to inform purchasing, menu planning and service delivery. The new EU directive makes food waste reduction a binding target, and you cannot reduce what you do not measure. With the new funding, Ganiga plans to expand its technical and commercial teams, further develop HooolyFood and its data platform, and increase recurring revenue. The company will initially focus on expanding within contract catering alongside Vivenda, before targeting event catering, hotels and other foodservice settings.

items.title: Exa 3.0 Search API Tops Perplexity, Brave and Parallel on 8 Benchmarks
items.summary: Exa has released Exa 3.0 , an upgrade to its web search API for AI agents. The Exa 3.0 search API ships a larger embedding model and a cheaper search type, Exa Lite. Dynamic Highlights is now generally available. Exa claims that it leads Perplexity, Brave and Parallel on 8 benchmarks. Those benchmarks were run by Exa, so you can treat them as self-reported. For developers, the practical change is cost: Lite costs $4 per 1,000 requests . TL;DR Size: Exa tracks over 2 trillion URLs and serves 100 billion pages. Embedding model size: Not disclosed. Runs on: Hosted API only. Exa lists configurable search latency of 450ms to 1s . No self-hosted option. Performance: Exa 3.0 Auto ranks first on all 8 Exa-run benchmarks against Perplexity, Brave and Parallel. Best: 91.8% on BrowseComp, plus the widest lead on ATLAS (42.0% vs 37.2% for Perplexity). Worst: 42.0% on ATLAS is its lowest percentage score. Its BrowseComp lead over Perplexity is only 0.3 points. What is Exa 3.0? Exa 3.0 is a search API release from Exa Labs that upgrades retrieval quality across every search type. It is available through the API. Exa runs its own crawler and an independent index. It is not a wrapper on Google or Bing results. How does Exa 3.0 improve retrieval? Exa attributes the gains to 3 changes in its retrieval stack: A larger embedding model : Exa trained it with more compute and data than any earlier model. Parameter count is not disclosed. Dynamic Highlights, now generally available : The model selects tokens across all results, not page by page. It gives more tokens to better pages and drops repeated information. Billions of new documents : New coverage includes products, local businesses, flights, events, sports and weather. According to the Exa’s post, Dynamic Highlights uses 95% fewer tokens than full page text while improving answer quality. Highlights carry no extra charge. That matters for agents, where context tokens often cost more than search calls. What is Exa Lite? Exa Lite is a new search type, set with type: "lite" on the /search endpoint, per the changelog . It runs on the same index as Exa Auto. Auto spends more compute on candidate generation, highlights and ranking. Lite supports query, result count, highlights, text, categories, domain and date filters, location and moderation. Unsupported parameters return a 400 error naming the field. Exa now recommends 3 search types: lite , auto and deep . The fast , instant and deep-reasoning types are legacy but still work. How does Exa 3.0 perform on benchmarks? Exa compared each provider’s highest-scoring single-step endpoint: Exa 3.0 Auto, Perplexity Web, Brave LLM Context and Parallel Advanced. All ran in one agentic harness. The agent was GPT-6 Luna, with up to 25 search rounds and 10 results per search. Evaluation happened in October 2026. && The margins vary widely. ATLAS and WebCode show the clearest leads, at 4.8 and 5.6 points over Perplexity. BrowseComp, DSQA and WideSearch leads are each under 1.5 points over the runner-up. ATLAS is a benchmark Exa published itself on October 8, 2026. On cost, Exa plots agentic search score against cost per task. Lite scores about 79 at about $0.045 per task. Auto scores about 80.5 at about $0.065. Exa says the pair sets a new Pareto frontier among tested providers. How does Exa 3.0 compare with Perplexity, Brave and Parallel? Feature Exa 3.0 Auto Perplexity Search API Brave Search API (LLM Context) Parallel Search API (Advanced) List price per 1K requests $7 (Lite $4) $5 $5 $5 BrowseComp (accuracy) 91.8% 91.5% 83.5% 63.1% DSQA (F1) 88.2% 87.6% 78.6% 82.8% WideSearch (F1) 56.1% 54.0% 54.8% 53.7% ATLAS 42.0% 37.2% 28.2% 24.8% WebCode 75.5% 69.9% 68.0% 64.5% FinSearchComp 68.0% 63.4% 57.6% 66.0% Company FindAll (mean entities) 15.4 14.2 13.3 9.7 People FindAll (mean entities) 7.6 6.8 3.8 3.8 Embedding model size Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed Not disclosed All benchmark scores come from Exa’s Exa 3.0 post and were run by Exa. No vendor has published matching results. Prices come from each vendor’s own pricing page. What data does the expanded index add? Exa states that it prioritized personal AI assistant use cases. The official technical page lists 1.27B ecommerce listings with prices and availability, and 211M+ local businesses . It also adds real-time news, sports, weather and market data, along with flights, events, transit and podcasts. The Exa Library structures this data into searchable collections. These include 320M people pages, 33M company pages and 500M research paper pages. It also lists 19M SEC filings, 10M patents and 9M court opinions. Where does Exa 3.0 fall short? Self-run evals : Exa picked the harness, endpoints and agent model. ATLAS is Exa’s own benchmark. Thin margins : Several leads are under 2 points, which may not survive other harnesses. Lite limits : Lite rejects unsupported parameters with a 400 , so some pipelines need Auto. Higher Auto list price : Auto costs $7 per 1,000 requests versus $5 for the 3 rivals. Opaque model details : Embedding model size and architecture are not disclosed. Key Takeaways Exa 3.0 leads 8 benchmarks, all run by Exa itself. Exa Lite costs $4 per 1,000 requests on the same index as Auto. Dynamic Highlights uses 95% fewer tokens than full pages, at no extra cost. Biggest leads: WebCode (+5.6) and ATLAS (+4.8) over Perplexity. Test on your own queries before switching providers. Check out the Exa 3.0 announcement , the Exa Library , the changelog and the API docs . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. Exa has released Exa 3.0, an upgrade to its web search API for AI agents. The Exa 3.0 search API ships a larger embedding model and a cheaper search type, Exa Lite. Dynamic Highlights is now generally available. Exa claims that it leads Perplexity, Brave and Parallel on 8 benchmarks. Those benchmarks were run by Exa, so you can treat them as self-reported. For developers, the practical change is cost: Lite costs $4 per 1,000 requests.

TL;DR
  • Size: Exa tracks over 2 trillion URLs and serves 100 billion pages. Embedding model size: Not disclosed.
  • Runs on: Hosted API only. Exa lists configurable search latency of 450ms to 1s. No self-hosted option.
  • Performance: Exa 3.0 Auto ranks first on all 8 Exa-run benchmarks against Perplexity, Brave and Parallel.
  • Best: 91.8% on BrowseComp, plus the widest lead on ATLAS (42.0% vs 37.2% for Perplexity).
  • Worst: 42.0% on ATLAS is its lowest percentage score. Its BrowseComp lead over Perplexity is only 0.3 points.
What is Exa 3.0?

Exa 3.0 is a search API release from Exa Labs that upgrades retrieval quality across every search type. It is available through the API. Exa runs its own crawler and an independent index. It is not a wrapper on Google or Bing results.

How does Exa 3.0 improve retrieval?

Exa attributes the gains to 3 changes in its retrieval stack:

  • A larger embedding model: Exa trained it with more compute and data than any earlier model. Parameter count is not disclosed.
  • Dynamic Highlights, now generally available: The model selects tokens across all results, not page by page. It gives more tokens to better pages and drops repeated information.
  • Billions of new documents: New coverage includes products, local businesses, flights, events, sports and weather.

According to the Exa’s post, Dynamic Highlights uses 95% fewer tokens than full page text while improving answer quality. Highlights carry no extra charge. That matters for agents, where context tokens often cost more than search calls.

What is Exa Lite?

Exa Lite is a new search type, set with type: "lite" on the /search endpoint, per the changelog. It runs on the same index as Exa Auto. Auto spends more compute on candidate generation, highlights and ranking. Lite supports query, result count, highlights, text, categories, domain and date filters, location and moderation. Unsupported parameters return a 400 error naming the field.

Exa now recommends 3 search types: lite, auto and deep. The fast, instant and deep-reasoning types are legacy but still work.

How does Exa 3.0 perform on benchmarks?

Exa compared each provider’s highest-scoring single-step endpoint: Exa 3.0 Auto, Perplexity Web, Brave LLM Context and Parallel Advanced. All ran in one agentic harness. The agent was GPT-6 Luna, with up to 25 search rounds and 10 results per search. Evaluation happened in October 2026.

&&

The margins vary widely. ATLAS and WebCode show the clearest leads, at 4.8 and 5.6 points over Perplexity. BrowseComp, DSQA and WideSearch leads are each under 1.5 points over the runner-up. ATLAS is a benchmark Exa published itself on October 8, 2026.

On cost, Exa plots agentic search score against cost per task. Lite scores about 79 at about $0.045 per task. Auto scores about 80.5 at about $0.065. Exa says the pair sets a new Pareto frontier among tested providers.

How does Exa 3.0 compare with Perplexity, Brave and Parallel? FeatureExa 3.0 AutoPerplexity Search APIBrave Search API (LLM Context)Parallel Search API (Advanced)List price per 1K requests$7 (Lite $4)$5$5$5BrowseComp (accuracy)91.8%91.5%83.5%63.1%DSQA (F1)88.2%87.6%78.6%82.8%WideSearch (F1)56.1%54.0%54.8%53.7%ATLAS42.0%37.2%28.2%24.8%WebCode75.5%69.9%68.0%64.5%FinSearchComp68.0%63.4%57.6%66.0%Company FindAll (mean entities)15.414.213.39.7People FindAll (mean entities)7.66.83.83.8Embedding model sizeNot disclosedNot disclosedNot disclosedNot disclosed

All benchmark scores come from Exa’s Exa 3.0 post and were run by Exa. No vendor has published matching results. Prices come from each vendor’s own pricing page.

What data does the expanded index add?

Exa states that it prioritized personal AI assistant use cases. The official technical page lists 1.27B ecommerce listings with prices and availability, and 211M+ local businesses. It also adds real-time news, sports, weather and market data, along with flights, events, transit and podcasts.

The Exa Library structures this data into searchable collections. These include 320M people pages, 33M company pages and 500M research paper pages. It also lists 19M SEC filings, 10M patents and 9M court opinions.

Where does Exa 3.0 fall short?
  • Self-run evals: Exa picked the harness, endpoints and agent model. ATLAS is Exa’s own benchmark.
  • Thin margins: Several leads are under 2 points, which may not survive other harnesses.
  • Lite limits: Lite rejects unsupported parameters with a 400, so some pipelines need Auto.
  • Higher Auto list price: Auto costs $7 per 1,000 requests versus $5 for the 3 rivals.
  • Opaque model details: Embedding model size and architecture are not disclosed.
Key Takeaways
  • Exa 3.0 leads 8 benchmarks, all run by Exa itself.
  • Exa Lite costs $4 per 1,000 requests on the same index as Auto.
  • Dynamic Highlights uses 95% fewer tokens than full pages, at no extra cost.
  • Biggest leads: WebCode (+5.6) and ATLAS (+4.8) over Perplexity.
  • Test on your own queries before switching providers.

Check out the Exa 3.0 announcement, the Exa Library, the changelog and the API docs. All credit goes to the researcher of this project. items.title: Cloudflare Releases Clairic, a System One Extraction Model on Workers AI
items.summary: Cloudflare has released a preview of Clairic , a new System One extraction model on Workers AI. The Cloudflare Clairic extraction model reads text or images and returns typed values, not generated text. It targets a job developers usually give to LLMs: pulling totals, dates and IDs into JSON. Clairic answers every requested field in 1 forward pass, with no reasoning and no output tokens. TL;DR Size: Parameter count not disclosed. 65,536-token context window , up to 4 images per request. Runs on: Cloudflare-hosted GPUs via Workers AI ( @cf/cloudflare/clairic ). No local option until weights ship. Performance: Sub-second extraction in Cloudflare’s tests. No standard accuracy benchmark is published yet. Best: Extraction step took 0.46 s vs 16.1 s for GLM-5.3 in Cloudflare’s claims pipeline. Worst: 4 of 21 TSA next-day forecasts fell outside its 80% interval. Multi-step arithmetic is unreliable. What is Clairic? Clairic is a Cloudflare model that extracts, computes, estimates and forecasts typed values from unstructured inputs. It builds on the System One idea from TypeSafe’s Jev , named for Kahneman’s fast, intuitive thinking. Jev and Cloudflare’s own Clef are decision models. They score options you list in advance. Clairic covers answers you cannot list, such as an invoice total, a date or a repair cost. Cloudflare frames a 3-part stack. Extraction models turn raw input into typed values. Decision models turn values into decisions. LLMs turn decisions into words. How does a Clairic request work? A request has a state (text plus up to 4 images) and a map of named, typed fields . Each field can carry plain-language instructions. Supported types are text, number, date, time, datetime, duration, list, estimate and forecast, per the Workers AI changelog . Every scalar answer includes p_null , the probability that the value is absent, plus a confidence score. Text answers return exact spans with character offsets. Estimates and forecasts return a median and an 80% interval, from p10 to p90. Forecasts cover up to 64 steps. There is no field limit. Fields that do not fit beside the input in one 8,192-token pass split into parallel passes. Each pass sees the whole input. In the docs example, a 61-token invoice ran in 3 passes. It billed 655 input tokens, including 472 schema tokens. Wide schemas can cost more than the document itself. What did Cloudflare’s tests show? In a support-email example, Clairic added price and tax into $701.10. It also computed 11 days since delivery. Neither number appears in the email. A missing tracking number returned null instead of a plausible guess. On a skewed receipt photo, it read all 7 present values and returned null for the absent discount. Its lowest confidence was 0.776, on the order number. For forecasting, Cloudflare predicted daily TSA checkpoint counts for 21 days. Average error was 3.3%. 17 of 21 actual counts fell inside the 80% interval. 3 of the 4 misses fell on Columbus Day weekend. The main test is a damaged-product claims pipeline. Clairic extracted facts, Clef chose refund or repair, and GLM-5.3 wrote the reply. Cloudflare compared this against GLM-5.3 handling all 3 steps. &&& The cascade finished in 19.3 s versus 61.7 s, about 3.2x faster. Extraction took 0.46 s against 16.1 s. The decision step took 0.22 s against 21.9 s. Cost per million claims fell 49%, from $11,740 to $6,032. The reply step still dominated, at 18.6 of the 19.3 s. Both pipelines got the facts and decision right. Clairic’s repair estimate was identical across runs. GLM-5.3 returned $250, $250 and $220. Cloudflare says Gemma 4 and Qwen failed the all-LLM version. How does Clairic compare with Clef, Jev and GLM-5.3? Metrics Clairic Clef Jev GLM-5.3 Developer Cloudflare Cloudflare TypeSafe AI Z.ai Class System One extraction System One decision System One decision System Two LLM (reasoning) Output Typed values: spans, numbers, dates, durations, lists, estimates, forecasts Probabilities over options you list Typed decisions with calibrated probabilities Free-form text Parameters Not disclosed 27B Not disclosed Not disclosed Context window 65,536 tokens 65,536 tokens Not disclosed 1,048,576 tokens Image input Yes, up to 4 Yes (text, JSON, images, video) Not disclosed Not disclosed Input price $0.10 / M tokens $0.24 / M tokens $0.042 / M tokens $1.40 / M tokens Output price None None Free $4.40 / M tokens Speed 0.46 s extraction step ( Cloudflare test ) 209.3 ms median ( Cloudflare evals ) 70 to 500 ms end to end (TypeSafe) 16.1 s extraction step ( Cloudflare test ) Availability Workers AI preview; open weights planned Workers AI; Apache 2.0 weights TypeSafe API, early access Workers AI, Paid plan Where can developers use it, and what does it cost? Clairic is live as a preview at @cf/cloudflare/clairic . Call it through the Workers AI binding with env.AI.run() or the REST API. AI Gateway works with the same endpoints. Pricing is $0.10 per million input tokens with no output charge. That undercuts Clef’s $0.24 but sits above Jev’s $0.042. Weights are promised but not yet released. Key Takeaways Clairic returns typed values, not text, in 1 forward pass. $0.10 per million input tokens; output tokens cost nothing. Extraction ran in 0.46 s vs 16.1 s for GLM-5.3. Every answer carries confidence, p_null , spans or intervals. Check out the Cloudflare blog post , the Clairic model docs , the extraction models explainer and the Workers AI changelog . Also read our earlier coverage of Drex 1.5 . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. items.summary_html:
Cloudflare has released a preview of Clairic, a new System One extraction model on Workers AI. The Cloudflare Clairic extraction model reads text or images and returns typed values, not generated text. It targets a job developers usually give to LLMs: pulling totals, dates and IDs into JSON. Clairic answers every requested field in 1 forward pass, with no reasoning and no output tokens.

TL;DR
  • Size: Parameter count not disclosed. 65,536-token context window, up to 4 images per request.
  • Runs on: Cloudflare-hosted GPUs via Workers AI (@cf/cloudflare/clairic). No local option until weights ship.
  • Performance: Sub-second extraction in Cloudflare’s tests. No standard accuracy benchmark is published yet.
  • Best: Extraction step took 0.46 s vs 16.1 s for GLM-5.3 in Cloudflare’s claims pipeline.
  • Worst: 4 of 21 TSA next-day forecasts fell outside its 80% interval. Multi-step arithmetic is unreliable.
What is Clairic?

Clairic is a Cloudflare model that extracts, computes, estimates and forecasts typed values from unstructured inputs. It builds on the System One idea from TypeSafe’s Jev, named for Kahneman’s fast, intuitive thinking.

Jev and Cloudflare’s own Clef are decision models. They score options you list in advance. Clairic covers answers you cannot list, such as an invoice total, a date or a repair cost.

Cloudflare frames a 3-part stack. Extraction models turn raw input into typed values. Decision models turn values into decisions. LLMs turn decisions into words.

How does a Clairic request work?

A request has a state (text plus up to 4 images) and a map of named, typed fields. Each field can carry plain-language instructions. Supported types are text, number, date, time, datetime, duration, list, estimate and forecast, per the Workers AI changelog.

Every scalar answer includes p_null, the probability that the value is absent, plus a confidence score. Text answers return exact spans with character offsets. Estimates and forecasts return a median and an 80% interval, from p10 to p90. Forecasts cover up to 64 steps.

There is no field limit. Fields that do not fit beside the input in one 8,192-token pass split into parallel passes. Each pass sees the whole input. In the docs example, a 61-token invoice ran in 3 passes. It billed 655 input tokens, including 472 schema tokens. Wide schemas can cost more than the document itself.

What did Cloudflare’s tests show?

In a support-email example, Clairic added price and tax into $701.10. It also computed 11 days since delivery. Neither number appears in the email. A missing tracking number returned null instead of a plausible guess.

On a skewed receipt photo, it read all 7 present values and returned null for the absent discount. Its lowest confidence was 0.776, on the order number.

For forecasting, Cloudflare predicted daily TSA checkpoint counts for 21 days. Average error was 3.3%. 17 of 21 actual counts fell inside the 80% interval. 3 of the 4 misses fell on Columbus Day weekend.

The main test is a damaged-product claims pipeline. Clairic extracted facts, Clef chose refund or repair, and GLM-5.3 wrote the reply. Cloudflare compared this against GLM-5.3 handling all 3 steps.

&&&

The cascade finished in 19.3 s versus 61.7 s, about 3.2x faster. Extraction took 0.46 s against 16.1 s. The decision step took 0.22 s against 21.9 s. Cost per million claims fell 49%, from $11,740 to $6,032. The reply step still dominated, at 18.6 of the 19.3 s.

Both pipelines got the facts and decision right. Clairic’s repair estimate was identical across runs. GLM-5.3 returned $250, $250 and $220. Cloudflare says Gemma 4 and Qwen failed the all-LLM version.

How does Clairic compare with Clef, Jev and GLM-5.3? MetricsClairicClefJevGLM-5.3 DeveloperCloudflareCloudflareTypeSafe AIZ.aiClassSystem One extractionSystem One decisionSystem One decisionSystem Two LLM (reasoning)OutputTyped values: spans, numbers, dates, durations, lists, estimates, forecastsProbabilities over options you listTyped decisions with calibrated probabilitiesFree-form textParametersNot disclosed27BNot disclosedNot disclosedContext window65,536 tokens65,536 tokensNot disclosed1,048,576 tokensImage inputYes, up to 4Yes (text, JSON, images, video)Not disclosedNot disclosedInput price$0.10 / M tokens$0.24 / M tokens$0.042 / M tokens$1.40 / M tokensOutput priceNoneNoneFree$4.40 / M tokensSpeed0.46 s extraction step (Cloudflare test)209.3 ms median (Cloudflare evals)70 to 500 ms end to end (TypeSafe)16.1 s extraction step (Cloudflare test)AvailabilityWorkers AI preview; open weights plannedWorkers AI; Apache 2.0 weightsTypeSafe API, early accessWorkers AI, Paid plan Where can developers use it, and what does it cost?

Clairic is live as a preview at @cf/cloudflare/clairic. Call it through the Workers AI binding with env.AI.run() or the REST API. AI Gateway works with the same endpoints.

Pricing is $0.10 per million input tokens with no output charge. That undercuts Clef’s $0.24 but sits above Jev’s $0.042. Weights are promised but not yet released.

Key Takeaways
  • Clairic returns typed values, not text, in 1 forward pass.
  • $0.10 per million input tokens; output tokens cost nothing.
  • Extraction ran in 0.46 s vs 16.1 s for GLM-5.3.
  • Every answer carries confidence, p_null, spans or intervals.

Check out the Cloudflare blog post, the Clairic model docs, the extraction models explainer and the Workers AI changelog. Also read our earlier coverage of Drex 1.5. items.title: Parallel Coding Agents: What to Delegate First
items.summary: Dynamic concurrency helps when the work can separate — and the results have somewhere to meet. Parallel contributions, one integrated result Codex finished 15 of 26 tasks with parallel agents, versus 9 without them. The average run still took longer. In Han Li and colleagues’ October 7 study of dynamic concurrency , those NL2Repo runs used a July GPT-5.4 configuration. Mean runtime increased from 9.4 to 9.9 minutes. More completed tasks and faster delivery were different outcomes. When your coding tool offers another agent, the choice is what to give it. Consider a hypothetical CSV export feature: a serializer and a download button can progress together once the input format is agreed. Before that, a second writer must wait or guess. Following that feature through shared files, handoffs, and the final download gives you a way to choose the next assignment: a second writer, an independent reviewer, or a single owner for the unresolved decision. What the benchmark actually improved Dynamic concurrency lets the main agent decide during execution when to create workers and what to assign them. The authors compared this policy enabled and disabled across 354 tasks and 2,124 executions. NL2Repo was one subset of that broader evaluation. NL2Repo outcomes and execution time in the published study This small subset distinguishes completion from speed. It cannot establish an October product ranking; extensive repeated runs were outside the study’s scope. Before choosing an orchestration pattern, decide which improvement matters for the task. A larger implementation may justify extra coordination if it produces a complete feature. A short repair with an obvious next edit has less independent work to distribute. The model’s ability to write code is one layer. The product’s scheduling and state handling are another. Dividing a particular feature into useful assignments is a workflow decision. More capable models still receive whatever dependencies that workflow creates. Find the input that both workers need In the hypothetical export feature, the button downloads the currently visible table rows as comma-separated values (CSV). “Build the CSV exporter” and “wire up the button” sound like separate jobs. They become separate once both workers know what crosses the boundary. Does the exporter receive already filtered rows? Who selects and orders the columns? Does it return text or a downloadable file? How does an error reach the interface? Without those answers, the UI worker may pass every row while the serializer assumes filtering has already happened. Both pieces can look reasonable in isolation, yet the download contains records the user did not choose. Put the shared decision first. For this example, define an exporter that receives the visible rows and an ordered column list, and returns CSV text. Agree how commas, quotes, line breaks, empty values, and errors are represented. Keep download creation with the UI owner. This is a proposed division of responsibilities, not a tested implementation. Now the serializer worker can implement the conversion while the main agent connects the button to the agreed function. Neither needs to invent the other’s inputs. A shared contract before parallel CSV implementation The main agent still has useful work during that overlap: handle the button’s disabled state, follow the application’s existing download pattern, and collect edge cases for the combined check. Waiting for a worker should not silently become the entire plan. This gives a concrete rule for starting a branch: its required inputs must already exist. If the serializer’s return type is still being decided, a second implementation worker will either wait or guess. Assigning it a read-only investigation of existing export behavior creates a useful result without competing to settle the same interface. Separate conversations still share a working environment Anthropic’s dynamic-workflow documentation describes moving orchestration into a script. Intermediate results live in script variables, and the runtime coordinates sub-agents. That changes where the plan and returned information are held. It leaves a separate question for any deployment: what can those workers change together? Separate conversation histories do not, by themselves, create separate files, temporary directories, package manifests, databases, or running servers. In the CSV example, two workers could edit different source files while both writing a fixture called /tmp/export.csv. One worker’s check would then read the other’s output. A clean source-file split would not explain that interference. Give each worker its own output location for disposable artifacts. Keep shared configuration changes with the integration owner, or have workers return proposed changes for that owner to apply. When isolated checkouts are available, they can separate code edits; shared services and external state still need explicit ownership. The distinction also changes the assignment. “Only edit the serializer” says little about test fixtures or dependency updates. A usable brief names the allowed source files, the scratch location, and which shared resources the worker must leave for the main agent. Give returned work an integration owner A worker returning “done” leaves several decisions unresolved. The main agent needs the actual patch, the interface version it assumes, the checks performed, and anything still unfinished. For the serializer branch, a useful handoff identifies the changed files and includes output for a row containing a comma, a quote, and a line break. It also states whether the worker changed the agreed error behavior. The integration owner can then decide whether to accept the patch or resolve the disagreement before connecting it to the button. The final check belongs after that connection. Download the file through the feature’s actual entry point and compare its rows and column order with the visible table. Exercise the empty and error states agreed in the contract. A serializer check cannot establish that the UI passes the correct row set. Factory’s September 27 concurrency-testing guidance makes a related verification point: a successful dynamic detector run covers the paths exercised by its workload. The claim needs to match what the check actually reached. For this export, passing a conversion check and passing the click-to-download path support different conclusions. Leave room for integration inside the task budget. If a worker cannot finish in time, the main agent needs an explicit choice: take over the remaining change, reduce the deliverable with approval, or report the unresolved part. Waiting beyond the deadline cannot produce an integrated result within it. Choose where the extra worker earns its place For the export feature, a second writer becomes useful once the shared contract is settled and both branches have their inputs. Before that point, an independent reviewer has a clearer job: identify cases the proposed contract misses, using the feature requirement rather than editing the same implementation. That reviewer should return a concrete case and the behavior it expects — for example, a filtered-out record appearing in the downloaded file. The implementation owner can act on that finding. A generic request to “review quality” gives the main agent less to integrate. Keep a tightly coupled repair with one implementation owner when every proposed branch needs the same unresolved decision. Split a larger feature when the branches can proceed from stable inputs and return distinct artifacts. In either case, name who will assemble and check the final result before the workers start. For the next CSV export assignment, the first parallel task should therefore follow the feature’s state: an independent requirements review while the interface is unsettled, or serializer implementation once it is agreed. The main agent keeps the button and the final download. That allocation gives each worker a useful place to finish. Parallel Coding Agents: What to Delegate First was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

Dynamic concurrency helps when the work can separate — and the results have somewhere to meet.Parallel contributions, one integrated result

Codex finished 15 of 26 tasks with parallel agents, versus 9 without them. The average run still took longer.

In Han Li and colleagues’ October 7 study of dynamic concurrency, those NL2Repo runs used a July GPT-5.4 configuration. Mean runtime increased from 9.4 to 9.9 minutes. More completed tasks and faster delivery were different outcomes.

When your coding tool offers another agent, the choice is what to give it. Consider a hypothetical CSV export feature: a serializer and a download button can progress together once the input format is agreed. Before that, a second writer must wait or guess.

Following that feature through shared files, handoffs, and the final download gives you a way to choose the next assignment: a second writer, an independent reviewer, or a single owner for the unresolved decision.

What the benchmark actually improved

Dynamic concurrency lets the main agent decide during execution when to create workers and what to assign them. The authors compared this policy enabled and disabled across 354 tasks and 2,124 executions. NL2Repo was one subset of that broader evaluation.

NL2Repo outcomes and execution time in the published study

This small subset distinguishes completion from speed. It cannot establish an October product ranking; extensive repeated runs were outside the study’s scope.

Before choosing an orchestration pattern, decide which improvement matters for the task. A larger implementation may justify extra coordination if it produces a complete feature. A short repair with an obvious next edit has less independent work to distribute.

The model’s ability to write code is one layer. The product’s scheduling and state handling are another. Dividing a particular feature into useful assignments is a workflow decision. More capable models still receive whatever dependencies that workflow creates.

Find the input that both workers need

In the hypothetical export feature, the button downloads the currently visible table rows as comma-separated values (CSV).

“Build the CSV exporter” and “wire up the button” sound like separate jobs. They become separate once both workers know what crosses the boundary. Does the exporter receive already filtered rows? Who selects and orders the columns? Does it return text or a downloadable file? How does an error reach the interface?

Without those answers, the UI worker may pass every row while the serializer assumes filtering has already happened. Both pieces can look reasonable in isolation, yet the download contains records the user did not choose.

Put the shared decision first. For this example, define an exporter that receives the visible rows and an ordered column list, and returns CSV text. Agree how commas, quotes, line breaks, empty values, and errors are represented. Keep download creation with the UI owner. This is a proposed division of responsibilities, not a tested implementation.

Now the serializer worker can implement the conversion while the main agent connects the button to the agreed function. Neither needs to invent the other’s inputs.

A shared contract before parallel CSV implementation

The main agent still has useful work during that overlap: handle the button’s disabled state, follow the application’s existing download pattern, and collect edge cases for the combined check. Waiting for a worker should not silently become the entire plan.

This gives a concrete rule for starting a branch: its required inputs must already exist. If the serializer’s return type is still being decided, a second implementation worker will either wait or guess. Assigning it a read-only investigation of existing export behavior creates a useful result without competing to settle the same interface.

Separate conversations still share a working environment

Anthropic’s dynamic-workflow documentation describes moving orchestration into a script. Intermediate results live in script variables, and the runtime coordinates sub-agents. That changes where the plan and returned information are held.

It leaves a separate question for any deployment: what can those workers change together? Separate conversation histories do not, by themselves, create separate files, temporary directories, package manifests, databases, or running servers.

In the CSV example, two workers could edit different source files while both writing a fixture called /tmp/export.csv. One worker’s check would then read the other’s output. A clean source-file split would not explain that interference.

Give each worker its own output location for disposable artifacts. Keep shared configuration changes with the integration owner, or have workers return proposed changes for that owner to apply. When isolated checkouts are available, they can separate code edits; shared services and external state still need explicit ownership.

The distinction also changes the assignment. “Only edit the serializer” says little about test fixtures or dependency updates. A usable brief names the allowed source files, the scratch location, and which shared resources the worker must leave for the main agent.

Give returned work an integration owner

A worker returning “done” leaves several decisions unresolved. The main agent needs the actual patch, the interface version it assumes, the checks performed, and anything still unfinished.

For the serializer branch, a useful handoff identifies the changed files and includes output for a row containing a comma, a quote, and a line break. It also states whether the worker changed the agreed error behavior. The integration owner can then decide whether to accept the patch or resolve the disagreement before connecting it to the button.

The final check belongs after that connection. Download the file through the feature’s actual entry point and compare its rows and column order with the visible table. Exercise the empty and error states agreed in the contract. A serializer check cannot establish that the UI passes the correct row set.

Factory’s September 27 concurrency-testing guidance makes a related verification point: a successful dynamic detector run covers the paths exercised by its workload. The claim needs to match what the check actually reached. For this export, passing a conversion check and passing the click-to-download path support different conclusions.

Leave room for integration inside the task budget. If a worker cannot finish in time, the main agent needs an explicit choice: take over the remaining change, reduce the deliverable with approval, or report the unresolved part. Waiting beyond the deadline cannot produce an integrated result within it.

Choose where the extra worker earns its place

For the export feature, a second writer becomes useful once the shared contract is settled and both branches have their inputs. Before that point, an independent reviewer has a clearer job: identify cases the proposed contract misses, using the feature requirement rather than editing the same implementation.

That reviewer should return a concrete case and the behavior it expects — for example, a filtered-out record appearing in the downloaded file. The implementation owner can act on that finding. A generic request to “review quality” gives the main agent less to integrate.

  1. Keep a tightly coupled repair with one implementation owner when every proposed branch needs the same unresolved decision.
  2. Split a larger feature when the branches can proceed from stable inputs and return distinct artifacts.
  3. In either case, name who will assemble and check the final result before the workers start.

For the next CSV export assignment, the first parallel task should therefore follow the feature’s state: an independent requirements review while the interface is unsettled, or serializer implementation once it is agreed. The main agent keeps the button and the final download. That allocation gives each worker a useful place to finish.
