items.title: How I Made Local LLMs Up to 2.24× Faster on a 4GB NVIDIA GPU
items.summary: What two rounds of llama.cpp benchmarking taught me about GPU offloading, KV cache optimization, and running Gemma 4, Qwen3, and Qwen3.5 on a GTX 1650 Ti. Your GPU might be more capable than you think. When people talk about running large language models locally, the conversation usually starts with expensive hardware: RTX 4090s, 24GB of VRAM, or dedicated AI workstations. I wanted to answer a different question: How much performance can we extract from a laptop GPU with only 4GB of VRAM? My test machine uses an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650 Ti, a GPU released years before the current generative AI boom. With just 4GB of GDDR6 memory, it is hardly the first card anyone would recommend for running modern language models. Yet after two rounds of systematic benchmarking with llama.cpp, the results were surprisingly encouraging. By tuning GPU layer placement, CPU threads, microbatch sizes, and KV cache precision, I measured: 2.24× faster token generation for Qwen3.5–4B. 2.07× faster token generation for Qwen3–4B. Approximately 59 tokens per second from Gemma 4 E2B. A 260 MiB reduction in GPU memory usage for Qwen3 with Q8 KV cache, at approximately a 4% throughput penalty. Successful completion of every measured longer-response request in the validation experiment. No hardware upgrades. No retraining. No modifications to CUDA kernels. Just better configuration. The most important discovery was that the automatic GPU configuration was not always the fastest , even when llama.cpp was already running with CUDA acceleration. Here is how I tested it, what worked, and how to reproduce these I tested three approximately four-bit-quantized language models: Tested models Gemma 4 E2B IT Quantization: Q4_K_M GGUF size: 3.22 GiB Qwen3.5-4B Quantization: Q4_K_M GGUF size: 2.55 GiB Qwen3-4B Quantization: Q4_K_M GGUF size: 2.33 GiB The results refer specifically to quantized GGUF inference, not full-precision inference. An important lesson appeared early: a model’s file size does not tell us exactly how much GPU memory inference will require. Some tensors can remain in CPU-accessible memory, while others are placed on the GPU. Different model architectures can therefore behave quite differently on the same hardware. That became especially relevant when comparing Gemma 4 with the Qwen models. 2. Why GPU offloading matters so much llama.cpp allows us to control how many model layers are assigned to the GPU using the --gpu-layers option. The configurations I tested included: --gpu-layers auto --gpu-layers 12 --gpu-layers 24 --gpu-layers all Automatic selection is a sensible starting point on memory-constrained hardware. But it is not necessarily the configuration with the highest throughput. Initially, I used auto for every model. All three models could generate responses, but the Qwen models were performing well below what the GPU could actually deliver. When I switched to --gpu-layers all, Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 became dramatically faster. Gemma 4, however, saw almost no improvement. This gave us the central finding of the study: GPU offloading should be tuned for each model rather than treated as one universal setting. 3. The benchmark methodology I designed two rounds of experiments rather than relying on a few manually timed prompts. The benchmark was automated with PowerShell scripts that launched llama-server, waited for readiness, issued API requests, collected timing information, recorded GPU memory usage, and saved results to CSV files. Phase one: searching the parameter space The first experiment tested four GPU offloading strategies, two CPU thread counts, and two microbatch sizes. GPU layers: auto, 12, 24, all CPU threads: 4, 6 Microbatch: 128, 256 4 × 2 × 2 = 16 configs/model 3 models × 16 = 48 configurations The test ran under a two-hour time budget, with up to three repetitions of each configuration. We used five types of prompts: factual questions, humor, Serbian-to-English translation, English-to-Serbian translation, and prompt improvement. The core inference settings remained consistent: Context size: 4096 Batch size: 512 Concurrent servers: 1 Warm-up: enabled Temperature: 0 GPU monitoring: enabled For each request, the script captured generation throughput, total latency, completion status, GPU memory usage, and related performance information. One methodological issue became apparent: the first benchmark limited output to 192 tokens, causing some longer responses to end before they were complete. Those samples still provided generation-speed observations, but they could not be treated as completed user tasks. Token generation throughput and task-completion time are different measurements. Phase two: validating the strongest configurations After identifying promising GPU/CPU parameters, I ran a second experiment focused on longer technical responses and KV cache optimization. The second phase evaluated ten model configurations in two rounds, comparing FP16, Q8_0, and Q4_0 cache formats where appropriate. Each configuration used one warm-up request and two measured requests. The output limit increased to 512 tokens. All 40 measured responses completed normally, with finish_reason=stop. This strengthened our confidence that the shortlisted configurations could handle more realistic requests without immediately exhausting the generation limit. 4. The biggest result: Qwen became more than twice as fast The most dramatic improvement came from GPU layer placement. For an apples-to-apples comparison, I used results with the same CPU thread count and microbatch size, changing only GPU offloading between auto and all. GPU offloading comparison Qwen3.5-4B GPU auto: 15.63 tok/s GPU all: 34.96 tok/s Speedup: 2.24× Qwen3-4B GPU auto: 20.46 tok/s GPU all: 42.41 tok/s Speedup: 2.07× Gemma 4 E2B GPU auto: 59.99 tok/s GPU all: 59.78 tok/s Speedup: ~1.00× For Qwen3.5, that represents approximately 124% more generation throughput. For Qwen3, approximately 107% more. These are substantial gains from configuration changes alone. The improvement did come with a GPU memory tradeoff. GPU memory use Auto All Qwen3.5-4B 2231 MiB 3089 MiB Qwen3-4B 2281 MiB 3163 MiB In other words, the fastest configurations used more of the available GPU memory. That is not necessarily a disadvantage when the GPU is dedicated to inference. Unused VRAM does not provide a performance benefit by itself. The question is whether using more VRAM reduces expensive CPU/GPU transfers and improves actual inference execution. In these measurements, it clearly did. But there is a limit. On a 4GB card, reserving enough GPU memory for runtime allocations, the operating system, and other applications remains important. 5. Why Gemma 4 behaved differently Gemma 4 E2B consistently achieved close to 60 generated tokens per second. Interestingly, changing its GPU setting from auto to all produced almost no difference. The runtime reported 36 of 36 relevant layers as offloaded, while still retaining substantial tensor data in CPU-mapped memory. Observed model buffers Gemma 4 E2B GPU model buffer: ~1450 MiB CPU-mapped buffer: ~2153 MiB GPU layers: 36 / 36 This does not mean that the entire model occupies only 1450 MiB. It means the runtime divides its tensors between different memory locations. In a separate exploratory test, I forced additional Gemma tensors onto the GPU. The GPU model buffer increased to roughly 3602 MiB, leaving very little VRAM headroom. That did not improve practical responsiveness. The lesson was clear: More GPU-resident tensors do not guarantee faster inference if the resulting memory pressure harms execution. I also compared microbatch values of 256 and 128. Gemma 4 microbatch comparison ub=256 ub=128 Speed 58.99 59.31 tok/s Latency 7.05 7.00 sec GPU memory 1813 1685 MiB Completed 4/4 4/4 The smaller microbatch saved approximately 128 MiB with effectively unchanged performance. Therefore, I selected -ub 128 for Gemma. One useful implication is that microbatch size should not simply be maximized because more GPU memory is available. On a single-user workload, a smaller value may be equally fast while providing more memory headroom. 6. KV cache quantization: an unexpected memory optimization Once the strongest GPU offload configurations were identified, I wanted to reduce VRAM usage without losing too much throughput. That led to the second major part of the study: KV cache quantization. Autoregressive transformer inference stores information from earlier tokens in a key-value cache. As context length grows, this cache can use substantial memory. llama.cpp allows the cache formats to be configured with: --cache-type-k --cache-type-v The experiment compared FP16, Q8_0, and Q4_0. Qwen3.5: quantization saves comparatively little The Qwen3.5 results were: Qwen3.5-4B KV cache Speed GPU memory --------------------------------- FP16 34.58 tok/s 3090 MiB Q8_0 34.21 tok/s 3041 MiB Q4_0 34.14 tok/s 3009 MiB Q4_0 reduced observed GPU memory use by approximately 81 MiB, while generation speed decreased by about 1.3%. This is a reasonable tradeoff, but not an especially compelling one for this configuration. The server logs also showed that Qwen3.5 uses additional recurrent state, alongside its KV cache. My conclusion was to retain FP16 for Qwen3.5, unless a particular application requires additional VRAM headroom. Qwen3: hundreds of megabytes saved Qwen3 showed a much larger benefit. Qwen3-4B KV cache Speed GPU memory --------------------------------- FP16 41.59 tok/s 3163 MiB Q8_0 39.92 tok/s 2903 MiB Q4_0 39.80 tok/s 2759 MiB The tradeoffs were striking. Q8_0 saved 260 MiB, with a generation-speed reduction of approximately 4%. Q4_0 saved 404 MiB, with a roughly 4.3% reduction. On a GPU with only 4GB of VRAM, hundreds of megabytes are meaningful. Q8_0 became my preferred balance: nearly all the measured performance of FP16, but with substantially more free GPU memory. There is a caveat: this experiment measured timing, memory, and successful completion. It did not formally evaluate whether KV quantization changed semantic accuracy or reasoning quality. That would require a separate task-quality benchmark. 7. Thinking versus non-thinking models: another source of latency While benchmarking, I encountered a practical issue familiar to anyone using reasoning-capable LLMs. Some models can spend a large number of tokens on internal reasoning before producing visible output. For complex mathematical reasoning or difficult planning tasks, this can be useful. But for basic coding questions, translations, summaries, and direct explanations, the additional delay may be undesirable. The tested llama.cpp build supports these options: --reasoning off --reasoning-budget 0 I used them to configure the models for direct responses. In practice, this made short interactive exchanges more usable and helped avoid cases where the output-token allowance was exhausted before the visible answer was complete. However, there is an important distinction. Disabling thinking does not necessarily make the GPU generate individual tokens faster. Instead, it can reduce the total number of generated tokens required before the user receives an answer. The 2.24× and 2.07× GPU-offloading gains reported earlier should not be attributed to reasoning settings. I also would not recommend disabling reasoning for every possible task. For problems where deliberate multi-step reasoning matters, a reasoning-enabled configuration may be the better choice. The best setting depends on the purpose of the model. 8. The optimized settings I ultimately selected Combining the results of both experiments, I selected the following practical configurations. Recommended llama.cpp profiles GEMMA 4 E2B GPU layers: auto CPU threads: 4 Context: 4096 Batch: 512 Microbatch: 128 KV cache: f16 / f16 Reasoning: off QWEN3.5-4B GPU layers: all CPU threads: 6 Context: 4096 Batch: 512 Microbatch: 256 KV cache: f16 / f16 Reasoning: off QWEN3-4B GPU layers: all CPU threads: 6 Context: 4096 Batch: 512 Microbatch: 256 KV cache: q8_0 / q8_0 Reasoning: off These should be viewed as tested profiles for my hardware, not universal defaults. Different GPUs, driver versions, model quantizations, context sizes, and concurrency settings can produce different outcomes. 9. Practical guide: running these models with llama.cpp Here is how to reproduce the configuration on Windows. I used the following directory structure: C:\llama.cpp\ bin\ llama-cli.exe llama-server.exe models\ google_gemma-4-E2B-it-Q4_K_M.gguf Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf Qwen3-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf The executable names and directory layout may differ depending on how you install llama.cpp. Step 1: check CUDA and driver compatibility First, open PowerShell and verify that Windows detects the NVIDIA GPU: nvidia-smi Then check your llama.cpp installation: cd C:\llama.cpp .\bin\llama-cli.exe --help Review the available flags before copying any configuration. One practical challenge I encountered was CUDA toolchain compatibility. A newer prebuilt llama.cpp binary failed with an unsupported PTX toolchain error on my machine, while build b8729 worked correctly. The important point is not that everyone should use b8729. It is that a binary and its packaged CUDA components must be compatible with the installed NVIDIA driver. Step 2: run Gemma 4 in CLI mode .\bin\llama-cli.exe ` -m ".\models\google_gemma-4-E2B-it-Q4_K_M.gguf" ` --gpu-layers auto ` -t 4 ` -c 4096 ` -b 512 ` -ub 128 ` --cache-type-k f16 ` --cache-type-v f16 ` --reasoning off ` --reasoning-budget 0 This profile produced approximately 59 tokens per second in the validation experiment. Step 3: run Qwen3.5 in CLI mode .\bin\llama-cli.exe ` -m ".\models\Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf" ` --gpu-layers all ` -t 6 ` -c 4096 ` -b 512 ` -ub 256 ` --cache-type-k f16 ` --cache-type-v f16 ` --reasoning off ` --reasoning-budget 0 With maximum GPU layer offloading requested, Qwen3.5 achieved about 34.6 generated tokens per second in the longer-response validation experiment. Step 4: run Qwen3 with Q8 KV cache .\bin\llama-cli.exe ` -m ".\models\Qwen3-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf" ` --gpu-layers all ` -t 6 ` -c 4096 ` -b 512 ` -ub 256 ` --cache-type-k q8_0 ` --cache-type-v q8_0 ` --reasoning off ` --reasoning-budget 0 This configuration achieved approximately 39.9 generated tokens per second while using roughly 2,903 MiB of GPU memory. For the highest measured Qwen3 throughput, FP16 KV cache remains an alternative, at the cost of more VRAM. 10. Running an OpenAI-compatible local inference server For terminal interactions, llama-cli is convenient. But if you want to integrate local inference with your own software, llama-server offers an OpenAI-compatible API. For example, here is the optimized Qwen3 server configuration: .\bin\llama-server.exe ` -m ".\models\Qwen3-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf" ` --host 127.0.0.1 ` --port 8080 ` --gpu-layers all ` -t 6 ` -c 4096 ` -b 512 ` -ub 256 ` --cache-type-k q8_0 ` --cache-type-v q8_0 ` --reasoning off ` --reasoning-budget 0 ` --no-webui Once started, the API base URL is: http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1 To check that the server is responding: Invoke-RestMethod ` http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/models To send a chat completion request: $body = @{ model = "Qwen3-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf" messages = @( @{ role = "user" content = "Explain AES-256 simply." } ) temperature = 0 max_tokens = 256 } | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 5 $result = Invoke-RestMethod ` -Uri "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions" ` -Method Post ` -ContentType "application/json" ` -Body $body $result.choices[0].message.content If your server reports a different model identifier from /v1/models, use that identifier instead. To use the built-in browser interface, omit --no-webui on builds that include the web interface. This example binds the server to 127.0.0.1, restricting access to the local machine. Do not expose an unauthenticated inference server directly to the internet. 11. How to benchmark your own low-VRAM GPU If you have a GTX 1650, GTX 1660, RTX 3050 4GB, or another memory-constrained NVIDIA GPU, I would recommend the following approach. Start with a correctness baseline. Verify that the model loads, completes prompts, and produces sensible answers before measuring performance. Test GPU offloading independently. Compare automatic layer selection with explicitly requested layer counts. Do not assume maximum offloading is always fastest or always feasible. Tune CPU threads and microbatch size. Higher numbers may increase memory pressure without improving single-user token generation. Inspect memory allocation. Separate model weights, KV cache, compute buffers, and other runtime allocations wherever logs permit. Evaluate cache quantization. Especially on smaller GPUs, the savings from Q8_0 or Q4_0 can be worth considering. Measure complete answers. Report token generation speed and total response latency separately. A truncated response should not be counted as a fully completed task. Repeat measurements. A configuration should be selected based on reproducible observations, not one unusually fast run. Most importantly, record the exact model file, quantization, inference engine version, driver, and GPU for every benchmark. Without that context, performance comparisons become difficult to reproduce. 12. What the experiment does not prove There are limits to what can be concluded from this study. All measurements came from one Windows 10 laptop with an NVIDIA GTX 1650 Ti and a single llama.cpp build. Other GPUs and software versions may behave differently. The three tested models also have different architectures. A higher tokens-per-second figure does not establish superior model quality. The experiment focused on one inference request at a time, not concurrent multi-user serving. The validation workload contained two technical prompt types and four measured responses per configuration, providing useful repeatability checks but not a large-scale statistical characterization. And although the quantized KV configurations completed requests successfully, we did not formally benchmark answer quality under different cache precisions. Finally, disabling thinking may improve responsiveness for simple tasks while weakening performance on difficult reasoning problems. These results should therefore be interpreted as measurements of local inference performance, not general model-quality rankings. 13. Conclusion: optimize before you upgrade Before running these experiments, I expected a 4GB laptop GPU to impose severe limits on local LLM inference. Those limits are real. But the performance available within them turned out to be more useful than I initially expected. With carefully chosen configurations, I measured: Gemma 4 E2B ~59 tok/s GPU auto, FP16 KV Qwen3.5-4B ~35 tok/s GPU all, FP16 KV Qwen3-4B ~42 tok/s GPU all, FP16 KV Qwen3-4B (memory-balanced) ~40 tok/s GPU all, Q8 KV 260 MiB less GPU memory than FP16 The biggest performance improvement came from requesting more GPU layer offloading for models that could benefit from it. KV cache quantization offered a second optimization opportunity: recovering GPU memory with a relatively small reduction in throughput. And disabling unnecessary reasoning helped keep interactive conversations focused on direct answers. None of these adjustments required purchasing additional hardware. The broader takeaway is straightforward: Before buying a faster GPU, measure whether your inference engine is making effective use of the one you already own. On hardware with only 4GB of VRAM, the right settings can make the difference between a sluggish local model and a genuinely usable one. Technical references llama.cpp — GitHub repository llama.cpp server documentation llama.cpp CLI documentation Experimental setup: NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650 Ti Laptop GPU (4GB), Intel Core i5–10300H, Windows 10, llama.cpp build b8729, October 2026. Performance measurements are rounded medians from the two experimental phases. How I Made Local LLMs Up to 2.24× Faster on a 4GB NVIDIA GPU was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
items.summary_html:
What two rounds of llama.cpp benchmarking taught me about GPU offloading, KV cache optimization, and running Gemma 4, Qwen3, and Qwen3.5 on a GTX 1650 Ti.Your GPU might be more capable than you think.

When people talk about running large language models locally, the conversation usually starts with expensive hardware: RTX 4090s, 24GB of VRAM, or dedicated AI workstations.

I wanted to answer a different question:

How much performance can we extract from a laptop GPU with only 4GB of VRAM?

My test machine uses an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650 Ti, a GPU released years before the current generative AI boom. With just 4GB of GDDR6 memory, it is hardly the first card anyone would recommend for running modern language models.

Yet after two rounds of systematic benchmarking with llama.cpp, the results were surprisingly encouraging.

By tuning GPU layer placement, CPU threads, microbatch sizes, and KV cache precision, I measured:

  • 2.24× faster token generation for Qwen3.5–4B.
  • 2.07× faster token generation for Qwen3–4B.
  • Approximately 59 tokens per second from Gemma 4 E2B.
  • A 260 MiB reduction in GPU memory usage for Qwen3 with Q8 KV cache, at approximately a 4% throughput penalty.
  • Successful completion of every measured longer-response request in the validation experiment.

No hardware upgrades. No retraining. No modifications to CUDA kernels.

Just better configuration.

The most important discovery was that the automatic GPU configuration was not always the fastest, even when llama.cpp was already running with CUDA acceleration.

Here is how I tested it, what worked, and how to reproduce these

I tested three approximately four-bit-quantized language models:

Tested models

Gemma 4 E2B IT
  Quantization: Q4_K_M
  GGUF size:    3.22 GiB

Qwen3.5-4B
  Quantization: Q4_K_M
  GGUF size:    2.55 GiB

Qwen3-4B
  Quantization: Q4_K_M
  GGUF size:    2.33 GiB

The results refer specifically to quantized GGUF inference, not full-precision inference.

An important lesson appeared early: a model’s file size does not tell us exactly how much GPU memory inference will require.

Some tensors can remain in CPU-accessible memory, while others are placed on the GPU. Different model architectures can therefore behave quite differently on the same hardware.

That became especially relevant when comparing Gemma 4 with the Qwen models.

2. Why GPU offloading matters so much

llama.cpp allows us to control how many model layers are assigned to the GPU using the --gpu-layers option.

The configurations I tested included:

--gpu-layers auto
--gpu-layers 12
--gpu-layers 24
--gpu-layers all

Automatic selection is a sensible starting point on memory-constrained hardware.

But it is not necessarily the configuration with the highest throughput.

Initially, I used auto for every model. All three models could generate responses, but the Qwen models were performing well below what the GPU could actually deliver.

When I switched to --gpu-layers all, Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 became dramatically faster.

Gemma 4, however, saw almost no improvement.

This gave us the central finding of the study:

GPU offloading should be tuned for each model rather than treated as one universal setting.

3. The benchmark methodology

I designed two rounds of experiments rather than relying on a few manually timed prompts.

The benchmark was automated with PowerShell scripts that launched llama-server, waited for readiness, issued API requests, collected timing information, recorded GPU memory usage, and saved results to CSV files.

Phase one: searching the parameter space

The first experiment tested four GPU offloading strategies, two CPU thread counts, and two microbatch sizes.

GPU layers:   auto, 12, 24, all
CPU threads:  4, 6
Microbatch:   128, 256
4 × 2 × 2 = 16 configs/model
3 models × 16 = 48 configurations

The test ran under a two-hour time budget, with up to three repetitions of each configuration.

We used five types of prompts: factual questions, humor, Serbian-to-English translation, English-to-Serbian translation, and prompt improvement.

The core inference settings remained consistent:

Context size:         4096
Batch size:           512
Concurrent servers:   1
Warm-up:              enabled
Temperature:          0
GPU monitoring:       enabled

For each request, the script captured generation throughput, total latency, completion status, GPU memory usage, and related performance information.

One methodological issue became apparent: the first benchmark limited output to 192 tokens, causing some longer responses to end before they were complete.

Those samples still provided generation-speed observations, but they could not be treated as completed user tasks.

Token generation throughput and task-completion time are different measurements.

Phase two: validating the strongest configurations

After identifying promising GPU/CPU parameters, I ran a second experiment focused on longer technical responses and KV cache optimization.

The second phase evaluated ten model configurations in two rounds, comparing FP16, Q8_0, and Q4_0 cache formats where appropriate.

Each configuration used one warm-up request and two measured requests.

The output limit increased to 512 tokens.

All 40 measured responses completed normally, with finish_reason=stop.

This strengthened our confidence that the shortlisted configurations could handle more realistic requests without immediately exhausting the generation limit.

4. The biggest result: Qwen became more than twice as fast

The most dramatic improvement came from GPU layer placement.

For an apples-to-apples comparison, I used results with the same CPU thread count and microbatch size, changing only GPU offloading between auto and all.

GPU offloading comparison

Qwen3.5-4B
  GPU auto:    15.63 tok/s
  GPU all:     34.96 tok/s
  Speedup:      2.24×
Qwen3-4B
  GPU auto:    20.46 tok/s
  GPU all:     42.41 tok/s
  Speedup:      2.07×
Gemma 4 E2B
  GPU auto:    59.99 tok/s
  GPU all:     59.78 tok/s
  Speedup:     ~1.00×

For Qwen3.5, that represents approximately 124% more generation throughput.

For Qwen3, approximately 107% more.

These are substantial gains from configuration changes alone.

The improvement did come with a GPU memory tradeoff.

GPU memory use

Auto       All
Qwen3.5-4B      2231 MiB   3089 MiB
Qwen3-4B        2281 MiB   3163 MiB

In other words, the fastest configurations used more of the available GPU memory.

That is not necessarily a disadvantage when the GPU is dedicated to inference.

Unused VRAM does not provide a performance benefit by itself. The question is whether using more VRAM reduces expensive CPU/GPU transfers and improves actual inference execution.

In these measurements, it clearly did.

But there is a limit. On a 4GB card, reserving enough GPU memory for runtime allocations, the operating system, and other applications remains important.

5. Why Gemma 4 behaved differently

Gemma 4 E2B consistently achieved close to 60 generated tokens per second.

Interestingly, changing its GPU setting from auto to all produced almost no difference.

The runtime reported 36 of 36 relevant layers as offloaded, while still retaining substantial tensor data in CPU-mapped memory.

Observed model buffers

Gemma 4 E2B
GPU model buffer:   ~1450 MiB
CPU-mapped buffer:  ~2153 MiB
GPU layers:         36 / 36

This does not mean that the entire model occupies only 1450 MiB. It means the runtime divides its tensors between different memory locations.

In a separate exploratory test, I forced additional Gemma tensors onto the GPU.

The GPU model buffer increased to roughly 3602 MiB, leaving very little VRAM headroom.

That did not improve practical responsiveness.

The lesson was clear:

More GPU-resident tensors do not guarantee faster inference if the resulting memory pressure harms execution.

I also compared microbatch values of 256 and 128.

Gemma 4 microbatch comparison

ub=256     ub=128
Speed           58.99      59.31 tok/s
Latency          7.05       7.00 sec
GPU memory       1813       1685 MiB
Completed        4/4        4/4

The smaller microbatch saved approximately 128 MiB with effectively unchanged performance.

Therefore, I selected -ub 128 for Gemma.

One useful implication is that microbatch size should not simply be maximized because more GPU memory is available. On a single-user workload, a smaller value may be equally fast while providing more memory headroom.

6. KV cache quantization: an unexpected memory optimization

Once the strongest GPU offload configurations were identified, I wanted to reduce VRAM usage without losing too much throughput.

That led to the second major part of the study: KV cache quantization.

Autoregressive transformer inference stores information from earlier tokens in a key-value cache.

As context length grows, this cache can use substantial memory.

llama.cpp allows the cache formats to be configured with:

--cache-type-k
--cache-type-v

The experiment compared FP16, Q8_0, and Q4_0.

Qwen3.5: quantization saves comparatively little

The Qwen3.5 results were:

Qwen3.5-4B
KV cache   Speed       GPU memory
---------------------------------
FP16       34.58 tok/s   3090 MiB
Q8_0       34.21 tok/s   3041 MiB
Q4_0       34.14 tok/s   3009 MiB

Q4_0 reduced observed GPU memory use by approximately 81 MiB, while generation speed decreased by about 1.3%.

This is a reasonable tradeoff, but not an especially compelling one for this configuration.

The server logs also showed that Qwen3.5 uses additional recurrent state, alongside its KV cache.

My conclusion was to retain FP16 for Qwen3.5, unless a particular application requires additional VRAM headroom.

Qwen3: hundreds of megabytes saved

Qwen3 showed a much larger benefit.

Qwen3-4B
KV cache   Speed       GPU memory
---------------------------------
FP16       41.59 tok/s   3163 MiB
Q8_0       39.92 tok/s   2903 MiB
Q4_0       39.80 tok/s   2759 MiB

The tradeoffs were striking.

Q8_0 saved 260 MiB, with a generation-speed reduction of approximately 4%.

Q4_0 saved 404 MiB, with a roughly 4.3% reduction.

On a GPU with only 4GB of VRAM, hundreds of megabytes are meaningful.

Q8_0 became my preferred balance: nearly all the measured performance of FP16, but with substantially more free GPU memory.

There is a caveat: this experiment measured timing, memory, and successful completion. It did not formally evaluate whether KV quantization changed semantic accuracy or reasoning quality.

That would require a separate task-quality benchmark.

7. Thinking versus non-thinking models: another source of latency

While benchmarking, I encountered a practical issue familiar to anyone using reasoning-capable LLMs.

Some models can spend a large number of tokens on internal reasoning before producing visible output.

For complex mathematical reasoning or difficult planning tasks, this can be useful.

But for basic coding questions, translations, summaries, and direct explanations, the additional delay may be undesirable.

The tested llama.cpp build supports these options:

--reasoning off --reasoning-budget 0

I used them to configure the models for direct responses.

In practice, this made short interactive exchanges more usable and helped avoid cases where the output-token allowance was exhausted before the visible answer was complete.

However, there is an important distinction.

Disabling thinking does not necessarily make the GPU generate individual tokens faster. Instead, it can reduce the total number of generated tokens required before the user receives an answer.

The 2.24× and 2.07× GPU-offloading gains reported earlier should not be attributed to reasoning settings.

I also would not recommend disabling reasoning for every possible task. For problems where deliberate multi-step reasoning matters, a reasoning-enabled configuration may be the better choice.

The best setting depends on the purpose of the model.

8. The optimized settings I ultimately selected

Combining the results of both experiments, I selected the following practical configurations.

Recommended llama.cpp profiles

GEMMA 4 E2B
  GPU layers:   auto
  CPU threads:  4
  Context:      4096
  Batch:        512
  Microbatch:   128
  KV cache:     f16 / f16
  Reasoning:    off
QWEN3.5-4B
  GPU layers:   all
  CPU threads:  6
  Context:      4096
  Batch:        512
  Microbatch:   256
  KV cache:     f16 / f16
  Reasoning:    off
QWEN3-4B
  GPU layers:   all
  CPU threads:  6
  Context:      4096
  Batch:        512
  Microbatch:   256
  KV cache:     q8_0 / q8_0
  Reasoning:    off

These should be viewed as tested profiles for my hardware, not universal defaults.

Different GPUs, driver versions, model quantizations, context sizes, and concurrency settings can produce different outcomes.

9. Practical guide: running these models with llama.cpp

Here is how to reproduce the configuration on Windows.

I used the following directory structure:

C:\llama.cpp\
  bin\
    llama-cli.exe
    llama-server.exe
  models\
    google_gemma-4-E2B-it-Q4_K_M.gguf
    Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf
    Qwen3-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf

The executable names and directory layout may differ depending on how you install llama.cpp.

Step 1: check CUDA and driver compatibility

First, open PowerShell and verify that Windows detects the NVIDIA GPU:

nvidia-smi

Then check your llama.cpp installation:

cd C:\llama.cpp
.\bin\llama-cli.exe --help

Review the available flags before copying any configuration.

One practical challenge I encountered was CUDA toolchain compatibility. A newer prebuilt llama.cpp binary failed with an unsupported PTX toolchain error on my machine, while build b8729 worked correctly.

The important point is not that everyone should use b8729. It is that a binary and its packaged CUDA components must be compatible with the installed NVIDIA driver.

Step 2: run Gemma 4 in CLI mode
.\bin\llama-cli.exe `
  -m ".\models\google_gemma-4-E2B-it-Q4_K_M.gguf" `
  --gpu-layers auto `
  -t 4 `
  -c 4096 `
  -b 512 `
  -ub 128 `
  --cache-type-k f16 `
  --cache-type-v f16 `
  --reasoning off `
  --reasoning-budget 0

This profile produced approximately 59 tokens per second in the validation experiment.

Step 3: run Qwen3.5 in CLI mode
.\bin\llama-cli.exe `
  -m ".\models\Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf" `
  --gpu-layers all `
  -t 6 `
  -c 4096 `
  -b 512 `
  -ub 256 `
  --cache-type-k f16 `
  --cache-type-v f16 `
  --reasoning off `
  --reasoning-budget 0

With maximum GPU layer offloading requested, Qwen3.5 achieved about 34.6 generated tokens per second in the longer-response validation experiment.

Step 4: run Qwen3 with Q8 KV cache
.\bin\llama-cli.exe `
  -m ".\models\Qwen3-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf" `
  --gpu-layers all `
  -t 6 `
  -c 4096 `
  -b 512 `
  -ub 256 `
  --cache-type-k q8_0 `
  --cache-type-v q8_0 `
  --reasoning off `
  --reasoning-budget 0

This configuration achieved approximately 39.9 generated tokens per second while using roughly 2,903 MiB of GPU memory.

For the highest measured Qwen3 throughput, FP16 KV cache remains an alternative, at the cost of more VRAM.

10. Running an OpenAI-compatible local inference server

For terminal interactions, llama-cli is convenient.

But if you want to integrate local inference with your own software, llama-server offers an OpenAI-compatible API.

For example, here is the optimized Qwen3 server configuration:

.\bin\llama-server.exe `
  -m ".\models\Qwen3-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf" `
  --host 127.0.0.1 `
  --port 8080 `
  --gpu-layers all `
  -t 6 `
  -c 4096 `
  -b 512 `
  -ub 256 `
  --cache-type-k q8_0 `
  --cache-type-v q8_0 `
  --reasoning off `
  --reasoning-budget 0 `
  --no-webui

Once started, the API base URL is:

http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1

To check that the server is responding:

Invoke-RestMethod `
  http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/models

To send a chat completion request:

$body = @{
    model = "Qwen3-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf"
    messages = @(
        @{
            role = "user"
            content = "Explain AES-256 simply."
        }
    )
    temperature = 0
    max_tokens = 256
} | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 5
$result = Invoke-RestMethod `
    -Uri "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions" `
    -Method Post `
    -ContentType "application/json" `
    -Body $body
$result.choices[0].message.content

If your server reports a different model identifier from /v1/models, use that identifier instead.

To use the built-in browser interface, omit --no-webui on builds that include the web interface.

This example binds the server to 127.0.0.1, restricting access to the local machine. Do not expose an unauthenticated inference server directly to the internet.

11. How to benchmark your own low-VRAM GPU

If you have a GTX 1650, GTX 1660, RTX 3050 4GB, or another memory-constrained NVIDIA GPU, I would recommend the following approach.

Start with a correctness baseline. Verify that the model loads, completes prompts, and produces sensible answers before measuring performance.

Test GPU offloading independently. Compare automatic layer selection with explicitly requested layer counts. Do not assume maximum offloading is always fastest or always feasible.

Tune CPU threads and microbatch size. Higher numbers may increase memory pressure without improving single-user token generation.

Inspect memory allocation. Separate model weights, KV cache, compute buffers, and other runtime allocations wherever logs permit.

Evaluate cache quantization. Especially on smaller GPUs, the savings from Q8_0 or Q4_0 can be worth considering.

Measure complete answers. Report token generation speed and total response latency separately. A truncated response should not be counted as a fully completed task.

Repeat measurements. A configuration should be selected based on reproducible observations, not one unusually fast run.

Most importantly, record the exact model file, quantization, inference engine version, driver, and GPU for every benchmark.

Without that context, performance comparisons become difficult to reproduce.

12. What the experiment does not prove

There are limits to what can be concluded from this study.

All measurements came from one Windows 10 laptop with an NVIDIA GTX 1650 Ti and a single llama.cpp build. Other GPUs and software versions may behave differently.

The three tested models also have different architectures. A higher tokens-per-second figure does not establish superior model quality.

The experiment focused on one inference request at a time, not concurrent multi-user serving.

The validation workload contained two technical prompt types and four measured responses per configuration, providing useful repeatability checks but not a large-scale statistical characterization.

And although the quantized KV configurations completed requests successfully, we did not formally benchmark answer quality under different cache precisions.

Finally, disabling thinking may improve responsiveness for simple tasks while weakening performance on difficult reasoning problems.

These results should therefore be interpreted as measurements of local inference performance, not general model-quality rankings.

13. Conclusion: optimize before you upgrade

Before running these experiments, I expected a 4GB laptop GPU to impose severe limits on local LLM inference.

Those limits are real. But the performance available within them turned out to be more useful than I initially expected.

With carefully chosen configurations, I measured:

Gemma 4 E2B
  ~59 tok/s
  GPU auto, FP16 KV
Qwen3.5-4B
  ~35 tok/s
  GPU all, FP16 KV
Qwen3-4B
  ~42 tok/s
  GPU all, FP16 KV
Qwen3-4B (memory-balanced)
  ~40 tok/s
  GPU all, Q8 KV
  260 MiB less GPU memory than FP16

The biggest performance improvement came from requesting more GPU layer offloading for models that could benefit from it.

KV cache quantization offered a second optimization opportunity: recovering GPU memory with a relatively small reduction in throughput.

And disabling unnecessary reasoning helped keep interactive conversations focused on direct answers.

None of these adjustments required purchasing additional hardware.

The broader takeaway is straightforward:

Before buying a faster GPU, measure whether your inference engine is making effective use of the one you already own.

On hardware with only 4GB of VRAM, the right settings can make the difference between a sluggish local model and a genuinely usable one.

Technical references
  • llama.cpp — GitHub repository
  • llama.cpp server documentation
  • llama.cpp CLI documentation

Experimental setup: NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650 Ti Laptop GPU (4GB), Intel Core i5–10300H, Windows 10, llama.cpp build b8729, October 2026. Performance measurements are rounded medians from the two experimental phases.

items.title: Hollywood AI-listers: is the technology ready to rival flesh-and-blood film stars?
items.summary: As a freaky Val Kilmer doppelganger stars in a new western and faux starlet Tilly Norwood is set for her feature debut, experts are split on whether mainstream adoption is a long way down the line – or just around the corner ‘Don’t fear the dead – and don’t fear me.” An exact facsimile of a young Val Kilmer, not quite dead and not quite alive, utters that baiting line in the trailer for the new western As Deep as the Grave. Director Coerte Voorhees knows exactly what he is doing – this is an AI-created version of the late actor, approved by his family but bringing with it a heap of controversy about whether such technology could make flesh-and-blood thespians redundant. Not just yet, judging by the extended glimpse of the film released earlier this year : it looks like a thirtysomething Kilmer, if a robot version had been sent back to the 1920s American wilderness by Skynet and, as well as being strangely rigid, had forgotten to download his voice, let alone his signature air of spacey shrewdness. Kilmer’s estate signed off on it, citing his enthusiasm for new technology that expands storytelling, but surely he would have been dismayed by this freaky doppelganger.

‘Don’t fear the dead – and don’t fear me.” An exact facsimile of a young Val Kilmer, not quite dead and not quite alive, utters that baiting line in the trailer for the new western As Deep as the Grave. Director Coerte Voorhees knows exactly what he is doing – this is an AI-created version of the late actor, approved by his family but bringing with it a heap of controversy about whether such technology could make flesh-and-blood thespians redundant.

Not just yet, judging by the extended glimpse of the film released earlier this year: it looks like a thirtysomething Kilmer, if a robot version had been sent back to the 1920s American wilderness by Skynet and, as well as being strangely rigid, had forgotten to download his voice, let alone his signature air of spacey shrewdness. Kilmer’s estate signed off on it, citing his enthusiasm for new technology that expands storytelling, but surely he would have been dismayed by this freaky doppelganger.

items.title: Japan launches mission to bring home a piece of the Martian moon Phobos
items.summary: Japan launched a $578 million mission Monday on a five-year expedition to land on the largest moon of Mars and retrieve samples for return to Earth, a daring international project that could yield new insights into the formation of the Solar System. The robotic Martian Moons eXploration mission, known as MMX, lifted off at 3:41 pm EDT Monday (4:41 am Japan Standard Time Tuesday) from Tanegashima Space Center in southern Japan. The MMX spacecraft rode into orbit atop a 207-foot-tall (63-meter) H3 rocket, Japan's flagship launch vehicle. The rocket assigned to MMX debuted a new souped-up configuration with four strap-on solid rocket boosters, full-throttle main engines, and an extended payload shroud to accommodate the demands of Japan's heaviest and most ambitious interplanetary mission to date. Read full article Comments

items.title: SlothPlan: the to-do list that does less
items.summary: SlothPlan: the to-do list that does less My entry for the Hacktoberfest Week 3 "Slow and Steady" challenge — built for International Sloth Day, with open-weight models, zero API costs, and a philosophy I'd actually live by. The problem My to-do list has 47 items. Yours probably does too. And here's the dirty secret of productivity culture: the list isn't the work. Triaging the list is the work — the staring, the re-ordering, the guilt-math of "is learning Spanish more important than calling the dentist?" I have spent entire Sunday mornings reorganizing tasks instead of doing them, which is just procrastination wearing a planner's clothes. Every to-do app on the planet answers this with more features: priorities, tags, Eisenhower matrices, AI scheduling assistants that need your calendar, your email, your soul, and a $12/month subscription. They make the triage heavier . Nobody built the app that does the triage for you and then — this is the important part — tells you to do less. So for "Slow and Steady" I built exactly that: a tool that rewards laziness by doing the one piece of work you were avoiding (deciding what matters), capping your day at three things, and granting you written permission to delete the rest. What I built SlothPlan — a command-line tool where you dump a messy to-do list and get back three buckets: DO TODAY (max 3, non-negotiable), DEFER (officially not today's problem), and DELETE (permission granted, let it go). Each item gets a one-line reason. The judgment comes from a local open-weight model; the guarantees come from deterministic code. python3 -m slothplan triage -f my-messy-todos.txt The twist, same as my Week 2 entry: the model, the inference engine, and all the code run on your own machine. No account. No API key. No subscription. Your to-do list — which is, let's be honest, a map of your anxieties — never touches a network. The demo (real transcript, unedited) I fed it a 12-item Tuesday dump. Here is what the recorded run produced (full transcript in the repo's demo-output.txt — nothing cherry-picked): === SLOTHPLAN triage === method: rule-based fallback (--no-llm was passed; no model was run) DO TODAY (max 3) — your only decisions today: 1. Pay electricity bill, due Friday or they cut the power -> looks time-sensitive — it names a deadline, payment, or an urgent event 2. Reply to Priya about the wedding RSVP — deadline is tomorrow -> looks time-sensitive — it names a deadline, payment, or an urgent event 3. Submit the Hacktoberfest Week 3 entry README tonight -> looks time-sensitive — it names a deadline, payment, or an urgent event DEFER — officially not today's problem: 4. Call dentist to reschedule the appointment -> looks time-sensitive ... [moved from today: the 3-item cap keeps your day lazy] 12. Call mom back — she called twice today -> looks time-sensitive ... [moved from today: the 3-item cap keeps your day lazy] DELETE — permission granted, let it go: 10. Delete that crypto spam email from "DOUBLE YOUR COINS" -> matches a junk pattern — nothing of value is lost 11. Reorganize my Netflix watchlist -> matches a junk pattern — nothing of value is lost That's the deterministic mode ( --no-llm ), and it's the mode I'd actually use daily: three real obligations surfaced, the dentist and mom politely bounced by the cap with an explanation, and the crypto spam and the Netflix-watchlist reorganization sentenced to death. Twelve decisions I didn't have to make. Now the confession, because the transcript has two runs and I'm not hiding the first one: when I let the 0.5B model judge all 12 items itself, it took "rewards laziness" as a personal mission. It deleted the electricity bill . It called buying milk "spam". It deleted calling my mother. Every verdict parsed cleanly — 12/12, zero fallbacks — but its judgment was a sloth with an agenda. The transcript shows it exactly as it happened, which is the point of the architecture below: the model's opinions are suggestions; the deterministic layer holds the guarantees. How it works Deliberately boring architecture, because boring ships: Parsing (stdlib only): every non-empty line is a task; # comments and bullet/checkbox markers are stripped. My sample file's header comment got triaged as a task in the first build — fixed, and there's a test for it now. Judgment ( slothplan/llm.py ): one verdict per task from Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (Apache 2.0 open weights, Q4_K_M quantized) through the llama.cpp binary (MIT). Greedy decoding, ~3 seconds per item on two CPU cores. The model emits a single bucket word plus a short reason — a shape small enough for a 0.5B model to hold. This was a discovery , not the plan: my first prototype asked for one big JSON object covering all tasks, and the model hallucinated item numbers 13–20 for a 12-item list and stuffed 12 entries into a 3-item bucket. So the model judges one task at a time, and structure is enforced by code. Enforcement ( slothplan/triage.py ): every verdict is parsed and validated. Max 3 in "today" — overflow is moved to defer with the reason printed , so the cap is visible, not silent. Unparseable verdicts fall back to keyword rules and are labeled as fallback in the output . Nothing fails silently, ever. Zero third-party Python dependencies. Python 3.8, two downloaded files, and it runs. 29 unit tests, all passing. Why open innovation matters This tool cannot exist on a closed API, for two reasons — one practical, one philosophical. Practically: SlothPlan's entire design is a bet that a small model is enough. A 0.5B model is honest about what it is — opinionated, sometimes wrong, occasionally deleting your electricity bill — and the whole architecture (deterministic guardrails, labeled fallbacks, a --no-llm mode) is built around that honesty. You can only build that way if you can run the model locally, iterate on prompts for free at 3 a.m., and ship something whose marginal cost per triage is exactly zero. A closed API charges per token, which means every design decision bends toward fewer, bigger calls — the opposite of this architecture. And a to-do list is personal enough that "send it to someone's cloud" was never on the table. Philosophically: the open-weights ecosystem is what lets a student with a $0 budget and a borrowed VM build something in a day that would have been a research project five years ago. Qwen2.5's weights are public under Apache 2.0. llama.cpp is MIT. My code is MIT. Anyone can audit every layer, swap in a bigger GGUF with one flag, or fork the whole thing. That composability — weights, engine, and app all inspectable and replaceable — is open innovation working exactly as advertised. The moat isn't the model; it's the trust that comes from everything being auditable. Honest limitations I'd rather tell you than have you discover them: The bundled model is 0.5 billion parameters — tiny on purpose, so it runs on any laptop CPU. Its verdicts are opinions , and sometimes bad ones (see: the electricity bill incident). Any GGUF drops in via --model ; a bigger model would judge better. Reasons are sometimes missing ( (no reason given) ) — the model often emits just the bucket word despite being shown examples. The rule-based fallback is keyword heuristics, not understanding. It won't catch "renew the thingy before the thing expires." Prototype built in a day for a challenge, not a hardened product. 24 items max per run, .txt input, CLI only. Bonus-points honesty: I have no first user yet — this was built for the challenge this week, starting Monday morning. The demo above is real output from the actual tool, and the limitations section is real too. Try it Repo: https://github.com/swarnnim/slothplan ./scripts/download-llamacpp.sh ./scripts/download-model.sh python3 -m slothplan triage -f sample_todos/messy.txt If you also have a 47-item list you're avoiding: what's the one task on it you'd secretly love an app to delete for you? items.summary_html:
SlothPlan: the to-do list that does less

My entry for the Hacktoberfest Week 3 "Slow and Steady" challenge — built for International Sloth Day, with open-weight models, zero API costs, and a philosophy I'd actually live by.

The problem

My to-do list has 47 items. Yours probably does too. And here's the dirty secret of productivity culture: the list isn't the work. Triaging the list is the work — the staring, the re-ordering, the guilt-math of "is learning Spanish more important than calling the dentist?" I have spent entire Sunday mornings reorganizing tasks instead of doing them, which is just procrastination wearing a planner's clothes.

Every to-do app on the planet answers this with more features: priorities, tags, Eisenhower matrices, AI scheduling assistants that need your calendar, your email, your soul, and a $12/month subscription. They make the triage heavier. Nobody built the app that does the triage for you and then — this is the important part — tells you to do less.

So for "Slow and Steady" I built exactly that: a tool that rewards laziness by doing the one piece of work you were avoiding (deciding what matters), capping your day at three things, and granting you written permission to delete the rest.

What I built

SlothPlan — a command-line tool where you dump a messy to-do list and get back three buckets: DO TODAY (max 3, non-negotiable), DEFER (officially not today's problem), and DELETE (permission granted, let it go). Each item gets a one-line reason. The judgment comes from a local open-weight model; the guarantees come from deterministic code.

python3 -m slothplan triage -f my-messy-todos.txt

The twist, same as my Week 2 entry: the model, the inference engine, and all the code run on your own machine. No account. No API key. No subscription. Your to-do list — which is, let's be honest, a map of your anxieties — never touches a network.

The demo (real transcript, unedited)

I fed it a 12-item Tuesday dump. Here is what the recorded run produced (full transcript in the repo's demo-output.txt — nothing cherry-picked):

=== SLOTHPLAN triage ===
method: rule-based fallback (--no-llm was passed; no model was run)

DO TODAY (max 3) — your only decisions today:
  1. Pay electricity bill, due Friday or they cut the power
     -> looks time-sensitive — it names a deadline, payment, or an urgent event
  2. Reply to Priya about the wedding RSVP — deadline is tomorrow
     -> looks time-sensitive — it names a deadline, payment, or an urgent event
  3. Submit the Hacktoberfest Week 3 entry README tonight
     -> looks time-sensitive — it names a deadline, payment, or an urgent event

DEFER — officially not today's problem:
  4. Call dentist to reschedule the appointment
     -> looks time-sensitive ... [moved from today: the 3-item cap keeps your day lazy]
  12. Call mom back — she called twice today
     -> looks time-sensitive ... [moved from today: the 3-item cap keeps your day lazy]

DELETE — permission granted, let it go:
  10. Delete that crypto spam email from "DOUBLE YOUR COINS"
     -> matches a junk pattern — nothing of value is lost
  11. Reorganize my Netflix watchlist
     -> matches a junk pattern — nothing of value is lost

That's the deterministic mode (--no-llm), and it's the mode I'd actually use daily: three real obligations surfaced, the dentist and mom politely bounced by the cap with an explanation, and the crypto spam and the Netflix-watchlist reorganization sentenced to death. Twelve decisions I didn't have to make.

Now the confession, because the transcript has two runs and I'm not hiding the first one: when I let the 0.5B model judge all 12 items itself, it took "rewards laziness" as a personal mission. It deleted the electricity bill. It called buying milk "spam". It deleted calling my mother. Every verdict parsed cleanly — 12/12, zero fallbacks — but its judgment was a sloth with an agenda. The transcript shows it exactly as it happened, which is the point of the architecture below: the model's opinions are suggestions; the deterministic layer holds the guarantees.

How it works

Deliberately boring architecture, because boring ships:

  • Parsing (stdlib only): every non-empty line is a task; # comments and bullet/checkbox markers are stripped. My sample file's header comment got triaged as a task in the first build — fixed, and there's a test for it now.
  • Judgment (slothplan/llm.py): one verdict per task from Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct (Apache 2.0 open weights, Q4_K_M quantized) through the llama.cpp binary (MIT). Greedy decoding, ~3 seconds per item on two CPU cores. The model emits a single bucket word plus a short reason — a shape small enough for a 0.5B model to hold. This was a discovery, not the plan: my first prototype asked for one big JSON object covering all tasks, and the model hallucinated item numbers 13–20 for a 12-item list and stuffed 12 entries into a 3-item bucket. So the model judges one task at a time, and structure is enforced by code.
  • Enforcement (slothplan/triage.py): every verdict is parsed and validated. Max 3 in "today" — overflow is moved to defer with the reason printed, so the cap is visible, not silent. Unparseable verdicts fall back to keyword rules and are labeled as fallback in the output. Nothing fails silently, ever.
  • Zero third-party Python dependencies. Python 3.8, two downloaded files, and it runs. 29 unit tests, all passing.
Why open innovation matters

This tool cannot exist on a closed API, for two reasons — one practical, one philosophical.

Practically: SlothPlan's entire design is a bet that a small model is enough. A 0.5B model is honest about what it is — opinionated, sometimes wrong, occasionally deleting your electricity bill — and the whole architecture (deterministic guardrails, labeled fallbacks, a --no-llm mode) is built around that honesty. You can only build that way if you can run the model locally, iterate on prompts for free at 3 a.m., and ship something whose marginal cost per triage is exactly zero. A closed API charges per token, which means every design decision bends toward fewer, bigger calls — the opposite of this architecture. And a to-do list is personal enough that "send it to someone's cloud" was never on the table.

Philosophically: the open-weights ecosystem is what lets a student with a $0 budget and a borrowed VM build something in a day that would have been a research project five years ago. Qwen2.5's weights are public under Apache 2.0. llama.cpp is MIT. My code is MIT. Anyone can audit every layer, swap in a bigger GGUF with one flag, or fork the whole thing. That composability — weights, engine, and app all inspectable and replaceable — is open innovation working exactly as advertised. The moat isn't the model; it's the trust that comes from everything being auditable.

Honest limitations

I'd rather tell you than have you discover them:

  • The bundled model is 0.5 billion parameters — tiny on purpose, so it runs on any laptop CPU. Its verdicts are opinions, and sometimes bad ones (see: the electricity bill incident). Any GGUF drops in via --model; a bigger model would judge better.
  • Reasons are sometimes missing ((no reason given)) — the model often emits just the bucket word despite being shown examples.
  • The rule-based fallback is keyword heuristics, not understanding. It won't catch "renew the thingy before the thing expires."
  • Prototype built in a day for a challenge, not a hardened product. 24 items max per run, .txt input, CLI only.

Bonus-points honesty: I have no first user yet — this was built for the challenge this week, starting Monday morning. The demo above is real output from the actual tool, and the limitations section is real too.

Try it

Repo: https://github.com/swarnnim/slothplan

./scripts/download-llamacpp.sh
./scripts/download-model.sh
python3 -m slothplan triage -f sample_todos/messy.txt

If you also have a 47-item list you're avoiding: what's the one task on it you'd secretly love an app to delete for you? That's the roadmap — a bigger delete bucket.

items.title: Your Go Service Gets a Third Front Door: An MCP Adapter That Never Touches the Domain
items.summary: Book: Hexagonal Architecture in Go Also by me: Pocket Guides for Developers — the 8-book series My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub The ticket says: "Make refunds callable from the AI assistant." Your refund service already has two ways in. Support staff hit POST /orders/{id}/refund , and the on-call engineer runs shop refund A-100 --cents 4999 from a terminal. Now a coding agent or a chat client wants a third way in, and it speaks the Model Context Protocol . There are two ways this goes. In one, somebody adds jsonschema tags to the domain structs, threads an *mcp.CallToolRequest into the service layer "just for the metadata", and the refund rules now import an SDK. In the other, you write one new package next to the HTTP handler, and git diff --stat shows zero lines of production code changed under internal/domain and internal/app . This post builds the second one with the official MCP Go SDK , at v1.8.0 as I write this, down to a CI check that fails if the inner packages ever import it. The service you already have Here is the domain. It knows what a refund is and when one is allowed. It imports errors and nothing else. // internal/domain/order.go package domain import "errors" var ( ErrOrderNotFound = errors . New ( "order not found" ) ErrAlreadyRefunded = errors . New ( "order was already refunded" ) ErrInvalidAmount = errors . New ( "refund must be between 1 cent and the amount paid" ) ) type Order struct { ID string PaidCents int64 Refunded bool } func ( o * Order ) Refund ( cents int64 ) error { if o . Refunded { return ErrAlreadyRefunded } if cents < 1 || cents > o . PaidCents { return ErrInvalidAmount } o . Refunded = true return nil } The application layer owns two ports. Orders is the driven port, the storage the use case needs. Refunder is the driving port, the one every front door calls. // internal/app/refund.go package app import ( "context" "example.com/shop/internal/domain" ) // Orders is the driven port: storage the use case needs. type Orders interface { Get ( ctx context . Context , id string ) ( domain . Order , error ) Save ( ctx context . Context , o domain . Order ) error } // RefundOrder is the command every driving adapter builds. type RefundOrder struct { OrderID string Cents int64 } type Refunded struct { OrderID string Cents int64 } // Refunder is the driving port. HTTP, CLI and MCP call this. type Refunder interface { Refund ( ctx context . Context , c RefundOrder ) ( Refunded , error ) } The service is the only thing that implements it: // internal/app/refund.go (continued) type RefundService struct { Orders Orders } func ( s RefundService ) Refund ( ctx context . Context , c RefundOrder , ) ( Refunded , error ) { o , err := s . Orders . Get ( ctx , c . OrderID ) if err != nil { return Refunded {}, err } if err := o . Refund ( c . Cents ); err != nil { return Refunded {}, err } if err := s . Orders . Save ( ctx , o ); err != nil { return Refunded {}, err } return Refunded { OrderID : o . ID , Cents : c . Cents }, nil } The HTTP adapter decodes a JSON body, builds an app.RefundOrder , calls Refund , and translates domain errors into status codes. The translation is the only part worth showing, because the MCP adapter will need its own version of it: // internal/adapter/httpapi/status.go package httpapi import ( "errors" "net/http" "example.com/shop/internal/domain" ) func statusFor ( err error ) int { switch { case errors . Is ( err , domain . ErrOrderNotFound ) : return http . StatusNotFound case errors . Is ( err , domain . ErrAlreadyRefunded ) : return http . StatusConflict case errors . Is ( err , domain . ErrInvalidAmount ) : return http . StatusUnprocessableEntity } return http . StatusInternalServerError } The CLI adapter does the same thing with flags and exit codes. Two adapters, one port, and neither one is visible from internal/domain . The third adapter: an MCP tool handler An MCP server exposes tools. A client lists them, the model picks one, and the client sends tools/call with JSON arguments, as the tools section of the spec describes. In the Go SDK, mcp.AddTool registers a typed handler. The package docs say the input schema is inferred from the In type, descriptions come from jsonschema struct tags, and inputs are validated before your handler runs. Those struct tags are wire format, so they belong to the adapter. The domain Order has no json tags and it will not get jsonschema tags either. The adapter defines its own input and output types and copies fields across: // internal/adapter/mcpserver/server.go package mcpserver import ( "context" "github.com/modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk/mcp" "example.com/shop/internal/app" ) type refundIn struct { OrderID string `json:"order_id" jsonschema:"order to refund"` Cents int64 `json:"cents" jsonschema:"amount in cents"` } type refundOut struct { OrderID string `json:"order_id"` Cents int64 `json:"cents"` } type refundHandler = mcp . ToolHandlerFor [ refundIn , refundOut ] func New ( r app . Refunder ) * mcp . Server { s := mcp . NewServer ( & mcp . Implementation { Name : "shop" , Version : "v0.1.0" , }, nil ) mcp . AddTool ( s , & mcp . Tool { Name : "refund_order" , Description : "Refund a paid order once, " + "for at most the amount paid." , }, refund ( r )) return s } The handler is a translator and nothing more: // internal/adapter/mcpserver/server.go (continued) func refund ( r app . Refunder ) refundHandler { return func ( ctx context . Context , _ * mcp . CallToolRequest , in refundIn , ) ( * mcp . CallToolResult , refundOut , error ) { res , err := r . Refund ( ctx , app . RefundOrder { OrderID : in . OrderID , Cents : in . Cents , }) if err != nil { return nil , refundOut {}, toolError ( err ) } out := refundOut { OrderID : res . OrderID , Cents : res . Cents } return nil , out , nil } } Look at what New takes: app.Refunder , the same interface the HTTP handler takes. The handler ignores the *mcp.CallToolRequest . If you ever need something from it, such as the caller's client info, read it here and pass a plain value into the command. Do not pass the request type inward. Returning a nil result with a typed out is fine. In the SDK source , a nil result is replaced with an empty one, the output is marshaled into StructuredContent , and a JSON text copy goes into Content , which matches the spec's advice that structured results also ship as text for older clients. Domain errors become tool errors, not protocol errors The spec defines two kinds of failure . Protocol errors are JSON-RPC errors for unknown tools, malformed requests and server faults. Tool execution errors come back as a normal result with isError: true , and they cover business logic errors like "already refunded". The spec says clients SHOULD pass tool execution errors to the model so it can self-correct. That maps neatly onto the HTTP split between a 409 and a 500. "Order was already refunded" is information the model can act on: stop, or tell the user. A database timeout is not, and its text may contain a host name or a query you do not want in a model's context. The SDK does the plumbing. When a ToolHandlerFor returns an ordinary Go error, the CallToolResult docs say IsError is set and the error string goes into Content as text. Only a *jsonrpc.Error is sent as a protocol error, per the server code . So the adapter's job is to decide which error text the model is allowed to read: // internal/adapter/mcpserver/errors.go package mcpserver import ( "errors" "log" "example.com/shop/internal/domain" ) func toolError ( err error ) error { switch { case errors . Is ( err , domain . ErrOrderNotFound ), errors . Is ( err , domain . ErrAlreadyRefunded ), errors . Is ( err , domain . ErrInvalidAmount ) : return err } log . Printf ( "refund_order: %v" , err ) return errors . New ( "internal error" ) } The log.Printf is deliberate. Over stdio, the spec says the server MUST NOT write anything to stdout that is not a valid MCP message, and MAY log to stderr. Go's default logger writes to standard error , so it is safe. A stray fmt.Println in an adapter is not: it corrupts the message stream. The binary is a few lines of wiring. Here the in-memory store stands in for your real Postgres adapter: // cmd/shop-mcp/main.go package main import ( "context" "log" "github.com/modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk/mcp" "example.com/shop/internal/adapter/mcpserver" "example.com/shop/internal/adapter/memstore" "example.com/shop/internal/app" "example.com/shop/internal/domain" ) func main () { orders := memstore . New ( domain . Order { ID : "A-100" , PaidCents : 4999 }) svc := app . RefundService { Orders : orders } srv := mcpserver . New ( svc ) ctx := context . Background () if err := srv . Run ( ctx , & mcp . StdioTransport {}); err != nil { log . Fatal ( err ) } } To try it from Claude Code, build it and register it as a local stdio server with claude mcp add : go get github.com/modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk@v1.8.0 go build -o bin/shop-mcp ./cmd/shop-mcp claude mcp add --transport stdio shop -- " $PWD /bin/shop-mcp" Prove the domain stayed clean "We didn't touch the domain" is a claim. Make it a check. go list -deps walks a package and everything it imports, as the go command docs describe. Run it on the inner packages and grep for anything that should not be there: # from the module root; fails if go list fails or anything matches deps = $( go list -deps ./internal/domain ./internal/app ) && ! grep -E 'modelcontextprotocol|/adapter/' <<< " $deps " go.mod did change, because the module now requires the SDK. The domain's dependency list did not. That is the distinction this check enforces. A stricter version lives in the domain package as a test. go list -json reports a Standard field on every package, true for the standard library, so the test fails if the domain depends on anything outside the standard library except itself: // internal/domain/imports_test.go package domain_test import ( "bytes" "encoding/json" "os/exec" "testing" ) const self = "example.com/shop/internal/domain" func TestDomainImportsOnlyStdlib ( t * testing . T ) { cmd := exec . Command ( "go" , "list" , "-deps" , "-json" , "." ) out , err := cmd . Output () if err != nil { t . Fatal ( err ) } dec := json . NewDecoder ( bytes . NewReader ( out )) for dec . More () { var p struct { ImportPath string Standard bool } if err := dec . Decode ( & p ); err != nil { t . Fatal ( err ) } if ! p . Standard && p . ImportPath != self { t . Errorf ( "domain depends on %s" , p . ImportPath ) } } } The . works because go test runs each test binary from inside the package's source directory. And because the command has no -test flag, go list reports the package itself rather than its test binary, so the test's own imports ( os/exec , encoding/json ) are not part of what it checks. Test the use case through the fake, then the adapter in memory The fake is a driven adapter that keeps orders in a map. It implements app.Orders and returns the domain's not-found error: // internal/adapter/memstore/orders.go package memstore import ( "context" "sync" "example.com/shop/internal/domain" ) type Orders struct { mu sync . Mutex m map [ string ] domain . Order } func New ( seed ... domain . Order ) * Orders { s := & Orders { m : make ( map [ string ] domain . Order )} for _ , o := range seed { s . m [ o . ID ] = o } return s } func ( s * Orders ) Get ( _ context . Context , id string , ) ( domain . Order , error ) { s . mu . Lock () defer s . mu . Unlock () o , ok := s . m [ id ] if ! ok { return domain . Order {}, domain . ErrOrderNotFound } return o , nil } func ( s * Orders ) Save ( _ context . Context , o domain . Order ) error { s . mu . Lock () defer s . mu . Unlock () s . m [ o . ID ] = o return nil } The use case test runs steps in order against one order, because the second refund depends on the first: // internal/app/refund_test.go package app_test import ( "context" "errors" "testing" "example.com/shop/internal/adapter/memstore" "example.com/shop/internal/app" "example.com/shop/internal/domain" ) func TestRefund ( t * testing . T ) { ctx := context . Background () orders := memstore . New ( domain . Order { ID : "A-1" , PaidCents : 500 }) svc := app . RefundService { Orders : orders } steps := [] struct { id string cents int64 want error }{ { "missing" , 100 , domain . ErrOrderNotFound }, { "A-1" , 501 , domain . ErrInvalidAmount }, { "A-1" , 0 , domain . ErrInvalidAmount }, { "A-1" , 200 , nil }, { "A-1" , 100 , domain . ErrAlreadyRefunded }, } for _ , s := range steps { _ , err := svc . Refund ( ctx , app . RefundOrder { OrderID : s . id , Cents : s . cents , }) if ! errors . Is ( err , s . want ) { t . Errorf ( "Refund(%s, %d) = %v, want %v" , s . id , s . cents , err , s . want ) } } } No MCP anywhere in it. That test was true before the third door existed and it stays true after. The adapter gets its own test, over the SDK's in-memory transports so no process is spawned. The package examples connect the server to one end of NewInMemoryTransports and a client to the other. The assertion is the one that matters for agents: a missing order comes back as a tool result with IsError set, not as a protocol failure. // internal/adapter/mcpserver/server_test.go package mcpserver_test import ( "context" "testing" "github.com/modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk/mcp" "example.com/shop/internal/adapter/mcpserver" "example.com/shop/internal/adapter/memstore" "example.com/shop/internal/app" "example.com/shop/internal/domain" ) func TestUnknownOrderIsToolError ( t * testing . T ) { ctx := context . Background () svc := app . RefundService { Orders : memstore . New ()} st , ct := mcp . NewInMemoryTransports () _ , err := mcpserver . New ( svc ) . Connect ( ctx , st , nil ) if err != nil { t . Fatal ( err ) } c := mcp . NewClient ( & mcp . Implementation { Name : "test" , Version : "v0" , }, nil ) cs , err := c . Connect ( ctx , ct , nil ) if err != nil { t . Fatal ( err ) } defer cs . Close () res , err := cs . CallTool ( ctx , & mcp . CallToolParams { Name : "refund_order" , Arguments : map [ string ] any { "order_id" : "nope" , "cents" : 100 , }, }) if err != nil { t . Fatalf ( "got a protocol error: %v" , err ) } if ! res . IsError { t . Fatal ( "want IsError on the tool result" ) } text := res . Content [ 0 ] . ( * mcp . TextContent ) . Text if text != domain . ErrOrderNotFound . Error () { t . Fatalf ( "model would read %q" , text ) } } What the diff looks like Count the files. New: internal/adapter/mcpserver/server.go , errors.go , server_test.go , cmd/shop-mcp/main.go , and one test-only guard, internal/domain/imports_test.go . Changed: go.mod and go.sum .
